UK Bookkeeping, Accounting
& Taxation — Master Course

A 150-hour, ACCA/ACA-grade programme covering every UK compliance scenario from incorporation through cessation, with full FRS 102/105 disclosure reasoning, end-of-section MCQ assessments, and step-by-step software walkthroughs.
How to use this course

This is a single, self-contained reference text. Each Module follows the same pattern: (1) Learning objectives — what you will be able to do after the module; (2) Technical content with worked numerical examples, journal entries, legislation references and FRS citations; (3) Module summary; and (4) Knowledge-check MCQs with click-to-reveal feedback. Work top-to-bottom in order — later modules assume earlier knowledge.

The interactive quiz tracker (sidebar) updates as you complete sections. Your progress is stored only in the page memory for the session.

Tax-year currency

All numerical examples use 2024/25 rates as the primary teaching year, with 2025/26 uplifts noted where the change is material. Rates revise annually at the Spring & Autumn statements — always confirm current rates against gov.uk before applying to a live client.

Educational use

This course is a technical reference for trainee accountants and bookkeepers. It does not constitute regulated tax or legal advice for any specific person or business. Anyone advising clients commercially must be appropriately qualified and supervised by a recognised body (ICAEW, ACCA, AAT, CIMA, CIOT, ATT or equivalent), or be HMRC-supervised for AML.

Visual mockups are embedded throughout

This course interleaves visual mockups with the technical content. When a module covers a software workflow (Xero, QBO, Dext, BrightPay, TaxCalc), you'll find a faithful HTML mockup of the relevant screen alongside the explanation. When Part 5 covers year-end accounts, each balance sheet line has a working-paper visual showing how to evidence and tie back the figure.

Part One

Foundations

7 modules · ~20 hours · UK regulators, structures & bookkeeping fundamentals

Part 1 lays the rails. You will not understand any later module — VAT, Corporation Tax, FRS 102 disclosures, or cessation accounting — without first understanding who regulates UK businesses, what the four main business structures look like under the law, and how the double-entry bookkeeping system records every transaction. We start here.

Module 1 · Part 1 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

UK Compliance Landscape — Who Regulates What, and Why

It’s Tuesday. A new client signs your engagement letter — a one-shop café owner who wants to incorporate next quarter. You haven’t done a single piece of compliance work yet. Already in motion: HMRC will want a VAT registration and quarterly returns through MTD; an EPS submission on every payroll run; a CT600 within 12 months of incorporation. Companies House will demand a confirmation statement, abbreviated accounts, and a PSC register annually. The ICO needs the data-protection fee, paid before the till starts processing a single card. The Pensions Regulator watches the auto-enrolment duties from the day staff one is hired. Your professional body — ACCA, ICAEW, CIOT, AAT, ICB, IFA — supervises your AML compliance and your CPD. And OPBAS supervises them. Miss any one deadline and an automatic, daily-compounding penalty starts — no court order, no warning. Skip AML supervision entirely and that’s a criminal offence under MLR 2017, up to two years inside. This module is the seven-regulator map every UK accountant must hold in their head — not as trivia but as the operating system on which every client’s entire compliance year runs.

Learning Objectives

  • Name the seven UK regulators and supervisory bodies an accountant interacts with on a daily basis and describe each one's statutory remit.
  • Distinguish HMRC's role (tax collection, AML supervision of unsupervised agents) from Companies House's role (registry of companies, public record of accounts).
  • Explain the role of the Financial Reporting Council (FRC), its sub-bodies, and the standards it sets.
  • List the recognised professional bodies for accountants and bookkeepers and the AML supervision each performs.
  • Map a typical client engagement to the regulators that will receive filings.
  • Identify when an accountant becomes “in scope” for AML supervision and the consequences of operating without it.

1.1 Why “compliance” is the centre of gravity for UK accountants

The UK does not have a single Inland Revenue and Companies Office; it has a layered system of regulators, each with statutory powers, distinct deadlines, and distinct penalty regimes. As an accountant you do not simply “keep books” — you operate as the bridge between your client and these regulators. Failure to meet a deadline triggers automatic penalties, often on a daily basis, and serious failures can result in director disqualification, professional sanction, or criminal prosecution.

Compliance has three operational pillars:

  1. Record-keeping — capturing every business transaction in a form that satisfies HMRC's and (for companies) Companies Act record requirements.
  2. Reporting — transforming those records into the statutory returns and accounts each regulator requires, on the deadline they set.
  3. Paying — settling liabilities (Income Tax, Corporation Tax, VAT, NI, PAYE, etc.) by the legally specified date.

The technical work of bookkeeping (debits and credits) is in service of these three pillars. A trial balance is not an end in itself; it is the input to a CT600, an SA100 or a set of FRS 102 accounts. From day one of this course, every ledger entry should be evaluated by the question: “Where will this end up on the statutory return, and is it correctly classified for that purpose?”

1.2 HMRC — His Majesty's Revenue and Customs

HMRC is the UK's tax authority, formed in 2005 by the merger of Inland Revenue and HM Customs & Excise. It sits as a non-ministerial department of government, responsible to Parliament via the Treasury but not directly part of any minister's portfolio. This independence matters: Parliament sets the law (the Taxes Acts); HMRC administers it.

1.2.1 What HMRC actually does

Function Detail & legislative basis
Income Tax collection Income Tax (Earnings & Pensions) Act 2003 (ITEPA), Income Tax (Trading & Other Income) Act 2005 (ITTOIA), Income Tax Act 2007 (ITA). Collected via PAYE for employees, Self Assessment for the self-employed and complex cases.
Corporation Tax Corporation Tax Act 2009 (CTA 2009), Corporation Tax Act 2010 (CTA 2010). Filed on form CT600 within 12 months of period end.
VAT Value Added Tax Act 1994 (VATA 1994). Quarterly (sometimes monthly or annually) returns filed under MTD.
National Insurance Social Security Contributions & Benefits Act 1992; Classes 1, 1A, 1B, 2, 3 and 4 each with a different statutory basis.
Capital Gains Tax Taxation of Chargeable Gains Act 1992 (TCGA 1992). UK residential property disposals require a 60-day return separate to Self Assessment.
Inheritance Tax Inheritance Tax Act 1984 (IHTA 1984). Form IHT400 filed by personal representatives within 12 months of death.
Stamp Duty Land Tax (England & NI) Finance Act 2003 Part 4. (Wales: LTT — WRA; Scotland: LBTT — Revenue Scotland.)
Customs duties & excise UK Borders/Customs framework, particularly important post-Brexit for goods movement.
National Minimum Wage enforcement National Minimum Wage Act 1998. HMRC investigates underpayment and can name & shame employers.
Tax credits / Universal Credit liaison Tax credits being phased out into UC (DWP) but legacy elements still administered.
AML supervision Supervises tax advisers and accountants who are not supervised by a recognised professional body. See §1.7.
Legal status

HMRC is established by the Commissioners for Revenue & Customs Act 2005 (CRCA). Its Commissioners (currently a small board) hold delegated statutory power; their officers act “under the care and management of the Commissioners” (CRCA s.5). When you write to HMRC, you are technically writing to an Officer of the Board.

1.2.2 HMRC's structure and how to interact with it

From a practitioner's point of view, HMRC is split into a series of tax silos, each with its own helpline, address and online portal. The silo you need depends on the client and the issue:

Silo Online service Postal address (current at 2024/25)
Self Assessment SA online via Government Gateway / Agent Services Account Self Assessment, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1AS
Corporation Tax CT600 e-filing (third-party software only) Corporation Tax Services, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1AX
VAT MTD VAT through API-enabled software (Xero, QBO, etc.) VAT Written Enquiries Team, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1WR
PAYE / Employer PAYE Online, RTI submissions via payroll software PT Operations North East England, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1BX
CIS CIS Online for monthly returns Construction Industry Scheme, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1BX
Agent Authorisation Agent Services Account (ASA) plus “old” Online Agent Services for SA & CT Central Agent Authorisation Team, HM Revenue & Customs, BX9 1AU
Working tip

The “BX9” postcode is not a real geographic location — it routes to HMRC's centralised digital mail-handling. Never address physical post to HMRC's Whitehall headquarters; it will sit in a tray for weeks. Use the BX9 + sub-code for the relevant silo.

1.2.3 The Government Gateway and Agent Services Account (ASA)

Every individual and business that interacts digitally with HMRC needs a Government Gateway account. As an agent you will hold:

  • A personal Government Gateway for your own Self Assessment.
  • An Agent Online Services Account — the “old” account — used for filing SA100, CT600 and managing 64-8 authorisations.
  • An Agent Services Account (ASA) — the “new” account, mandatory for MTD VAT, MTD ITSA, Trust Registration Service, and CGT-on-property reporting.

You authorise an agent relationship by either: (a) the client signing form 64-8 (legacy method, for SA, CT, PAYE, VAT pre-MTD); or (b) the digital authorisation request via the ASA, where the client receives a code from HMRC that they pass to you to enter in your ASA. The digital authorisation has overtaken paper 64-8s for most live filing services.

1.3 Companies House — The Registry

Companies House (CH) is the registrar of companies in the UK. It is an executive agency of the Department for Business and Trade. Crucially, Companies House is a registry, not a regulator: it records what is filed but historically does not validate the truthfulness of filings beyond formal completeness. The Economic Crime & Corporate Transparency Act 2023 (ECCTA) is now changing that — CH gains identity-verification, query and rejection powers in phased rollouts from 2024 to 2027.

1.3.1 What Companies House does

Function Detail
Incorporation Registers limited companies (private & public), LLPs, Limited Partnerships, Community Interest Companies (CICs) and Overseas Companies. Form IN01 (paper) or web/software incorporation.
Statutory accounts Receives annual accounts from every active company (full, abridged, micro-entity or filleted). Public on the CH register.
Confirmation Statement Annual snapshot (form CS01) confirming SIC code, registered office, officers, shareholders and PSC. £34 digital filing fee (£62 paper) from 1 May 2024.
People with Significant Control (PSC) register Public register of individuals owning >25% of shares/voting rights or with significant influence over the company.
Director and Secretary appointments / changes Forms AP01 (appoint director), TM01 (terminate), CH01 (change details). Must be filed within 14 days of the change.
Share allotments & capital changes SH01 (allotment of shares), SH06 (cancellation), SH19 (statement of capital), and the various return forms for capital reductions.
Charges (security) MR01 to register a fixed/floating charge over company assets within 21 days of creation. Failure to register makes the charge void against a liquidator.
Strike-off Voluntary strike-off via DS01 for solvent dormant companies; compulsory strike-off where filings are overdue.
ECCTA reforms — be aware

The Economic Crime & Corporate Transparency Act 2023 introduces:

  • Mandatory identity verification (IDV) for directors, PSCs and people filing on behalf of companies.
  • Removal of the option to file abridged accounts (only filleted accounts will remain — full accounts must be prepared even if some pages aren't filed publicly).
  • Mandatory software-only filing (paper and CH WebFiling routes will be phased out).
  • Enhanced CH powers to query, reject and remove incorrect information.

Rollout is staged 2024–2027. Always check the latest CH transition timetable when advising clients on first-year filings.

1.3.2 Statutory deadlines — Companies House

Filing Deadline Penalty for missed filing
First accounts (private company) 21 months after date of incorporation £150 (≤1 month late) → £1,500 (>6 months); doubled if late in 2 consecutive years
Subsequent accounts (private company) 9 months after accounting reference date (ARD) As above
Public company accounts 6 months after ARD £750 → £7,500; doubled if late twice
Confirmation statement Annually, within 14 days of due date (review period) No fine, but company can be struck off and directors can be prosecuted
Director/officer changes 14 days from change Criminal offence; directors prosecutable
Charge registration (MR01) 21 days from creation Charge void against liquidator if late; court application required to register out of time

1.4 The Financial Reporting Council (FRC) and its successor ARGA

The FRC sets UK accounting standards (FRS 100 to FRS 105), audit standards (ISAs UK), corporate governance code, and the actuarial standards. It is in the process of being replaced by the Audit, Reporting and Governance Authority (ARGA) following the post-Carillion Kingman Review. ARGA will have stronger statutory powers including direct sanction of company directors over financial reporting failures.

For day-to-day bookkeeping the FRC matters because it owns the financial reporting standards you must apply when preparing accounts:

  • FRS 100 — framework: which standard applies to which entity.
  • FRS 101 — reduced disclosure for subsidiaries of IFRS groups.
  • FRS 102 — the main UK GAAP standard, most clients you will work on.
  • FRS 102 Section 1A — reduced disclosures for small entities (qualifying as small under Companies Act).
  • FRS 103 — insurance contracts (specialist).
  • FRS 104 — interim financial reporting.
  • FRS 105 — the micro-entities regime: simplest, fewest disclosures, no fair value model.

We will spend modules 29 to 32 on FRS 105, FRS 102 Section 1A and FRS 102 in granular detail, including why each disclosure is required by the standard.

1.5 Professional bodies and AML supervisors

To call yourself a “Chartered Accountant” you must be a member of a chartered body. These bodies set entry standards, run the qualification, monitor CPD, and supervise members for AML purposes.

Body Designation Scope
ICAEW ACA / FCA Institute of Chartered Accountants in England & Wales. Full audit-recognised body. Practising certificate required to operate in public practice.
ICAS CA Institute of Chartered Accountants of Scotland. Same scope as ICAEW within Scotland.
Chartered Accountants Ireland ACA / FCA Cross-border (NI / RoI).
ACCA ACCA / FCCA Association of Chartered Certified Accountants. Audit-recognised. Largest UK body by membership.
CIMA ACMA / FCMA, CGMA Chartered Institute of Management Accountants. Focus on management accounting; not audit-recognised in the UK.
AAT MAAT / FMAAT Association of Accounting Technicians. Recognised AML supervisor. Ideal for bookkeeping and small-business accounting.
CIOT / ATT CTA / ATT Chartered Institute of Taxation / Association of Taxation Technicians — tax-only specialism.
ICB MICB / FICB Institute of Certified Bookkeepers. Bookkeeping focus; AML supervisor.
IAB AIAB / MIAB International Association of Bookkeepers; AML supervisor.

1.6 The Office for Professional Body AML Supervision (OPBAS)

OPBAS sits within the FCA and supervises the AML supervisors. It does not directly supervise accountants, but it ensures the professional bodies do their AML supervisory job consistently.

1.7 Anti-Money Laundering (AML) supervision — you must be supervised

Critical legal point

Under the Money Laundering Regulations 2017 (as amended), any person providing accountancy services or tax services by way of business must be supervised for AML — either by their professional body or, if not in a body, directly by HMRC. Operating without supervision is a criminal offence carrying up to two years' imprisonment (MLR 2017, reg.56).

HMRC's AML registration costs around £300 per premises per year (2024/25) plus a £40 registration fee and a £150 fit-and-proper test for senior staff. If you are AAT, ACCA, ICAEW etc. you do not additionally register with HMRC for AML — your body covers it. We cover AML in depth in Module 83.

1.8 Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) — data protection

If your business processes personal data (and as an accountant you process names, NINOs, salaries, bank details, addresses), you must register with the ICO (a notification fee, currently £40–£2,900 a year depending on size) and comply with the UK GDPR & Data Protection Act 2018. Module 86 covers this in detail.

1.9 The Pensions Regulator (TPR)

TPR enforces auto-enrolment compliance. Every employer (regardless of size) must auto-enrol eligible jobholders into a qualifying pension scheme, contribute the statutory minimum, and file an annual re-declaration of compliance. Penalties for non-compliance start at £400 fixed and escalate to £10,000/day for the largest employers (Module 23).

1.10 The Charity Commission & OSCR

Charities in England & Wales register with the Charity Commission for England & Wales (CCEW) once income exceeds £5,000 (or any income for CIOs). Scotland uses OSCR; Northern Ireland uses the Charity Commission for Northern Ireland (CCNI). Charity accounts follow the Charities SORP — the Statement of Recommended Practice based on FRS 102 — with extensive narrative disclosures (Trustees' Annual Report). Module 71 covers charity conversion in depth.

1.11 Insolvency Service

Part of the Department for Business and Trade. Investigates bankruptcies, supervises liquidators, oversees director disqualifications, and runs the Bankruptcy Restrictions / Director Disqualification regimes. We meet the Insolvency Service in modules 60–64 (cessation routes).

1.12 Putting it together — a typical client's regulator map

Imagine you take on a brand-new private limited company — a husband-and-wife consultancy:

Filing Regulator Frequency
VAT return (if registered) HMRC Quarterly
RTI / Full Payment Submission HMRC On or before each pay date
Re-declaration of pension compliance The Pensions Regulator Every 3 years
Self Assessment for each director HMRC Annual (31 Jan)
P11D (if any benefits in kind) HMRC Annual (6 Jul)
P60 to each employee via employer to employee Annual (31 May)
Confirmation statement Companies House Annual
Statutory accounts Companies House & HMRC (with CT600) Annual
CT600 HMRC Annual (12m after PE)
ICO notification ICO Annual
Your own AML supervision Professional body or HMRC Annual

Eleven distinct compliance points for a tiny consultancy. Multiply across thirty clients and you can see why workflow software (Karbon, Senta, Pixie, etc.) has become essential to practice management.

Module 1 — Summary

  • HMRC administers tax (Income Tax, CT, VAT, NI, CGT, IHT). Authority comes from Parliament via the Taxes Acts; HMRC writes guidance but only Parliament makes law.
  • Companies House is a registry of companies and LLPs. ECCTA 2023 is currently turning it into a more active gatekeeper with identity verification and query powers.
  • FRC sets accounting and audit standards (FRS 100–105). Being replaced by ARGA with stronger statutory powers.
  • Accountants must be supervised for AML — by their professional body (ICAEW, ACCA, AAT, etc.) or directly by HMRC. Unsupervised practice is a criminal offence.
  • Other regulators in the orbit: TPR (pensions), ICO (data protection), Charity Commission/OSCR/CCNI, Insolvency Service.
  • A typical small-company client triggers a dozen distinct annual compliance points spread across at least four regulators.
Knowledge Check

Module 1 — End-of-Section MCQ (10 questions)

Click the option you believe is correct. Feedback appears immediately. Aim for 8/10.

Q1
Which of the following is not administered by HMRC?
Strike-off (DS01) is processed by Companies House. HMRC may object to a strike-off if tax is owed, but it does not administer the process.
Q2
A new private limited company is incorporated on 14 March 2024. When are its first statutory accounts due at Companies House?
First accounts of a private company are due 21 months after incorporation. Subsequent accounts are due 9 months after the accounting reference date (ARD).
Q3
Which standard is most commonly applied to small UK private companies that do not qualify as micro-entities?
FRS 102 Section 1A reduces disclosures for entities qualifying as small under the Companies Act size limits while still applying FRS 102 recognition and measurement.
Q4
Operating as a paid bookkeeper without AML supervision is:
MLR 2017 reg.56 makes unsupervised practice a criminal offence punishable by up to 2 years' imprisonment.
Q5
The Confirmation Statement (CS01) is filed at:
CS01 confirms the registered office, officers, shareholders, PSC and SIC code. Filing fee £34 (digital) from May 2024.
Q6
A “BX9” HMRC postcode refers to:
BX9 is a non-geographic mail routing code. Correspondence is sub-routed by the address line (e.g. “Self Assessment”, “Corporation Tax Services”, “PT Operations North East England”).
Q7
Which body is the AML supervisor for AAT-qualified bookkeepers in independent practice?
AAT is a recognised AML supervisory body and supervises members in practice. Members do not also need HMRC supervision.
Q8
A fixed charge over a company's premises is created on 1 February. By when must it be registered at Companies House under the standard rule?
21 days — CA 2006 s.859A. Out of time, the charge is void against a liquidator and the company would need a court order to register late.
Q9
Which of the following is a non-ministerial department?
HMRC is a non-ministerial department reporting to Parliament via the Treasury, established by CRCA 2005. The others are executive agencies or arm's-length bodies.
Q10
Which Act is replacing the FRC with a stronger regulator (ARGA)?
The Audit Reform Bill (post-Kingman) creates ARGA. As of 2024/25 the FRC continues to operate while transition occurs.
Module 2 · Part 1 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

UK Business Structures — Deep Dive

A client comes in with the same question every accountant hears: “sole trader or ltd?” The honest answer is never a one-liner — it depends on profit profile, liability exposure, growth plan, exit intent, and how the owner wants to extract cash. Two builders with identical £80k profits can rationally choose differently: one stays sole trader (simpler, full Class 4 NI exposure, unlimited liability accepted because the work isn’t litigation-prone); the other incorporates (Corp Tax + dividend tax, slightly lower total tax at this band, limited liability against a client who sues over a structural defect, professional credibility, easier sale at exit). The wrong structure costs real money — and the cost compounds. Pick sole-trader when a Ltd would have saved £4k/year in tax and the owner pays £40k of unnecessary tax over a decade. Pick Ltd when sole-trader would have saved £1.5k/year in admin and accountancy fees and the owner pays £15k of compliance overhead they didn’t need. Choose CIC when a charity would have unlocked Gift Aid and rate relief, or choose a charity when a CIC would have allowed dividends to fund the founders. Get the structure right at incorporation and every later decision sits on a sound foundation. Get it wrong and you spend years working around it. This module is the seven-structure map: sole trader, general partnership, LLP, private limited (Ltd), public limited (PLC), Community Interest Company (CIC), and charity/CIO — with the legal personality, liability exposure, tax regime, public-disclosure burden, and governance documents that distinguish each.

The cross-over: at low profits sole trader is often cheaper; as profit rises Ltd typically wins on tax, but the exact cross-over depends on extraction strategy and the dividend tax rates — rerun the calculation annually. If yes, C I C lets founders be paid; charity or C I O gives full tax exemption with stricter governance. Five: none of the above, low-risk solo trade? Learning Objectives

  • Compare the seven main UK business structures (sole trader, general partnership, LLP, private limited, public limited, CIC, charity/CIO) on legal personality, liability, taxation, governance, public disclosure and cost.
  • Calculate the all-in tax cost (Income Tax + NI + Corporation Tax + dividend tax) of a £50,000 / £100,000 / £200,000 profit business under sole-trader vs Ltd vs LLP structures.
  • Identify the structure that best fits a given client scenario based on liability exposure, profit profile, growth plans and exit strategy.
  • Explain the regulatory and reporting consequences of each structure.
  • List the documents constitutionally governing each structure.

2.1 The seven UK business structures at a glance

Structure Separate legal entity? Liability Income tax Public accounts? Govt. body
Sole Trader No Unlimited personal IT + Class 2 & 4 NI No HMRC only
General Partnership No (England); separate (Scotland) Unlimited; joint & several IT + Class 2 & 4 NI on each partner's share No HMRC only
LLP Yes Limited to capital contribution IT + Class 2 & 4 NI on each member's share (transparent) Yes HMRC + CH
Limited (Ltd) Yes Limited to share capital Corporation Tax (company); IT/dividend tax (shareholders) Yes HMRC + CH
PLC Yes Limited to share capital Corporation Tax Yes (extensive) HMRC + CH + (if listed) FCA
CIC Yes Limited (Ltd or company limited by guarantee) Corporation Tax Yes + CIC34 report HMRC + CH + CIC Regulator
Charity / CIO Yes Limited Generally exempt; trading subsidiary often used Yes (Charities SORP) HMRC + Charity Commission/OSCR/CCNI (+ CH for charitable companies)

2.2 Sole trader — the legal nuts and bolts

A sole trader (or “self-employed individual”) is a person who carries on a trade, profession or vocation in their own name. There is no legal separation between the person and the business. Their assets and the “business” assets are the same in law — if the business goes bankrupt, the personal assets follow.

2.2.1 Registering as a sole trader

You must register for Self Assessment with HMRC by 5 October following the end of the tax year in which you started self-employment. Registration is online at gov.uk/register-for-self-assessment; HMRC issues a UTR (Unique Taxpayer Reference) within ~10 working days, and a separate Government Gateway login.

2.2.2 Tax footprint of a sole trader

Profits from self-employment are charged to:

  • Income Tax on profits above the Personal Allowance (£12,570 for 2024/25): 20% basic, 40% higher, 45% additional. Personal Allowance tapers away at £1 for every £2 of income above £100,000 — fully eroded at £125,140.
  • Class 4 NI: 6% on profits between £12,570 and £50,270; 2% above. (Reduced from 9% to 6% from 6 April 2024 in the Spring Budget; check current year for 2025/26.)
  • Class 2 NI: abolished as a flat-rate weekly charge from 6 April 2024. Voluntary Class 2 contributions remain available for self-employed earning below the Small Profits Threshold (currently £6,725) who wish to maintain a state pension contribution year — £3.45/week (2024/25 rate).
Worked Example 2.1

Sarah, freelance graphic designer (sole trader)

Year ended 5 April 2025. Trading profit: £40,000. No other income.

Trading profit 40,000
Less Personal Allowance (12,570)
Taxable income 27,430
Income Tax (basic 20%) 5,486
Class 4 NI: (50,270 − 12,570) × 6% = 2,262 capped to:
(40,000 − 12,570) × 6%		 1,646
Total tax & NI 7,132 17.8% effective

Sarah pays this through Self Assessment by 31 January 2026 (along with first Payment on Account for 2025/26).

2.2.3 Advantages and disadvantages of sole trader status

Advantage Disadvantage
Cheapest and simplest to set up — no Companies House fee Unlimited personal liability for business debts
No requirement to publish accounts — complete privacy Cannot raise external equity finance
Losses can be offset against other income (sideways loss relief, ITA 2007 s.64) Often perceived as less “professional” than a Ltd by larger customers
Cash basis available if turnover <£150k (mandatory default from 6 April 2024 for new entrants) Profits are taxed each year regardless of withdrawals — no flexibility to defer income recognition like a company can with retained earnings
No Corporation Tax administration; one annual SA100 Class 4 NI applies on top of Income Tax — total marginal rate ~28% for basic-rate earners

2.3 General Partnership

Two or more persons (individuals or corporates) carrying on business in common with a view to profit (Partnership Act 1890 s.1). No legal personality in England & Wales (the partnership is not a separate person); each partner is jointly and severally liable for partnership debts.

2.3.1 The partnership agreement

The PA 1890 provides default rules — equal sharing of profits, equal contribution to capital, no entitlement to remuneration for working in the business, etc. Almost all clients will want to override these by a written Partnership Agreement covering:

  • Profit-sharing ratio (PSR) and changes in PSR
  • Capital contributions and interest on capital
  • Salaries to partners (a P&L charge in commercial accounts but added back for tax)
  • Drawings limits and policies
  • Admission of new partners and retirement of existing partners
  • Dispute resolution
  • Continuation/dissolution on death of a partner

2.3.2 Tax for a general partnership

The partnership itself does not pay tax. It files an SA800 Partnership Tax Return that reports the partnership's profit; that profit is then allocated among the partners according to their PSR for the period and each partner reports their share on form SA104 (partnership pages) within their personal SA100.

2.3.3 Limited Partnership (LP) — specialist structure

An LP is a partnership with at least one general partner (unlimited liability) and one or more limited partners (limited to capital contribution). LPs are registered at Companies House under the Limited Partnerships Act 1907. Mostly used by private equity / VC funds. Not to be confused with LLP (next).

2.4 Limited Liability Partnership (LLP)

Created by the Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000. An LLP is a separate legal entity (like a company) but is taxed like a partnership (transparent, members pay IT & NI on their share). Designed for professional firms (law, accountancy) that wanted limited liability without becoming companies.

2.4.1 Key LLP attributes

  • Minimum 2 members; minimum 2 designated members (with statutory filing duties).
  • No share capital; capital contributions are accounted for as members' loans/equity per the LLP agreement.
  • Files annual accounts at Companies House (small/micro filing exemptions broadly mirror companies).
  • Files a confirmation statement annually.
  • Members are taxed personally on their share of LLP profits as if they were partners (ITTOIA 2005 s.863).
  • Salaried members rule (ITA 2007 s.863A) deems certain “disguised employees” in LLPs to be employees for PAYE/NI — you must apply the three-condition test annually.

2.5 Private Limited Company (Ltd)

The workhorse of UK business. Roughly 4.6 million companies on the register. The company is a separate legal person under CA 2006 s.16. Shareholders own; directors manage; their roles and the relationship between them are set out in the company's Articles of Association and (often) a separate Shareholders' Agreement.

2.5.1 Constitutional documents

  • Memorandum of Association — a now-very-short document signed by initial subscribers confirming intention to form a company. Replaced extensively in 2009 by simpler form.
  • Articles of Association — the company's internal rulebook. The Model Articles for private companies (Companies (Model Articles) Regulations 2008, Sch 1) are the default; can be modified or replaced by bespoke Articles.
  • Shareholders' Agreement — private contract between shareholders. Often covers pre-emption, drag/tag rights, exit mechanics, valuation. Not filed at Companies House (unlike Articles, which are public).

2.5.2 Tax footprint of a Ltd

Two layers of tax:

  1. Corporation Tax on company profits — 25% main rate above £250,000; 19% small profits rate up to £50,000; marginal relief in between (effective marginal rate ~26.5%).
  2. Income Tax on amounts extracted — salary (taxed under PAYE with Class 1 NI primary 8% / secondary 13.8%), or dividends (taxed at 8.75% basic / 33.75% higher / 39.35% additional, with a £500 dividend allowance for 2024/25, reducing to £500 in 2024/25 from £1,000 in 2023/24).

2.5.3 The salary/dividend mix — the classic owner-managed company question

For a director-shareholder, the optimal extraction structure depends on (a) whether they need NI credits, (b) the company's profit level, (c) their other income, and (d) personal allowance interactions. The traditional structure for a single-director company in 2024/25:

  • Pay a salary equal to the Secondary NI Threshold (£9,100 for 2024/25, raised to £5,000 for 2025/26 with Employer NI changes from April 2025) to maintain a qualifying year for the State Pension without triggering Employer or Employee NI.
  • Take the rest as dividends out of post-tax retained profits.
2025/26 watch — Employer NI changes

From 6 April 2025, the Secondary Threshold drops to £5,000 (from £9,100) and Employer NI rises to 15% (from 13.8%). The classic “£9,100 salary + dividends” strategy needs revisiting from 2025/26 — in many cases a higher salary (up to the Personal Allowance £12,570) becomes optimal because the Employer's Allowance (£10,500 from April 2025, where eligible) covers the resulting Employer NI, and the salary saves Corporation Tax at 19%–25%.

Worked Example 2.2

Director-shareholder — £40,000 profit company (2024/25)

Single director-shareholder, no other income, taking £9,100 salary + balance as dividend.

Profit before director's salary 40,000
Less salary (9,100)
Profit chargeable to CT 30,900
Corporation Tax @ 19% (small profits rate) (5,871)
Profit available as dividend 25,029
Personal tax position:
Salary 9,100 Personal Allowance covers
Dividend 25,029
Less remaining Personal Allowance (12,570 − 9,100) (3,470)
Less Dividend Allowance (500)
Taxable dividend 21,059
Dividend tax @ 8.75% 1,843
Total tax 5,871 + 1,843 = 7,714 ~19.3% effective

Compare Sarah (sole trader, Worked Example 2.1) at £7,132 on £40k profit. The Ltd is slightly more expensive at this profit level — the cross-over typically happens around £30k–£35k profit. The Ltd's value comes at higher profits, when retained earnings can be deferred, and when limited liability is genuinely useful.

2.6 Public Limited Company (PLC)

A company whose name ends in “plc”. The label means it can offer shares to the public — not that it must, and not that it is listed. Distinct features:

  • Minimum allotted share capital £50,000, of which 25% must be paid up.
  • Minimum 2 directors (vs 1 for Ltd) and a company secretary (mandatory).
  • Accounts due 6 months after ARD (vs 9 months for Ltd).
  • Cannot file abridged or filleted accounts — full accounts required.
  • If listed (LSE Main, AIM, AQUIS) — FCA rules apply on top.

2.7 Community Interest Company (CIC)

A limited company (Ltd or company limited by guarantee) with a community/social-purpose lock. Created by the Companies (Audit, Investigations & Community Enterprise) Act 2004. Regulated by the CIC Regulator (a small office within Companies House). Files a CIC34 community-interest report annually with the accounts. Asset lock means assets cannot be distributed to members — if dissolved, must transfer to another asset-locked body.

2.8 Charity, Charitable Incorporated Organisation (CIO) and Charitable Company

Three principal forms:

  • Unincorporated charity (charitable trust or association) — trustees personally liable; no separate legal personality.
  • Charitable company limited by guarantee — legal personality; dual-registered (Companies House + Charity Commission).
  • CIO — Charitable Incorporated Organisation, created by Charities Act 2011 Part 11. Single regulator (Charity Commission) so no Companies House filing burden. Two flavours: Foundation CIO (members are the trustees) and Association CIO (separate membership body with trustees elected by members).

Charity-specific tax treatment: most income exempt under CTA 2010 Part 11 (trading income exemption) provided used for charitable purposes; non-primary-purpose trading sometimes routed through a wholly-owned trading subsidiary which gift-aids profit up to the parent. Module 71 covers Ltd-to-CIO conversion in detail.

2.9 The choice tree — which structure for which client?

Client situation Recommended structure Rationale
Hobby income, <£10k profit, no liability risk Sole trader Simplest, cheapest. No CT or CH filings.
Freelance consultant, £20–£40k profit, low liability risk Sole trader Tax cost similar; admin cheaper. Revisit at £50k+.
Trades-person (electrician, builder) £30k+ Ltd Significant injury or property-damage liability protection worth limited liability cost.
Two-person consultancy with retained profit Ltd Income splitting via dividends; retained profit deferral.
Professional firm (law, accountancy) with multiple senior practitioners LLP Limited liability + tax transparency; easier to admit/retire members than for a Ltd.
Property landlord, single rental property Generally personal name Tax-driven analysis: SDLT 3% surcharge for company purchase, no Section 24 mortgage interest restriction in company, but extra 8% CGT on disposal of corporate. Modelling required.
Property landlord building a portfolio (5+ properties) Ltd Section 24 mortgage interest restriction in personal name very expensive at higher rates; companies fully deduct interest.
Social enterprise (community gym, food bank with paid trading) CIC or CIO Asset lock and clear social purpose; CIO if grant-funded mostly; CIC if mostly trading.
Charity raising funds for cause CIO Single regulator; trustee limited liability; cleaner constitutional framework than charitable trust.
Multi-director SME with VC funding Ltd or PLC Shares are the standard investment instrument; partnership structures don't accommodate equity investors.
The £50k profit pivot

A widely-used rule of thumb: profits up to £30k — sole trader is usually cheaper after software and accountancy costs; £30k–£50k — broadly equivalent; above £50k — Ltd starts to dominate provided the owner does not need to extract every penny each year. If they do extract everything, the dividend-tax layer narrows the advantage. Always model on actual numbers; never advise structurally without modelling.

Module 2 — Summary

  • Seven principal structures: sole trader, partnership, LLP, Ltd, PLC, CIC, charity/CIO. They differ on legal personality, liability, taxation and disclosure.
  • Sole trader and partnership offer simplicity and privacy but unlimited personal liability and an Income Tax + Class 4 NI tax footprint.
  • LLP combines partnership taxation transparency with limited liability — ideal for professional firms.
  • Ltd provides limited liability and access to dividend extraction at lower combined tax cost above ~£50k profit, at the cost of public filing and Corporation Tax administration.
  • PLC, CIC and charity forms are specialist — deployed for capital raising, social purpose and tax-exempt purposes respectively.
  • Always model the after-tax outcome on actual numbers. The 2024/25 to 2025/26 transition (Employer NI changes, dividend allowance erosion, Class 2 abolition) materially shifts the balance.
Knowledge Check

Module 2 — End-of-Section MCQ (10 questions)

Aim for 8/10. Click an option to see the verdict.

Q1
A sole trader's business assets are, in law:
A sole trader has no legal separation from the business; the assets are personal assets and the liabilities are personal liabilities.
Q2
By which date must a new sole trader register for Self Assessment for the tax year 2024/25?
Registration for SA is required by 5 October following the end of the tax year of commencement. Filing deadline is the following 31 January, but registration is earlier.
Q3
The Class 4 NI rate on profits between £12,570 and £50,270 in 2024/25 is:
Class 4 main rate cut from 9% to 6% from 6 April 2024 (Spring Budget 2024). 2% applies above £50,270.
Q4
A partnership return (SA800):
SA800 reports profit; the profit is allocated to partners by their PSR and each partner reports their share on SA104 in their personal SA100.
Q5
Which is true of an LLP?
LLPs combine the limited liability of a company with the tax transparency of a partnership.
Q6
The Corporation Tax rate on profits up to £50,000 (single company, 2024/25) is:
19% small profits rate applies up to £50k; 25% main rate above £250k; marginal relief in between with effective marginal of 26.5%.
Q7
The dividend allowance for 2024/25 is:
£500 for 2024/25 (down from £1,000 in 2023/24 and £2,000 in 2022/23).
Q8
A PLC must file its accounts at Companies House within:
PLC accounts: 6 months after ARD. Private companies: 9 months. (First accounts: 21 months from incorporation in either case.)
Q9
A CIC's defining legal feature is:
A CIC is a limited company with an asset lock, regulated by the CIC Regulator. It pays Corporation Tax like any company.
Q10
A property investor with 8 buy-to-let properties on residential mortgages and £80k other employment income is most likely better off:
Section 24 ITA 2007 restricts mortgage interest relief on residential property to a 20% basic-rate tax credit for individuals; companies deduct it in full. With the investor on higher-rate income, the saving is material.
Module 3 · Part 1 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Bookkeeping Fundamentals — Double-Entry from First Principles

A 15th-century Italian friar called Luca Pacioli wrote a 600-page maths book in 1494, and a small section — Summa de Arithmetica — codified the double-entry system that every UK SME’s books still run on today. The logic hasn’t changed in 530 years: every transaction touches at least two accounts, debits equal credits, and one equation holds true after every single posting: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. Software hides the mechanics — Xero shows you a bank rec, QuickBooks shows you a sales invoice — but underneath, every single line is still a debit and a credit. Understand the eight universal transaction patterns and you can post anything: a director’s loan repayment, a depreciation charge, a deferred revenue release, a wage accrual, a year-end CT provision. Don’t understand the patterns and you’ll spend a career copy-pasting from Google searches and second-guessing whether sales returns are a debit or a credit (debit). This module is the bedrock: the one equation, the five account types, the eight transaction patterns, the trial balance — including what a TB does and (critically) doesn’t detect. Skip this and every later module (FRS 102, CT computations, journals, year-end adjustments, going-concern reviews) is a struggle.

0:00–0:12 The equation, big. ASSETS = LIABILITIES + EQUITY centred in a gold box. Three small definition tiles below. “The only equation in accounting” “The accounting equation. The only equation in accounting. Assets equals Liabilities plus Equity. True after every single transaction, in every business, in every era — codified by Luca Pacioli in 1494 and still running every U K S M E’s books today. Assets are what the business OWNS — cash, debtors, stock, fixed assets. Liabilities are what the business OWES — creditors, loans, accruals. Equity is the owner’s share — the balancing figure. Re-arrange to Assets minus Liabilities equals Equity and you have the net-worth view of the balance sheet.” Open chord
0:13–0:28 Five account types. Three big tiles (Assets, Liabilities, Equity) row one. Two more (Income, Expenses) row two. Gold rules panel below. “Memorise the right column” “Five account types. Three balance-sheet: assets, liabilities, equity. Two profit-and-loss: income, expenses. The debit and credit rules. Assets and expenses go up with a debit. Liabilities, equity and income go up with a credit. Memorise the right column — the left is just the opposite. And the two rules you need: every transaction has equal debits and credits, the totals always balance; and assets and expenses up with debit, liabilities and equity and income up with credit. Every line in Xero, Q B O, Sage hides one of these in the background.” Rise
0:28–0:43 Eight pattern tiles. Green for income side (patterns 1-3), red for purchases (4-6), blue for capital/drawings (7-8). “Eight patterns. Post anything.” “The eight universal transaction patterns. Learn these and you can post anything. One: cash sale — debit cash, credit sales. Two: credit sale — debit debtors, credit sales and V A T. Three: receipt from debtor — debit cash, credit debtors. Four: cash purchase — debit expense, credit cash. Five: credit purchase — debit expense and V A T, credit creditors. Six: payment to creditor — debit creditors, credit cash. Seven: capital introduced — debit cash, credit capital or director loan. Eight: drawings or dividend — debit drawings or dividends, credit cash. Every business event collapses into one of these — or a compound combination. Depreciation, accruals, prepayments, deferred revenue are compound versions of the same logic. Learn the patterns — never Google ‘is sales returns a debit or credit’ again.” Discover
0:43–0:56 Trial balance. What it WILL catch (green) vs what it WON’T (red). Gold “the trap” panel: balanced ≠ correct. “Balanced is not correct” “The trial balance — your first integrity check. A two-column listing of every ledger balance: debits on one side, credits on the other. A T B will detect a one-sided entry, a maths or extraction error, and a wrong-way posting. A T B will NOT detect a completely missing transaction, an entry posted to the wrong account on the same side, or compensating errors. And the professional trap: a balanced T B does not mean the books are correct. Balance means the maths is internally consistent. Reconciliations, control accounts, and analytical review are what catch the things the T B cannot.” Fixed
0:56–1:10 Universal method. Four stacked rows: SOURCE, DEBIT, CREDIT, NARRATIVE. Bottom: worked example of a £1,200 supplier payment. “Same method. Every transaction. 530 years.” “The universal method to translate any business event into a journal: source, debit, credit, narrative. Step one, the source: what document? Invoice, receipt, bank entry, payslip, journal request? Step two, the debit: what goes up that’s asset or expense? Step three, the credit: what goes up that’s liability, equity, or income? Step four, the narrative: one sentence explaining why, for the person reading the books in three years. Worked example: paying a one thousand two hundred pound supplier invoice. Source: bank transfer receipt. Debit Creditors twelve hundred, credit Bank twelve hundred. Narrative: settled supplier invoice four-four-two-three in full per the accounts-payable run on the twelfth of March. Pattern six. Same logic for the three-point-four million invoice as for the hundred-and-twenty stationery one. For five hundred and thirty years and counting.” Triumph

Learning Objectives

  • State and explain the accounting equation, including its rearrangements.
  • Apply the rules of double-entry to record assets, liabilities, equity, income and expenses.
  • Post compound and reversing journals correctly.
  • Prepare a trial balance from a list of ledger balances and identify the types of error a TB will and will not detect.
  • Translate any business event into a journal using the “source → debit → credit → narrative” method.

3.1 What is bookkeeping?

Bookkeeping is the systematic recording of every financial transaction of a business, in chronological order, in a way that allows the business to: (a) know its financial position at any moment (balance sheet); (b) measure its performance over a period (P&L); (c) prove the figures to an external party (HMRC, Companies House, banks, investors); and (d) detect errors and fraud. The discipline is approximately 700 years old — codified by the Italian friar Luca Pacioli in Summa de Arithmetica (1494) — but the underlying logic has not changed since.

3.2 The accounting equation

Assets = Liabilities + Equity

This is the only equation in accounting. It is true after every single transaction, in every business, in every era. Variations:

  • Assets − Liabilities = Equity (net worth) — how the balance sheet is normally presented in the UK.
  • Equity = Capital introduced + Retained profits − Drawings/Dividends — expansion of the equity component over time.
  • Profit = Income − Expenses — measuring the change in equity from operations between two balance sheet dates (excluding capital introduced/withdrawn).

3.3 Double-entry — the symmetry rule

Every transaction has at least two equal and opposite entries: one debit and one credit (or several adding to balance). This guarantees the accounting equation remains true. The direction of debit/credit is fixed by the type of account:

Account type Increase Decrease Normal balance
Asset Debit Credit Debit
Expense Debit Credit Debit
Drawings Debit Credit Debit
Liability Credit Debit Credit
Equity / Capital Credit Debit Credit
Income / Revenue Credit Debit Credit

Mnemonic: DEAD CLIC — Debits go up for Expenses, Assets, Drawings; Credits go up for Liabilities, Income, Capital.

3.4 The 8 universal transaction patterns

Every UK business transaction reduces to one of these eight patterns. Memorise them and you can journalise anything.

Pattern 1 — Cash sale
BankDr 1,200
Sales (or Sales + VAT control)Cr 1,200
Records receipt of cash and recognition of revenue simultaneously.
Pattern 2 — Credit sale (invoice issued, money not yet received)
Trade Debtors (Accounts Receivable)Dr 1,200
SalesCr 1,000
VAT Output TaxCr 200
Recognises receivable and revenue at point of supply (FRS 102 Section 23 / IFRS 15 logic).
Pattern 3 — Receipt from credit customer
BankDr 1,200
Trade DebtorsCr 1,200
Settles the receivable; revenue was already recorded in pattern 2 — do not record sales again.
Pattern 4 — Cash purchase (expense)
Stationery (or appropriate expense)Dr 50
VAT Input Tax (if recoverable)Dr 10
BankCr 60
Pattern 5 — Credit purchase (supplier invoice received)
Expense (or Asset, e.g. inventory)Dr 100
VAT Input TaxDr 20
Trade Creditors (Accounts Payable)Cr 120
Pattern 6 — Payment to supplier
Trade CreditorsDr 120
BankCr 120
Pattern 7 — Capital introduced by owner
BankDr 10,000
Capital (sole trader) / Director's Loan / Share Capital (Ltd)Cr 10,000
Pattern 8 — Drawings / Dividend (distribution to owner)
Drawings (sole trader) / Dividends Paid (Ltd, charged against retained earnings)Dr 500
BankCr 500

3.5 Compound journals

Where a transaction needs more than two postings — e.g. payroll — we use a compound journal:

Payroll for the month — gross £10,000, tax £1,500, EE NI £700, ER NI £900, net pay £7,800
Wages & Salaries (P&L)Dr 10,000
Employer's NI (P&L)Dr 900
PAYE/NIC liabilityCr 3,100
Net wages payable / BankCr 7,800
Three credits, two debits — total debits 10,900 = total credits 10,900. Always check.

3.6 The trial balance

A trial balance lists every ledger account balance with debits in one column and credits in another. The columns must total to the same figure. If they do, you have arithmetic integrity (one of the three checks below).

Errors a TB will detect Errors a TB will not detect
One-sided entries (only Dr or only Cr posted) Errors of omission (transaction not recorded at all)
Different amounts on Dr and Cr Errors of commission (right side, wrong account)
Casting errors in a single ledger Errors of principle (e.g. capital expenditure expensed as repair)
Transposition errors that change a side total Compensating errors (two errors that cancel out)
Original entry errors (wrong amount on both sides)
Reversal errors (Dr and Cr swapped)

This is why the trial balance is a necessary but not sufficient check. The other two checks at month-end are: bank reconciliation (proves cash account against external bank statement) and control account reconciliations (proves debtor/creditor control accounts against the underlying sub-ledgers).

Module 3 — Summary

  • Accounting equation Assets = Liabilities + Equity holds after every transaction.
  • Double-entry: equal debits and credits per transaction. DEAD CLIC mnemonic.
  • Eight universal transaction patterns cover the bulk of bookkeeping.
  • Trial balance proves arithmetic but cannot detect errors of omission, commission, principle, compensation, original entry or reversal.
Knowledge Check

Module 3 — End-of-Section MCQ (8 questions)

Q1
A business pays £600 cash for a desk to use in the office (capitalised). Which is the correct journal?
An asset is acquired (Dr increases an asset) by paying out cash (Cr decreases an asset). Treating it as an expense would be an error of principle.
Q2
Which type of error will a balanced trial balance not detect?
Posting to the wrong account on the right side is an error of commission and the TB still balances.
Q3
A credit sale of £1,200 (incl. 20% VAT) generates which credit to VAT Output Tax?
£1,200 ÷ 1.2 = £1,000 net; £1,200 − £1,000 = £200 VAT.
Q4
Drawings are:
Drawings reduce the owner's equity. They are not an expense and do not affect profit.
Q5
A receipt from a credit customer is posted as:
Sales were recognised when the invoice was raised; the receipt only settles the debtor.
Q6
Equity at year-end equals:
Equity moves only via capital introduced/withdrawn (or share issues/buybacks for a Ltd) and retained profit/loss.
Q7
Compensating errors are:
Two errors of equal and opposite effect can leave the TB balanced. Only substantive checks (e.g. reconciliations) catch them.
Q8
In double-entry, an increase in a liability is recorded as:
Liabilities have a normal credit balance. Increases are credits, decreases are debits.

The Chart of Accounts & The General Ledger

A new client moves their books from a 20-year-old desktop Sage file to Xero. The migration runs “successfully”. Six months later the bookkeeper, the accountant and the owner are arguing about why the management accounts make no sense: rent is split across three different account codes, motor expenses sits in “general expenses”, and there are 11 different sales accounts the owner created over the years for “different product lines” that don’t actually exist any more. None of it’s wrong. None of it’s usable either. The chart of accounts is the backbone of every accounting system — every posting lands in one of its accounts — and its structure determines whether you can produce a clean P&L, a balance sheet that maps to the Companies Act formats, a VAT return that ties out, and management accounts the owner can read. Done well, the COA is invisible — numbers flow effortlessly into reports. Done badly, every month-end is a reconciliation puzzle and the statutory accounts re-classification at year-end takes three days. This module is the standard UK COA structure (Xero/QBO conventions), the control-account discipline that keeps debtors, creditors, VAT, PAYE and the bank reconciling, and the mapping from COA codes to FRS 102 Section 1A and Companies Act Schedule 1 statutory account lines. Get this right at setup and the rest of the year-end process flows.

Two: analysis lives in dimensions, not accounts — cost centres, tracking categories, jobs and projects, not a separate code for every project. Three: mappable to the statutory accounts — every code knows its Companies Act line and its F R S disclosure note. Four: archived, not deleted — stale codes get archived after year-end, never deleted with historic transactions still attached. Spend an hour on the C O A at setup. Save days every year-end after that.” Triumph

Learning Objectives

  • Design a chart of accounts that balances simplicity with the level of analysis needed for VAT, Corporation Tax, payroll and statutory accounts.
  • Distinguish a control account from a sub-ledger and reconcile between them.
  • Map every UK statutory account line (per FRS 102 Section 1A formats and the Companies Act Schedule 1) to a chart of accounts code range.

4.1 What is the chart of accounts (COA)?

The chart of accounts is the list of every account in the general ledger, organised by code or category. It is the backbone of the accounting system — everything that gets posted lands in one of these accounts. The COA structure determines how easily you can produce: a P&L (income/expense classification); a balance sheet (asset/liability/equity classification); a VAT return (VAT codes); and statutory accounts (mapped to the Companies Act formats).

4.2 Standard UK COA structure (Xero/QBO defaults)

Code range Category Examples
100–199 Sales / Revenue 200 Sales, 260 Other Income
300–399 Cost of Sales 310 Materials, 320 Direct Labour
400–599 Operating Expenses 404 Rent, 408 Utilities, 412 Insurance, 477 Salaries
600–699 Finance / Other 610 Interest Income, 620 Bank Charges, 625 Loan Interest
700–799 Depreciation, Tax Charges 710 Depreciation, 760 Corporation Tax
800–899 Non-current Assets 810 Office Equipment, 820 Plant & Machinery, 850 Motor Vehicles
900–989 Current Assets 910 Inventory, 920 Trade Debtors, 950 Bank, 960 Petty Cash
990–999 Prepayments & Accrued Income 995 Prepayments, 996 Accrued Income
1000–1099 Current Liabilities 1020 Trade Creditors, 1040 VAT Liability, 1050 PAYE/NIC Liability, 1060 Corporation Tax Liability
1100–1199 Accruals & Deferred Income 1110 Accruals, 1120 Deferred Income
1200–1299 Non-current Liabilities 1210 Bank Loans, 1230 Hire Purchase
1500–1599 Equity 1510 Share Capital, 1520 Share Premium, 1530 Retained Earnings, 1540 Director's Loan, 1560 Dividends Paid

Note: Xero, QBO, Sage, FreeAgent each use slightly different default code numbers but the categories are universal. When converting clients between platforms, the COA is the first thing to map and the most common source of conversion errors.

4.3 Control accounts and sub-ledgers

The general ledger contains control accounts (single-line balances summarising sub-ledgers). Examples:

  • Trade Debtors Control — summary; the underlying sub-ledger has every customer's balance broken out (Aged Debtors Report).
  • Trade Creditors Control — summary; underlying = supplier balances (Aged Creditors).
  • VAT Control — summary; underlying = transaction-level VAT detail by tax code.
  • PAYE/NIC Control — summary; underlying = month-by-month payroll detail.

Control accounts must reconcile to the sub-ledger every period. If they don't, an entry has been posted directly to the control account bypassing the sub-ledger — common in a manual journal that should have been done as a customer credit note instead.

Module 4 — Summary

  • The COA is the list of every ledger account, structured by category for reporting.
  • A control account summarises a sub-ledger; the two must always reconcile.
  • The COA design predicts whether you can produce a clean VAT return, CT600 and statutory accounts — design it with the end report in mind.
Knowledge Check

Module 4 — End-of-Section MCQ (5 questions)

Q1
Trade Debtors Control:
It is a single ledger balance summarising the customer sub-ledger; reconciliation is essential.
Q2
A code range of 800–899 is most likely used for:
Standard Xero numbering puts non-current assets in 800s.
Q3
Why does COA design matter for VAT?
Boxes 6 and 7 of the VAT return need supply-type breakdowns; the COA is where this is captured.
Q4
Director's Loan Account is best classified as:
If the director has lent the company money, it is a creditor. If the director owes the company money (overdrawn DLA), it is a debtor with potential s.455 tax consequences (Module 8).
Q5
When migrating from QBO to Xero, the most common issue at the COA level is:
Account category mismatches (e.g. an item that was “Cost of Sales” in QBO landing in “Direct Cost” or “Expense” in Xero) are the classic migration issue.

The Bookkeeping Cycle — From Source Document to Trial Balance

It’s the 5th of the month. Last month’s books need closing — and somewhere in the chaos sit 247 supplier invoices, 18 expense claims, a bank statement with 312 transactions, two payroll runs, a VAT return due in three weeks, and a director who’s just dropped a coffee receipt on your desk “for the books, ta.” What separates a bookkeeper who closes the month in two working days from one still chasing reconciliations a fortnight later isn’t speed — it’s the cycle. A defined nine-step sequence, run the same way every month, with controls embedded at each step. Capture · code · post · bank rec · control accounts · adjusting journals · trial balance · review · lock. Skip a step or do them out of order and the errors compound: a missed bank rec hides three duplicate invoices; an un-reconciled VAT control silently builds a £4,200 misstatement; an unrun analytical review lets a 14% gross-margin drift go unnoticed for a quarter. Run the cycle properly and the trial balance at step 7 is just the natural output of having done the previous six. This module is the nine-step monthly close, the controls at each step, and the bank reconciliation discipline that catches the issues every other step misses.

0:00–0:13 Nine numbered tiles in a 3-3-3 grid. Steps 3, 4, 6 highlighted as keystones. Bottom gold panel: why the order matters. “Discipline beats brilliance” “The monthly bookkeeping cycle in nine steps. One: capture the source documents. Two: code and post. Three: reconcile the bank. Four: reconcile the control accounts. Five: post the adjusting journals. Six: extract the trial balance. Seven: draft the P and L and balance sheet. Eight: run the analytical review. Nine: lock the period. The order matters. Reconciliations come BEFORE adjusting journals because adjusting on un-reconciled data is adjusting on noise. The trial balance inherits every earlier error. Skip a step now and spend three days finding the error in two months’ time. Same nine steps, the same way, every month.” Open chord
0:13–0:28 Bank reconciliation. Two top cards: bank statement (blue, independent record) vs bank ledger (green, our books). Below: two unmatched categories (red + purple). Bottom: closing position formula. “Independent record vs the books we keep” “Bank reconciliation. The highest-value control in the cycle. The bank statement is the independent record — it comes from the bank itself, with no client influence. The bank ledger is what your books say. The job is to match every line, and investigate every unmatched one. Items on the statement but not in the books mean a missed invoice, a direct debit nobody coded, a bank fee, or possibly fraud. Items in the books but not on the statement mean uncleared cheques or genuine timing differences. The closing position: statement balance plus or minus reconciling items must equal the ledger balance. If not, the reconciliation isn’t finished. Bank rec is what catches missed invoices, duplicate postings, supplier fraud, bank fees, and mis-codings — every other step misses these.” Discover
0:28–0:43 Four control account cards. Debtors (green) · Creditors (red) · VAT (purple) · PAYE (gold). Bottom: the rule banner. “If a control doesn’t reconcile, the period isn’t closed.” “Control account reconciliations — the four that always run. Debtors control reconciles to the aged-debtors listing — a mismatch means a mis-allocated receipt or a sales invoice posted to the wrong customer. Creditors control reconciles to the aged-creditors listing — a mismatch means duplicate bills or unallocated supplier payments. V A T control reconciles to the V A T return draft — a mismatch means misposted V A T or the wrong rate code. P A Y E control reconciles to the payroll summary and the H M R C P A Y E account — a mismatch means a missing F P S or an under or over-payment to H M R C. The rule: if any control doesn’t reconcile, the period isn’t closed. No exceptions, no ‘close enough’.” Fixed
0:43–0:56 Six adjusting journal tiles. Accruals, prepayments, depreciation, stock, payroll accruals, deferred income. Bottom: green template panel + reversal rule. “Source · DR · CR · Narrative · Reversal” “Adjusting journals — the true-up that turns cash-basis postings into accrual accounts. Accruals: expense incurred but invoice not yet in. Prepayments: paid this period but the benefit is future. Depreciation: this month’s slice of fixed-asset cost. Stock movement: closing minus opening stock as a cost-of-sales adjustment. Payroll accruals: period worked but not yet paid. Deferred income: received but not yet earned. Every adjusting journal follows the same template: source, debit, credit, narrative, and crucially — reversal? If it should reverse next month, schedule it now. Accruals and prepayments reverse on day one of the next month; depreciation does not. Track all open accruals on a schedule — never let one drift two months unreviewed.” Rise
0:56–1:10 Steps 6-9 stacked + target. TB · P&L+BS · analytical review (red) · lock (dark red) · green target panel. “Working day 5. Books closed. Cycle restarts.” “Close-out. The trial balance at step six is the natural output of having done the previous five — debits equal credits, the integrity check. Step seven: the P and L and balance sheet draft — a trial-balance export run through the C O A mapping from module four, not a manual rewrite. Step eight: analytical review — compare to last month, to budget, to prior year, investigate any big movement. Step nine: lock the period — no edits to closed periods, this protects the audit trail and ties the books to filed returns. The target: working day five. Books closed, management accounts out, cycle ready to restart. Discipline beats brilliance. The cycle, the same way, every month, is the moat.” Triumph

Learning Objectives

  • Sequence the steps in a monthly bookkeeping cycle.
  • Identify the controls embedded at each step.
  • Explain how a bank reconciliation works and why it matters.

5.1 The cycle in 9 steps

  1. Capture source documents — collect every invoice, receipt, bank statement, expense claim, payroll record. Source: Dext, supplier portals, bank feeds.
  2. Code & post transactions — assign each item to a COA account and a VAT code; post to the ledger.
  3. Reconcile the bank — match every line on the bank statement to a posting in the bank ledger; investigate unmatched items.
  4. Reconcile control accounts — debtors control to AR ageing; creditors control to AP ageing; VAT control to VAT return draft; PAYE control to payroll summary.
  5. Adjusting journals — accruals, prepayments, depreciation, stock movement, payroll accruals, deferred income.
  6. Run a trial balance — confirm Dr=Cr; review for unusual balances (negative assets, etc.).
  7. Run management accounts — P&L vs budget, balance sheet snapshot, key KPIs.
  8. Lock the period — set lock date in software so prior-period postings are blocked.
  9. File & archive — store source documents, save management pack, log version.

5.2 Bank reconciliation in depth

A bank reconciliation answers: does my cash book agree with the bank's record of my cash? The starting point is the bank statement closing balance. From it, you adjust for unpresented cheques, uncleared lodgements and bank-only items (charges, interest, direct debits not yet recorded), to arrive at the cash book balance. In the cloud-feed era this is largely automated, but the discipline must be understood.

Worked Example 5.1

Bank Reconciliation as at 31 March 2025

Bank statement closing balance £12,450
Add: lodgement banked 31/3 not yet credited 2,000
Less: unpresented cheques (#241, #243, #244) (1,800)
Adjusted bank balance 12,650
Cash book balance per ledger 12,650
Difference NIL

Action: post nothing — the items will clear next period. If the cash book balance had differed (after adjustments), investigate.

Module 5 — Summary

  • Nine repeating steps every month: capture, code, reconcile bank, reconcile controls, adjust, TB, MI, lock, archive.
  • Bank reconciliation is the cornerstone control. Never sign off accounts without one.
Knowledge Check

Module 5 — End-of-Section MCQ (5 questions)

Q1
An unpresented cheque is one that:
Correct — appears in cash book but not yet on bank statement.
Q2
Why lock the period after closing?
Lock dates protect the integrity of filed VAT returns and management accounts.
Q3
Which control account would you reconcile to the aged creditors report?
Aged creditors = supplier balances = trade creditors control sub-ledger.
Q4
A bank-only item not yet in the cash book is:
Bank charges, direct debits, standing orders and bank interest are common bank-only items requiring a journal to bring the cash book up to date.
Q5
A monthly P&L vs budget review is best done:
MI is meaningful only after the underlying ledger is corrected for accruals, prepayments, depreciation, etc.

Source Documents & the UK Record-Keeping Rules

Three years after a perfectly clean year-end, a client gets a Schedule 36 information notice from HMRC. The enquiry officer wants to see every invoice over £500 for the period, the contracts behind two specific supplier relationships, and the original mileage logs. The client shrugs — “you’ve got it all, right?” — and the bookkeeper’s heart sinks. Because they DON’T have it all. Half the supplier invoices were captured into Dext but the originals were thrown away. The contracts went into a folder that got deleted when someone reorganised the OneDrive. The mileage logs — well, the director kept them in a notebook in the van, and the van got sold last spring. The penalty regime doesn’t care whether you had good books once; it cares whether you can produce them now. UK record-keeping has three overlapping statutory regimes — HMRC, the Companies Act 2006, and the Limitation Act 1980 — with different periods and different categories. Add VAT’s 6-year rule, payroll’s 3-year rule, MTD’s digital-link requirement, GDPR’s retention principle, and AML’s 5-years-after-engagement-ends rule, and the question “how long do we keep this?” has at least five right answers depending on what the document is. This module is the map: every source document, who originates it, what posts it, how long you keep it, and why MTD doesn’t replace the source — it just demands the digital link from source to ledger to return.

0:00–0:13 Source → ledger → return. Three boxes with arrows, then a red Sch 36 panel + gold principle banner. “Every posting must trace back to a source” “The source-to-return audit trail. Every business transaction starts with a source document — an invoice, a receipt, a bank statement, a payslip. That source is posted into the ledger with a debit, credit, and narrative, and a link back to the source. The ledger then feeds the statutory returns — V A T, C T 600, S A 100, statutory accounts, F P S. HMRC’s test arrives years later. A Schedule 36 information notice names a posting. You must show the source behind it. No source means inadequate records, which means an automatic penalty — it doesn’t matter that the figure on the return was right. The principle: every posting must trace back to a source, and every source must survive long enough to be produced.” Open chord
0:13–0:28 Eight source-document tiles. Sales invoice/receipt (green), purchase invoice/payment (red), bank stmt (blue), payroll (purple), expense claim (gold), journal request (purple). Bottom: supporting docs banner. “Eight sources cover almost everything” “The eight principal source documents. Sales invoice and sales receipt: the income side — the invoice creates debtors and sales, the receipt clears the debtor. Purchase invoice and payment receipt: the spend side — the invoice creates the expense and the creditor, the payment clears it. Bank statement: the independent record, the bedrock of the bank rec. Payroll run: wages plus PAYE, plus NI, plus pension. Expense claim with receipts and mileage attached. Journal request — the manual entry, which needs a written reason. And supporting documents, equally important: contracts, engagement letters, loan agreements, insurance policies, HP and lease docs. Every one needs a date, a party, an amount, and where required a valid V A T number.” Rise
0:28–0:43 Retention grid. Eight retention tiles in a 2×4 grid (red, purple, gold, blue, green). Gold callout below: keep the longest. “Five overlapping regimes. Keep the longest.” “Retention periods. Five overlapping statutory regimes. HMRC self-assessment: five years after the thirty-first of January filing. HMRC Corporation Tax: six years from end of accounting period. HMRC V A T: six years from end of V A T period. HMRC P A Y E and payroll: three years after end of tax year. Companies Act 2006: three years for private, six for public, accounting records. Limitation Act 1980: six years for contracts, twelve for deeds. M L R 2017 A M L: five years after the end of the business relationship. U K G D P R: no longer than necessary, you justify. The safe practice: keep the longest of the applicable periods. For most things that’s six years. Document the policy.” Discover
0:43–0:56 MTD card. Top purple panel with the core rule. Then a red “what MTD does NOT do” and green “digital copy is acceptable”. Gold conditions banner. “MTD adds the link — doesn’t remove the source” “Making Tax Digital and digital links. The core requirement: records kept digitally with an unbroken digital link from the source to the V A T return. Re-typing a number into a spreadsheet breaks the chain — bridging software fixes it. What M T D does NOT do: it does not eliminate paper retention obligations, it does not replace original invoices, and it does not override the six-year rules. A digital copy is acceptable: Dext or Receipt Bank scans, PDFs from supplier portals, bank-feed C S V exports. The conditions for a digital copy to count: legible, complete, un-editable once captured, retrievable on demand.” Fixed
0:56–1:10 Five rules. Stacked policy rows: scan at point of receipt, link to ledger, retain longest, off-system backup, written policy reviewed yearly. “A defensible policy in five rules” “A defensible record-keeping policy in five rules. One: scan at the point of receipt. Dext or supplier portal or an email pull — never ‘file later’. Two: link source to posting in the ledger. Xero and Q B O have an attach feature; every line traces to its evidence. Three: retain for the longest applicable period. Default six years; longer for contracts, deeds, and loss claims. Four: back up. An immutable copy off-system, so a bookkeeping platform that fails or revokes access doesn’t take your records with it. Five: a written policy, reviewed annually — Schedule 36, M L R, G D P R, Companies Act — one document mapping each requirement.” Triumph

Learning Objectives

  • Identify each type of source document and the legal basis for retaining it.
  • State the retention periods required by HMRC, the Companies Act and the Limitation Act.
  • Explain how MTD digital-records rules interact with paper sources.

6.1 The principal source documents

Document Originator Posted into
Sales invoice Your business → customer Sales day book → Sales account + Trade Debtors
Sales credit note Your business → customer Sales returns day book
Purchase invoice Supplier → your business Purchase day book → Expense/Asset + Trade Creditors
Purchase credit note Supplier → your business Purchase returns day book
Bank statement Bank Cash book
Cheque counterfoil / paying-in slip Internal Cash book
Petty cash voucher Internal Petty cash book
Expense claim with receipts Employee → company Expense ledger / Director's Loan
Payroll summary (P32 / FPS) Payroll software Wages journal
Loan agreement Lender Loan account + interest expense
HP / lease agreement Lender HP/Lease creditor + asset cost

6.2 What makes a UK VAT invoice valid?

For input VAT to be recoverable, you need a valid VAT invoice from the supplier. Per VAT Regulations 1995 reg.14, a full VAT invoice must contain:

  1. An invoice sequential number
  2. Date of issue
  3. Tax point (time of supply)
  4. Supplier's name, address and VAT registration number
  5. Customer's name and address
  6. Description sufficient to identify the goods/services
  7. Quantity / extent of supply
  8. Unit price (if applicable)
  9. Net amount
  10. VAT rate(s) and amount(s) per rate
  11. Total VAT charged
  12. Gross amount payable

A simplified VAT invoice (used for retail supplies under £250 incl. VAT) needs fewer fields but must show supplier name/VRN, date, description, rate and the gross amount.

6.3 Retention periods

Records Minimum retention Source
Self-employed records 5 years from 31 January following tax year TMA 1970 s.12B
Company tax records 6 years from end of accounting period FA 1998 Sch.18 para.21
VAT records 6 years (or longer for capital goods scheme — 10 years) VATA 1994 Sch.11 para.6
Companies Act records 3 years (private), 6 years (public) CA 2006 s.388
Payroll records 3 years from end of tax year (also 6 years for AML purposes if you are an agent) Income Tax (PAYE) Regs 2003 reg.97
Pension auto-enrolment records 6 years (4 years for opt-out notices) Pensions Act 2008 / TPR guidance
AML client records 5 years from end of business relationship MLR 2017 reg.40
Practical advice

Default to 7 years for everything — it covers all the above and aligns with the Limitation Act 1980 (6 years for contractual claims). With cloud storage near-free, longer retention is the safe choice.

6.4 MTD digital records rules

Under MTD for VAT (and from 2026 onwards, MTD ITSA), records must be kept “digitally” and there must be a “digital link” between every step from source to filed return. Manual re-typing into a spreadsheet between two systems breaks the digital link and is non-compliant. Permitted digital links include:

  • API connections (the gold standard — Xero/QBO/etc. talking directly).
  • CSV import/export between systems.
  • Email of XLS/XLSX files (digital files), where the data is then imported (not retyped).
  • Linked cells within a spreadsheet (cell A1 in sheet 1 = A1 in sheet 2).

Not permitted: rekeying numbers; copy-paste of values (formula loss); transcribing a paper printout into a spreadsheet.

Module 6 — Summary

  • VAT invoice rules (reg.14) determine input tax recoverability.
  • Retention: 5 years SA, 6 years CT/VAT/CA, 7 years for safety.
  • MTD requires digital links throughout the workflow — copy-paste breaks the chain.
Knowledge Check

Q1

FA 1998 Sch.18 para.21. Many practices default to 7 years.
Q2

Without a valid VAT invoice, no input VAT recovery (subject to limited concessions).
Q3

Q4

Q5
