Module 7 · Part 1 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Cash vs Accruals Basis

A sole trader landscaper finishes a £14,000 garden project in March 2025. They invoice on the 28th. The customer pays on the 7th of April. Under cash basis the £14k falls into the 2025/26 tax year (year of receipt). Under accruals basis the £14k is taxable in 2024/25 (year of invoice / earning). Two different tax years, two different tax computations, two different payments-on-account profiles — same single invoice. From 6 April 2024 the rules flipped : cash basis is now the DEFAULT for every unincorporated business, regardless of turnover. The old £150k threshold is gone. The accruals basis — once standard — is now an election OUT. For most very small sole traders that’s fine. For anyone with stock, work-in-progress, large debtors at year-end, capital allowances on big assets, or losses they want to offset against general income — the cash basis can quietly cost them thousands. And if your client is already on accruals and you flip them (or vice versa), the transition adjustments alone can produce a tax shock that wasn’t in any forecast. Limited companies are unaffected — FRS 102 / FRS 105 require accruals, full stop. This module is the two bases properly defined, who can use what after the 2024 reform, the transition adjustments when moving between them, and the “which is better for this specific client?” calculation that should run at every year-end review.

Under cash basis the income is recognised when received — the fourteen thousand falls into the 2025-26 tax year. Under accruals basis, income is recognised when earned — the fourteen thousand falls into 2024-25. Different tax year, different liability, different payments on account, different cash-flow at the 31st of January. Same trader. Same invoice. The basis chosen is what decides when H M R C gets paid.” Open chord

From the 6th of April 2024, cash basis is the default. Accruals is now an opt-out election, and the turnover threshold is gone. Who it applies to: all unincorporated businesses — sole traders and partnerships. Limited companies are unaffected — F R S 105 and F R S 102 still require accruals. L L Ps cannot use cash basis. Stock and W I P heavy: there’s no carry-forward, profit timing becomes lumpy. Large year-end debtors: tax follows the cash, not the earnings. Big capex: capital allowances are restricted under cash. Loss sideways relief: also restricted on cash basis. Interest expense: the old five hundred pound cap was removed in 2024 but check the current position. Volatile income: cash basis distorts profit in big-win years. When cash basis genuinely helps: pure-service sole traders with no stock, no W I P, paid promptly — the bookkeeping is dramatically simpler and the tax answer ties to the bank. Transitional adjustments true-up the gap. Cash to accruals: add opening debtors, deduct opening creditors, plus stock and W I P at year-end. Accruals to cash: reverse opening debtors, reverse opening creditors, and stock is written off per section 226A. And there’s a spreading relief on cash-to-accruals: the positive transitional adjustment can be spread over six tax years, or you elect to accelerate. The spreading cushions the one-off tax shock from picking up previously-deferred income.” Fixed

Five stacked policy rows: current basis, lower-bill, three-year view, transition model, document the decision. “Run the review every year-end” “The year-end review question, for every unincorporated client. One: what basis are they on now? Check the actual return — box 9 or box 10 of S A 103 — not the bookkeeping system. Two: which basis would give a lower tax bill this year? Compute under both, considering debtors, creditors, stock, W I P, capex. Three: what’s the pattern over three years, not just this one? Cash basis can look great this year and cost next — project forward. Four: if switching, model the transition adjustment, the spreading election, the payments-on-account impact, the cash-flow at the 31st of January. Five: document the decision in the file. The conscious choice, not a default that nobody reviewed.” Triumph

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish cash basis from accruals (traditional) basis.
  • Identify which businesses must use accruals and which may use cash.
  • Apply the transition adjustments when moving from cash to accruals (or vice versa).

7.1 The two bases defined

Cash basis: income is recognised when cash is received; expenses are recognised when paid. No debtors, creditors, accruals or prepayments. Easier for the smallest businesses.

Accruals (traditional) basis: income is recognised when earned (invoice raised); expenses recognised when incurred (invoice received), regardless of cash flow. The standard required by FRS 102 / FRS 105 for company accounts and the default for income tax purposes for businesses above the cash basis threshold.

7.2 Cash basis — eligibility (FA 2013, ITTOIA 2005 s.25A onwards)

Until 5 April 2024 the cash basis was elective for sole traders and partnerships with turnover up to £150,000 (must leave at £300,000). From 6 April 2024 the cash basis is the default for all unincorporated businesses; you must elect out if you want accruals. Turnover thresholds were also abolished. This is a major change brought in by the Spring Budget 2024.

Cash basis is not available to: limited companies (must use accruals under FRS); LLPs; partnerships with a corporate partner; farms using herd basis; ministers of religion; managed service companies; Lloyd's underwriters.

7.3 Differences in practice

Item Cash basis Accruals basis
Sales invoice raised but unpaid at year-end Not income — wait for cash Income recognised; debtor created
Supplier invoice received but unpaid at year-end Not yet expense — wait for payment Expense recognised; creditor created
Stock at year-end Generally not adjusted (purchases expensed when paid) Closing stock asset; reduces cost of sales
Capital expenditure Capital allowances available for cars only; other capital items expensed when paid (cash-basis-specific rule) Capitalised; depreciation in P&L; capital allowances for tax
Loan interest Restricted to £500 deduction per year (cash basis cap) Fully deductible on accruals basis
Losses Carried forward only (no sideways relief) Sideways relief available (ITA 2007 s.64)

7.4 Transition adjustments

When moving from cash to accruals (or accruals to cash), a transition adjustment is required to avoid double-counting or non-counting of income and expenses across the changeover (ITTOIA 2005 ss.232–240).

Worked Example 7.1

Sole trader switching from cash to accruals

Year 1 (cash): Sales received £80,000. Year 2 (accruals): At end of Year 1 there were £8,000 of unpaid sales invoices and £3,000 of unpaid supplier invoices.

Transition adjustment in Year 2:

  • Add £8,000 to income (debtors created on transition date — would never have been counted under cash basis).
  • Add £3,000 to expenses (creditors created on transition date).

Net adjustment: +£5,000 added to taxable profit in Year 2 — spread over 6 years if on transition to MTD ITSA.

Module 7 — Summary

  • Cash basis is now the default for unincorporated UK businesses (from 2024/25).
  • Limited companies must use accruals (FRS 102/105 mandate).
  • Transition adjustments under ITTOIA 2005 prevent double-counting on basis change.
Knowledge Check

Module 7 — End-of-Section MCQ (5 questions)

Q1
From 6 April 2024 the cash basis for unincorporated businesses:
Spring Budget 2024 made cash basis the default; election out to accruals is now required.
Q2
A limited company can use the cash basis for tax:
Companies must use accruals basis under FRS standards; the cash basis is unincorporated only.
Q3
Loan interest deductible under the cash basis is capped at:
£500 cap on loan interest under the cash basis.
Q4
Sideways loss relief is available:
Sideways loss relief (ITA 2007 s.64) is restricted to accruals basis. Cash basis losses can only be carried forward.
Q5
A transition from cash to accruals creates an addition to income for:
Without the transition adjustment, those debtors would never be taxed (not received under cash, already invoiced before accruals starts).

Cloud Software Platforms

5 modules · ~12 hours · Dext, Xero, QuickBooks Online, Sage Business Cloud, FreeAgent
Visual mockups in this Part

Each platform module below includes inline software mockups: Dext (capture & publish), Xero (sales invoice, supplier bill, bank reconciliation, manual journal, MTD VAT submission, credit note, recurring invoice), QBO (invoice, bank rule with split), plus payroll software (BrightPay) and TaxCalc (CT600, SA100) appear later when their related tax topics are covered.

Modern UK bookkeeping is impossible without the major cloud platforms. Each module here treats one platform — what it does, who it suits, the day-one setup, the day-to-day workflow, troubleshooting and integrations. We are platform-agnostic: a competent UK bookkeeper should be able to work confidently in any of these.

Module 8 · Part 2 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Dext — Document Capture & Processing

A practice handling 60 SME clients used to spend an estimated two days a week re-typing supplier invoices and stapling receipts to expense claims. After Dext rollout: that drops to two hours. Same accuracy, better audit trail, and an MTD-compliant digital link from the supplier’s PDF to the line in Xero. Dext (formerly Receipt Bank) is the practice-grade document-capture layer that sits BEFORE the bookkeeping platform — it ingests receipts, supplier invoices, bank statements, and credit-card slips through four routes (mobile photo, email-in, drive sync, supplier fetch), runs OCR + machine learning to extract supplier, date, net, VAT, gross, line items, and currency, then publishes to Xero / QBO / Sage with the right account code and VAT rate. The compounding effect is what makes it transformative: every transaction that goes through Dext gets a permanent attached source document in the ledger — so when a Sch 36 notice arrives in 2028, you don’t hunt through a shoebox; you click the line in Xero and the original invoice opens. This module is what Dext is, the four upload routes, supplier rules that learn over time, multi-VAT invoice splits, the publish workflow into Xero/QBO/Sage, and the practice dashboard that lets one person manage 30+ clients without losing anyone.

Learning Objectives

  • Set up a Dext practice and onboard a client.
  • Configure document upload routes (mobile, email-in, drive sync, supplier fetch).
  • Process line-items, supplier rules and multi-VAT invoices.
  • Publish to Xero / QBO / Sage with the correct VAT and account coding.

8.1 What Dext is and why we use it

Dext (formerly Receipt Bank) is a document-capture and pre-accounting platform owned by HG Capital. It ingests source documents (receipts, supplier invoices, bank statements) by mobile photo, email, drive sync or supplier fetch, applies OCR and machine learning to extract data, and pushes the result into the accounting ledger. The value is two-fold: (1) eliminates re-keying — a digital link from source to ledger that satisfies MTD; (2) creates a permanent audit trail attached to each ledger transaction.

In a busy bookkeeping practice, Dext typically handles 70–90% of inbound transactions. The remainder come from bank-feed-only items (e.g. card payments without receipt) and direct supplier integrations (Amazon, eBay).

Dext · Visual Walkthrough

Capture & process a receipt — mobile to ledger in 4 clicks

Steps
  1. Open Dext mobile app → tap Camera
  2. Snap photo (auto-crops; all corners visible)
  3. Upload (auto on Wi-Fi)
  4. On desktop Costs Inbox, Dext has OCR'd the receipt
  5. Review: Supplier, Date, Total, VAT
  6. Assign Account, VAT code, Payment status
  7. Click Publish → posts to Xero/QBO + moves to Archive
Supplier Rules tip

After 3 same-supplier items, click Create Rule — Dext auto-codes future invoices. Review quarterly for drift.

8.2 Practice and client account hierarchy

A Dext Practice account sits above the client accounts. From the Practice dashboard you see all clients, their submission counts, and processing status. Each client account is a separate workspace with its own COA, suppliers, customers and integration. Pricing is per client per month with bands by document volume.

8.2.1 Adding a new client

  1. From the Practice dashboard → Add Client → enter business name and primary contact email.
  2. Choose plan tier (Streamline / Optimise / Advance based on document count).
  3. Connect to the accounting ledger (Xero / QBO / Sage / FreeAgent / Sage 50). The integration creates an OAuth link and pulls the client's COA, supplier list and tax rates.
  4. Set the default VAT rate and the default expense account for new suppliers (typically a holding account such as “Dext to be reviewed”).
  5. Set up upload routes (next section).
  6. Send the client their personalised email-in address and mobile-app login.

8.3 Document upload routes

Route How it works Best for
Mobile app Snap photo → auto-uploads when on Wi-Fi → arrives in Inbox Receipts paid by card on the go
Email-in Each client has unique clientname@dext.com address; forwarded emails (or attachments) are processed PDF supplier invoices arriving by email
Cloud drive sync Connect Google Drive, Dropbox or OneDrive folder; new files auto-import Suppliers who upload to a shared folder
Supplier fetch Dext logs into supplier portals (BT, EE, Amazon, AWS, etc.) and fetches monthly invoices Recurring portal-only suppliers
Web upload / drag-drop Bulk PDF upload from desktop Bookkeeper backfilling old documents

8.4 Processing items in the Inbox

An item arrives in Costs or Sales Inbox. Dext extracts: supplier, date, total, VAT, currency, and (with line-item add-on) individual lines. The bookkeeper then checks: supplier matches an existing supplier in the ledger; expense account is correct; VAT code is correct; project/tracking categories assigned where used; payment status set to Paid (with bank account selected) or Unpaid.

8.4.1 Supplier rules

Once you process a supplier the second or third time, click Create Rule to set: this supplier always codes to X account with Y VAT rate, and (if using auto-publish) push to ledger automatically. Rules slash processing time but require periodic review — a supplier can change its supply mix and break the assumption.

8.4.2 Multi-line items

A typical Amazon invoice contains both VATable goods, zero-rated goods (books) and possibly third-party seller items not yours to recover VAT on. Use the line-item splitter (Optimise/Advance plans) to divide the invoice into rows with separate accounts and VAT codes.

8.5 Publishing to Xero (worked walkthrough)

  1. In Inbox, select the item → review fields → click Publish.
  2. Dext creates a Bill in Xero with: contact = supplier; line item = your coded expense; tax rate = your selected VAT code; reference = Dext item number.
  3. If marked Paid in Dext, Dext also creates the bank payment matched to the bill.
  4. The original receipt PDF is attached to the Bill in Xero (visible in Attachments).
  5. The item moves to Archive in Dext.
Common error — duplicate publishing

If a supplier sends the invoice both by email and uploads to a synced drive, two items can land in Dext. Use the Possible Duplicates filter weekly to catch and merge these before publishing.

8.6 Bank statement processing in Dext

Dext will OCR a PDF/scan of a bank statement, extract transactions, and push to your ledger as a feed. Useful for: closed bank accounts where the live feed has been cancelled; old periods being reconstructed; or accounts with no Open Banking support.

8.7 The Practice Dashboard — managing 30+ clients

Key views: (1) Pending review by client — tells you who needs work; (2) Submission status — who's ahead/behind; (3) Auto-publish health — rules misfiring; (4) Task list — assignable items between team members.

Module 8 — Summary

  • Dext digitises source documents and creates a digital link satisfying MTD.
  • Five upload routes — mobile, email, drive, supplier fetch, web.
  • Supplier rules and line-items dramatically reduce processing time at scale.
  • Publishing creates the Bill (or Sales invoice) with the receipt attached for audit.

Module 9 · Part 2 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Xero — Setup, Reconciliation & Reporting

Xero is the platform UK SMEs and their accountants run on — ~4.4m subscribers globally, dominant in the UK SME segment, the default for any practice taking on a new owner-managed company. The strength isn’t any single feature; it’s how the bank feed, the invoice engine, the multi-VAT scheme support, the tracking categories, and the reporting layer plug into each other so a bookkeeper can close a month in hours, not days. The four buttons every Xero user learns first are Match · Create · Transfer · Discuss on the bank-reconciliation screen — and they are the productivity unlock. Match: the system already found the invoice or bill, click Yes. Create: it’s a new transaction, type the supplier and code. Transfer: it’s a movement between two bank accounts you own. Discuss: you don’t know — flag it, ask the director, come back. Plus the discipline pieces: chart-of-accounts customised to the client’s sector (not Xero’s blank default), lock dates set so closed periods can’t be tampered with, tracking categories handling analysis (jobs, departments, branches) without bloating the COA, and the report pack tailored once and reused monthly. This module is the new-org setup, the bank-reconciliation method, the bill / invoice workflow, lock dates and tracking categories, and the reports that turn Xero into a management-accounting platform — not just a bookkeeping system.

Learning Objectives

  • Set up a new Xero organisation, customised COA and bank feed.
  • Reconcile bank transactions using Match, Create, Transfer and Discuss.
  • Create and send sales invoices and bills, including recurring templates.
  • Use tracking categories and lock dates effectively.
  • Run the Reports (P&L, Balance Sheet, Aged Receivables, Aged Payables, VAT Return).

9.1 Creating a Xero organisation

From your Xero Partner dashboard → My Xero → Add an organisation. Enter:

  • Legal name and trading name
  • Country (UK)
  • Currency (GBP)
  • Industry (sets default COA template)
  • Time zone (London)
  • Financial year end
  • VAT registration status and scheme (Standard / Flat Rate / Cash / Standard with Flat Rate election)
  • Tax basis (accruals or cash)

9.2 Customising the Chart of Accounts

Xero ships a standard 200+ account template. Strip it back to what the client actually needs — an over-large COA fragments postings and obscures reporting. Recommended additions for almost every UK COA:

  • Director's Loan Account (separate per director if multiple)
  • Wages Control Account (clearing for net pay vs PAYE/NI vs pension)
  • Dividends Paid (current year, separate from retained earnings)
  • Sales analysis split by service line
  • Fixed Asset register categories: Office Equipment, Computer Equipment, Plant & Machinery, Motor Vehicles, Leasehold Improvements

9.3 Bank feeds

Xero connects to UK banks via Open Banking (regulated PSD2 connection): Lloyds, HSBC, Barclays, NatWest/RBS, Santander, Starling, Monzo, Tide, Revolut, Wise, etc. Authentication uses Strong Customer Authentication (SCA) requiring re-authorisation every 90 days. Tip: set a calendar reminder for 80 days from connection to re-authenticate before the feed lapses.

9.3.1 Setting up an Open Banking feed

  1. Bank Accounts → Add Bank Account → search for the bank.
  2. Choose Direct Bank Feed (Open Banking) where available.
  3. Authenticate with the client's online banking credentials and SCA.
  4. Select which accounts to share with Xero (current, savings, cards).
  5. Confirm consent for 90 days.
  6. Feed begins to flow — typically backfills 90 days of history.

9.4 Bank reconciliation in Xero

Xero presents each bank statement line on the left and proposes a match on the right. Four actions per line:

  • Match — line matches an existing invoice/bill/payment. Click OK.
  • Create — no existing record; create a new spend/receive money transaction.
  • Transfer — line is movement between two of the client's own bank accounts.
  • Discuss — flag for client/colleague (no posting until resolved).

Bank Rules automate Create for predictable transactions: e.g. “Any line containing ‘TfL Travel’ from this account → spend money to Travel Expenses, VAT N/A”.

Xero · Walkthrough X3

Reconcile a bank line — Match, Create, Transfer or Discuss

The 4 actions per line
  1. Match: line matches an existing invoice/bill → click OK
  2. Create: no existing record → fill Account, Tax, Description → OK
  3. Transfer: between two of client's own accounts
  4. Discuss: flag for client/colleague; no posting until resolved
Bank Rules

Bank Accounts → Bank Rules. Pattern-based auto-fill: e.g. any “TfL Travel” → Spend Money / 471 Travel / VAT N/A / contact TfL.

SCA re-auth Open Banking re-auth every 90 days. Set a calendar alert at day 80.

9.5 Bills and Sales Invoices

Bills (purchase invoices) are created either: (a) manually via Business → Bills to pay → New; (b) via Dext publish (Module 8); (c) imported by CSV; or (d) auto-created by a Hubdoc/scan extension. Sales invoices similarly: manual, recurring templates, or via integrations (e.g. WooCommerce, Shopify).

9.5.1 Recurring sales invoices

Set up under Business → Invoices → New Repeating Invoice: set frequency (weekly, monthly, quarterly), end date, contact, line items. Useful for retainer clients, rental income, subscription billing.

9.6 VAT in Xero

Xero is a recognised MTD-VAT software. The VAT Return view assembles the 9 boxes from posted transactions. To file: Accounting → Reports → VAT Return → period → Submit to HMRC. First-time filing requires HMRC authorisation via your Government Gateway.

Xero · Walkthrough X5

Submit MTD VAT return (Accounting → Reports → VAT Return)

Steps
  1. Accounting → Reports → VAT Return
  2. Pick the period (Q4 1 Jan – 31 Mar)
  3. Review 9 boxes; drill into any unusual figure
  4. Run Exception Report for late-posted items
  5. Reconcile VAT control to Box 5
  6. Click Submit to HMRC
  7. First time: Government Gateway auth (3-year grant)
  8. Save HMRC correlation ID
  9. Hard-lock the VAT period
Always lock after submit Otherwise backdated postings flow into “exceptions” in the next return — easy to miss.

9.7 Lock Dates

Two lock-date levels:

  • All users lock — prevents anyone (including the bookkeeper) backdating before this date.
  • Users without Adviser/Standard role — softer lock the bookkeeper can override.

Set the soft lock at month-end after MI is signed; set the hard lock when accounts are filed.

9.8 Key reports

Report Purpose
Profit & Loss Period income vs expense; comparable to prior period or budget
Balance Sheet Position at a date
Aged Receivables Detail Customer balances split into 30/60/90 day buckets
Aged Payables Detail Supplier equivalent
Bank Reconciliation Report Statement-balance reconciliation for audit/year-end
VAT Return 9-box return ready for MTD submission
Trial Balance For year-end accounts production
Account Transactions Drill-down on a single ledger account for a period

Module 9 — Summary

  • Customise the COA at setup; never inherit the default 200-account template untouched.
  • Use Open Banking feeds and re-authenticate every 90 days.
  • Reconcile via Match/Create/Transfer/Discuss; automate with Bank Rules.
  • Set hard lock dates after filings to protect period integrity.

Q2

Q3

Q4

Q5

Q6

QuickBooks Online (QBO) — Setup & Workflow

Intuit’s UK product runs roughly parallel to Xero in feature coverage and is the better fit for a sizeable minority of UK SMEs — particularly those with inventory, US-facing operations, or owners already familiar with the desktop QuickBooks of a decade ago. The plans ( Simple Start, Essentials, Plus, Advanced) scale from a one-person business to a 25-user operation; the practitioner access is QuickBooks Online Accountant — free with multiple client logins. The thing that surprises Xero migrants: QBO’s Banking screen auto-categorises bank lines from the moment the feed connects, using ML based on payee history across millions of files — so a bookkeeper’s job is often confirm-or-correct rather than code-from-scratch. The mental model is slightly different from Xero too: QBO has classes (1 dimension) and locations (1 dimension) where Xero has 2 tracking categories — same idea, different language. This module is the new-file setup, the Banking screen workflow, Bank Rules with class and location tracking, the Expense vs Bill distinction (cash-out vs accruals), and the MTD VAT submission directly from QBO.

One: company settings — legal entity, company number, address, financial year start, first month V A T period. Two: V A T — scheme, registration date, connect H M R C for M T D submissions. Three: chart of accounts — customise BEFORE the first posting; QBO’s default is even thinner than Xero’s. Four: classes and locations on before the first posting — QBO’s tracking dimensions, which can’t be retro-applied to bank lines later. Five: connect the bank feed via Open Banking, ninety-day consent, pull ninety days of history. Steps three and four before any data lands — or pay the re-classification price later.” Rise
0:28–0:43 Banking screen. Top ‘For Review’ banner. 4 action tiles: Add, Match, Transfer, Exclude. Bank Rules purple panel. “Confirm or correct — not code from scratch” “The Banking screen is the heart of QBO — with the M L engine that surprises Xero migrants. The For-Review row shows the payee QBO has already inferred and the category it proposes, trained across millions of files. Four actions: Add — accept QBO’s guess in one click. Match — an existing record is found, link them. Transfer — movement between owned accounts, never code as expense. Exclude — personal or non-business, never post. And Bank Rules capture the pattern once — money-out plus description contains ‘British Gas’ equals Utilities, V A T standard, Class Office — same line categorises itself every month after.” Discover
0:43–0:56 Expense vs Bill. Two cards, gold rule banner, red common-mistake panel. “If cash has left · Expense. If not · Bill.” “Expense versus Bill. An Expense is cash already out — a card payment, direct debit, standing order — it touches the bank and the expense ledger immediately. A Bill is cash not out yet — it sits in Accounts Payable until cleared by the pay-run. The rule: if cash has left, Expense. If it hasn’t, Bill. Same supplier, same purchase, different ledger story. The common mis-posting that destroys monthly profitability: a Bill paid this month, then ALSO an Expense for the same supplier — double-count. Always look up the bill before adding the bank line.” Fixed
0:56–1:10 VAT submission flow. Five stacked steps: pre-file checks, review 9 boxes, submit, schedule payment, lock date (red). “Submit, pay, lock” “M T D V A T from QBO closes the loop in five steps. One: pre-file checks — bank reconciled, control accounts agreed, V A T exception report run. Two: review the nine boxes — open V A T, check each against expectation, drill into anomalies. Three: submit to H M R C — QBO calls the H M R C A P I, receipt and reference are stored against the return. Four: schedule payment — direct debit if on file, or pay-dot-gov-dot-U K, then reconcile the bank movement against the return. Five: set a lock date — Account and Settings, Advanced, Close the books, lock with a password. The period is now closed — the return on file matches the books, permanently.” Triumph

Learning Objectives

  • Set up a UK QBO file with correct VAT scheme.
  • Use the Banking screen to add transactions efficiently.
  • Create Bank Rules with categorisation and class-tracking.
  • Submit MTD VAT returns from QBO.

10.1 QBO at a glance

Intuit's UK product. Three plan tiers (Simple Start, Essentials, Plus) plus QuickBooks Online Advanced for larger SMEs and QuickBooks Online Accountant for practitioners (free with multiple client logins). Strong on banking automation and inventory; sometimes weaker than Xero on multi-currency and project costing.

10.2 New company file

  1. From QuickBooks Online Accountant → Add client → enter details.
  2. Choose subscription tier (most UK SMEs land on Essentials or Plus).
  3. Set fiscal year end.
  4. Set VAT: registration status, VRN, scheme (Standard / Flat Rate / Cash). VAT scheme can be changed later but not retrospectively.
  5. Enable MTD: Settings → Taxes → set up MTD → connect to HMRC via Government Gateway.
QBO · Walkthrough Q1

Create a sales invoice (+ New → Invoice)

Steps
  1. Click + New in top-left → Invoice
  2. Select Customer (or quick-add)
  3. Choose Terms (Net 30 etc.)
  4. Set Invoice date and Due date
  5. Add Product/Service rows; choose VAT code per line
  6. Save and send
Product/Service setup matters Each P/S item has a default Income Account + VAT Rate. Set correctly once and every invoice posts right.

10.3 Banking and Bank Rules

QBO's banking screen lists each bank line with Suggested categorisation. Click Add to accept; Find Match to pair to an existing invoice or bill; Transfer for inter-account movements. Bank Rules are powerful: condition-based with multiple criteria (description contains, amount range, account, etc.) and can split a single bank line into multiple categories with VAT rates — useful for things like Amazon (some lines standard, some zero-rated).

10.4 VAT in QBO

The VAT Centre (Taxes → VAT) shows current return draft, due dates, and exception items. UK VAT codes:

Code Meaning
20.0% S Standard rate sales/purchases
5.0% R Reduced rate (domestic fuel, energy-saving materials)
0.0% Z Zero-rated (food, books, children's clothes)
Exempt Exempt supplies (insurance, education, healthcare)
No VAT Out of scope (wages, dividends, MOT pass-through)
20.0% RC SG Reverse charge for services (in scope for buyer)
20.0% RC CIS Domestic reverse charge for construction (CIS DRC)

10.5 Reports

Profit and Loss, Balance Sheet, A/R Ageing, A/P Ageing, VAT Liability Report, Transaction Detail by Account, Custom Summary Report. The Custom Summary is QBO's strength: pivot-style report builder for non-standard analysis (e.g. revenue by class × quarter).

Module 10 — Summary

  • QBO is a strong alternative to Xero, particularly for inventory-heavy SMEs.
  • Bank Rules can split a single line and apply different VAT codes — useful for marketplaces.
  • VAT codes follow standard UK structure (S/R/Z/E/No VAT) plus reverse-charge variants.

Module 11 · Part 2 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Sage Business Cloud Accounting

Sage is the legacy heavyweight of UK accounting software — founded in Newcastle in 1981 and dominant in mid-market UK accounting for two decades before Xero and QBO ate the SME segment. Today Sage runs two parallel products an accountant needs to know: Sage Business Cloud Accounting (the modern SaaS replacement for Sage 50, three tiers: Start, Standard, Plus) for the mid-SME, and Sage 50 Cloud (still desktop-installed with cloud sync) for clients with complex stock, multi-company, or legacy data they refuse to migrate off. A typical practitioner runs at least one of each. The strengths: deep functional coverage in stock and manufacturing; strong CIS handling out of the box; the project costing module is closer to ERP than to Xero or QBO; and the practitioner’s portal (Sage for Accountants ) is genuinely good. The weaknesses: the interface is older-feeling, the third-party app ecosystem is thinner than Xero’s, and migrating data off Sage to Xero/QBO is one of the more painful exercises in practice life. This module is the product range, Sage Business Cloud’s setup and bank reconciliation workflow, Sage 50’s desktop heritage and what makes it still preferable for certain clients, MTD-VAT, and the migration trade-off when a client wants to leave.

One: reconcile bank and control accounts — standard close-out discipline from module five. Two: prepare V A T return — V A T menu, Returns, Generate — Sage builds the nine boxes from posted tax codes. Three: review and submit — drill into each box, investigate anomalies, submit via the H M R C A P I. Four: pay by direct debit if on file or via pay-dot-gov-dot-U K, reconcile the outflow against the return reference. Five: close the period — Sage 50 has a hard year-end run, Cloud Accounting uses period lock, either way don’t skip it.” Fixed

Some clients are right on Sage.” “Migrating off Sage is one of the more painful exercises in practice life. What breaks: custom nominal codes, multi-currency historic balances, stock valuations and bill-of-materials links. What works: tools like Movemybooks or Jet Convert; year-end cutover for a clean start; two years history plus an opening trial balance is often the right scope. The parallel-run principle — in the first month after cutover, post into BOTH platforms and reconcile to a single trial balance on both. When the second-month T Bs match, you switch off Sage. Do NOT delete the Sage file. Archive it read-only for six years per the retention rules. And critically — some clients ARE right on Sage. Don’t reflexively migrate — assess the fit.” Triumph

Learning Objectives

  • Recognise where Sage sits in the UK SME market and its product range (Start / Standard / Plus / Sage 50).
  • Process sales invoices, expenses and bank reconciliation in Sage Business Cloud.
  • Submit MTD-VAT.

11.1 Product range

Product Position
Sage Business Cloud Accounting Start Sole trader / micro-business; basic invoicing and bank rec
Sage Business Cloud Accounting Standard Multi-user; full bookkeeping; CIS module
Sage Business Cloud Accounting Plus Adds inventory and multi-currency
Sage 50 Cloud (formerly Sage 50) Desktop product with cloud sync; deep features for £1m+ SMEs
Sage Intacct / Sage X3 Mid-market and enterprise; not in scope here

11.2 Workflow basics

Setup mirrors Xero/QBO — choose VAT scheme, set FY end, build COA. Bank reconciliation is via direct bank feed (Open Banking) with the same Match/Create/Transfer pattern. Sage's strength is CIS — the deductions are calculated automatically and the monthly CIS return submission is built in.

11.3 Sage 50 (the desktop legacy)

Many established UK practices still have clients on Sage 50. Differences from cloud: data lives on the local PC (with optional cloud backup); is more granular but less collaborative; uses tax codes T0–T9 rather than named codes (T1 = standard, T0 = zero, T2 = exempt, T9 = out of scope, T20 = CIS DRC, T21 = CIS DRC zero-rated).

Module 11 — Summary

  • Sage's cloud product is fully MTD-compliant and competitive with Xero/QBO at the SME level.
  • Sage 50 remains widespread in long-established practices; familiarity with T-codes useful.
  • CIS is a Sage strength.

FreeAgent

FreeAgent — Edinburgh-built, owned by NatWest since 2018 — is the platform purpose-built for UK contractors, freelancers, and very small Ltd companies. It’s free to NatWest, Royal Bank of Scotland, Ulster Bank, and Mettle business banking customers (which alone is roughly a million UK SMEs), and a paid subscription for everyone else. The pitch is opinionated: rather than be everything to everyone, FreeAgent strips down to what a one-person business actually needs — time tracking, project costing, invoicing with online payment, expenses with mileage, dividend records, payroll for up to a handful of employees, and the unique-among-the-majors feature: filing the Self Assessment SA100 (for sole traders) and Corporation Tax CT600 (for very small Ltds) directly to HMRC. No TaxCalc. No Iris. No separate filing software. The eligibility is strict — not for groups, not for FRS 102 full, not where complex computations are needed — but for the contractor who’s a director with a single PSC and straightforward results, FreeAgent handles compliance start to finish. The trade-off: limited scalability, thinner reporting than Xero/QBO, no real multi-currency. This module is what FreeAgent is, who it’s for, the integrated SA100/CT600 filing, the bank reconciliation flow, project-and-time tracking, and the upgrade decision point when a client outgrows it.

Learning Objectives

  • Position FreeAgent in the UK market — the contractor & freelancer-focused product.

12.1 What is FreeAgent?

UK-built product (Edinburgh) owned by NatWest. Free to NatWest/RBS/Mettle business banking customers; subscription for others. Targets sole traders, contractors and small Ltd companies. Unique: prepares and files SA100 (sole trader) and CT600 (Ltd) directly to HMRC for users meeting eligibility (small companies only; not for groups, not for FRS 102 full).

12.2 Why a contractor would prefer FreeAgent

  • End-to-end: bank rec → invoicing → expenses → MTD VAT → CT600 → final accounts → SA100 in one platform.
  • Time-tracking and project profitability built in.
  • Tax forecasting — predicts CT and SA liabilities live based on the year-to-date.
  • Director's loan account self-management interface.

12.3 Limitations

  • Not designed for large or complex SMEs — limited multi-user, no class tracking, basic inventory.
  • No FRS 102 full reporting — micro-entity FRS 105 only via the integrated final accounts.
  • Group/consolidation: not supported.

Module 12 — Summary

  • FreeAgent is the natural choice for owner-managed Ltd contractors and sole-trader freelancers.
  • Its built-in SA100 and CT600 modules are unique and remove the need for separate tax software at the small end.
  • Not suitable for complex SMEs — outgrow it at ~£500k turnover or when you add multiple departments.

Part Three

Value Added Tax (VAT)

8 modules · ~18 hours · The most technically complex tax administered by HMRC

VAT is the UK's third-largest tax revenue source (after Income Tax and National Insurance). It is also the area where bookkeepers make the most expensive mistakes — misclassifying a supply, missing a registration trigger, recovering input VAT without entitlement, or breaking the digital link required by Making Tax Digital. Part 3 walks through every dimension: the fundamentals, the alternative schemes, supplies of goods, supplies of services, property, partial exemption, errors and inspections, and MTD compliance.

Module 13 · Part 3 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

VAT Fundamentals — Registration, Rates, Tax Points & Returns

VAT is the UK’s most-administered tax — collected by every registered business on every sale, reclaimed on every input, and reported every quarter. Get it wrong and the penalties stack up faster than for any other tax. The fundamentals every accountant must hold: the four UK rates (20% standard, 5% reduced, 0% zero-rated, exempt — and the difference between “zero” and “exempt” matters enormously); the £90,000 registration threshold (rolling 12-month test PLUS forward look at next 30 days — the two triggers that catch every late registration); the tax point rules that decide which VAT period a supply falls into (basic tax point, actual tax point, advance payments, continuous supplies — not always the invoice date you’d guess); and the 9-box return that ties it all together. Plus: voluntary registration, group registration, de-registration thresholds, retrospective registration when you discover a client missed the trigger, and the difference between a VAT invoice (must contain 9 specific items) and a simplified one. This module is every fundamental that every other VAT module (schemes, place of supply, partial exemption, MTD) builds on.

Reduced at five — fuel and energy, child car seats, certain conversions. Zero-rated at zero — food, books, children’s clothing. And exempt — financial services, education, health, residential rent. The crucial difference: zero-rated supplies are still TAXABLE — no V A T charged on the sale, but you can reclaim input V A T in full, and they count toward the registration threshold. Exempt supplies are out of scope — no V A T charged AND you cannot reclaim related input V A T, AND they don’t count toward the threshold. 0:13–0:28 Threshold + two triggers + voluntary/dereg cards. “Two triggers. One threshold.” “Registration. Trigger one, the backward look: any rolling twelve-month period that exceeds ninety thousand. Register within thirty days of the end of that month. Trigger two, the forward look: the next thirty days alone expected to exceed ninety thousand — register immediately. Voluntary registration is available below the threshold — useful for B2B clients to reclaim input V A T. De-registration threshold is eighty-eight thousand — you can opt out if the fall is expected to be sustained. Late registration triggers backdated V A T, fifteen percent penalty, and interest.” Rise

The basic tax point: goods, the date physically supplied; services, the date performed. The actual tax point overrides the basic when EITHER an invoice is issued within fourteen days of the basic tax point OR a payment is received earlier — whichever is earliest applies. Advance payments: tax point is earlier of receipt or invoice. Continuous supplies: tax point is the V A T invoice or payment date. Worked example. A service delivered on the twenty-eighth of March is the basic tax point. Invoiced on the eighth of April, paid the fifteenth. Invoice within fourteen days, so the actual tax point is the eighth of April — goes into Q2, not Q1. If the invoice had been the eighteenth of April, more than fourteen days, the tax point reverts to the twenty-eighth of March, Q1.” Discover

Box 2: V A T due on N I Protocol acquisitions. Box 3: total V A T due, Box 1 plus Box 2. Box 4: V A T reclaimed on purchases. Box 5 is THE number — net V A T, Box 3 minus Box 4. Positive: you pay H M R C. Negative: H M R C pays you. Box 6: total sales excluding V A T — all supplies including zero-rated. Box 7: total purchases ex V A T. Boxes 8 and 9: N I Protocol dispatches and acquisitions — rarely used outside that specific scope.” Fixed

The deadline: quarter end plus one month plus seven days. A quarter ending the thirty-first of March, file and pay by the seventh of May. M T D is mandatory: digital link from source to box. Late filing and late payment now run on a points system — threshold reached, two hundred pound penalty. A V A T invoice must contain nine items: invoice number, date, supplier name address and V R N, customer name and address, description of goods or services, quantity, unit price, V A T rate per line, plus net, V A T, and gross totals. Missing items mean not a valid V A T invoice — the customer can’t reclaim. Simplified V A T invoices for supplies up to two hundred and fifty pounds use fewer items — the common retail receipt. These are the fundamentals every other module builds on.” Triumph

Learning Objectives

  • State the four VAT rates in the UK and identify supplies that fall in each.
  • Apply the registration thresholds (compulsory and voluntary) and identify the trigger for backwards/forwards registration.
  • Determine the tax point of any supply.
  • Complete a 9-box VAT return from a trial balance.
  • Calculate output and input VAT for any standard scenario.

13.1 What is VAT, conceptually?

VAT is a multi-stage transaction tax on the value added at each link of a supply chain. Each VAT-registered business charges output VAT on its sales, recovers input VAT on its purchases, and pays the net to HMRC. The economic burden falls on the final non-VAT-registered consumer; intermediate businesses are tax collectors, not taxpayers, on each transaction.

Legislative basis: Value Added Tax Act 1994 (VATA 1994); secondary legislation in the VAT Regulations 1995 (SI 1995/2518); HMRC public notices (Notice 700 series) provide interpretation but are not law.

13.2 The four UK VAT rates

Rate Description Examples
20% standard Default rate for almost all supplies Most goods and services; professional services; restaurant meals; clothing for adults; alcohol
5% reduced Specific listed supplies (VATA Sch 7A) Domestic gas/electricity; energy-saving materials; children's car seats; certain conversions of dwellings
0% zero-rated Listed supplies (VATA Sch 8) — taxable, just at 0% Most food (not catering); books, journals, e-books; children's clothing & footwear; new-build residential construction; passenger transport (10+ seat vehicles); newspapers & magazines
Exempt Listed supplies (VATA Sch 9) — outside the scope of VAT charge but block input recovery Insurance; finance (most); education; health & welfare; postal services; betting & gaming; sale of land/buildings unless opted
Zero-rated vs Exempt — the critical difference

Both result in £0 VAT being charged on the sale — but the consequence for input VAT recovery differs. Zero-rated sales are taxable supplies; the supplier can fully recover input VAT on costs incurred to make them. Exempt sales are non-taxable supplies; input VAT on costs to make exempt supplies is blocked (subject to partial-exemption rules — Module 18). A VAT-registered insurance broker recovers no input VAT on its overheads; a VAT-registered children's clothing retailer recovers all of it.

13.2.1 Out of scope (OoS)

A separate concept: the supply isn't made in the UK at all (place of supply is overseas), or it isn't a supply for VAT purposes (wages, dividends, statutory fines). OoS items don't appear in Box 6 of the VAT return at all (in most cases — cross-border services to UK businesses can be reverse-charged into Box 6).

13.3 Registration

13.3.1 Compulsory registration thresholds (2024/25)

£90,000 per rolling 12 months of taxable turnover (raised from £85,000 on 1 April 2024). Two tests:

  1. Historic test — at the end of any month, taxable supplies in the prior 12 months exceed £90,000. Must register within 30 days; effective date is the first day of the month after the breach.
  2. Future test — you reasonably expect taxable turnover in the next 30 days alone to exceed £90,000. Effective date is the start of that 30-day period.

13.3.2 Deregistration threshold

£88,000 (raised from £83,000 on 1 April 2024). Voluntary deregistration available when taxable turnover in next 12 months is reasonably expected to be below £88,000.

13.3.3 Voluntary registration

Available regardless of turnover, including for businesses making zero-rated supplies (often beneficial — can recover input VAT). Not available for businesses making only exempt supplies.

Worked Example 13.1 — Registration date

A consultancy crosses £90,000 cumulative taxable turnover on 18 May 2025 (a single big invoice tipped it over). What is the VAT registration deadline and effective date?

  • Threshold breached at end of May 2025 (historic test).
  • Must notify HMRC by 30 June 2025 (within 30 days of end of breach month).
  • Effective date of registration: 1 July 2025 (first day of second month after breach).
  • From 1 July 2025, must charge output VAT on all standard-rated sales.

13.4 The tax point

The tax point is the date a supply is treated as made for VAT purposes. It determines which VAT return the supply falls into.

Type of supply Basic tax point Actual tax point (overrides)
Goods When goods are removed or made available to the customer Earlier of: invoice issued or payment received (if before basic TP); OR invoice issued within 14 days of basic TP (becomes the actual TP)
Services When the service is performed Same actual TP rules as goods
Continuous services End of each period covered by an invoice Earlier of: invoice issued or payment received
Goods on sale or return Earlier of: customer adopts goods, or 12 months from removal

13.4.1 The 14-day rule (in detail)

For goods or services where invoice is issued within 14 days of the basic tax point, the actual tax point becomes the invoice date. Most businesses invoice within 14 days, so in practice the invoice date is the tax point. If invoice is issued later than 14 days, the basic tax point applies (unless HMRC agrees a longer period).

13.5 The 9-box VAT return

Box Content
Box 1 VAT due on sales and other outputs (output VAT charged)
Box 2 VAT due on acquisitions from EU member states (now NI-only post-Brexit)
Box 3 Total VAT due (Box 1 + Box 2)
Box 4 VAT reclaimed on purchases and other inputs (input VAT recoverable)
Box 5 Net VAT due to HMRC (Box 3 − Box 4) — payable if positive, repayment if negative
Box 6 Total value of sales and all other outputs excluding any VAT (net of VAT)
Box 7 Total value of purchases and all other inputs excluding any VAT (net of VAT)
Box 8 Total value of dispatches of goods to EU member states (NI-only post-Brexit)
Box 9 Total value of acquisitions of goods from EU member states (NI-only post-Brexit)

13.6 Filing & payment deadlines

  • Quarterly returns: filing & payment 1 month and 7 days after the end of the VAT quarter (e.g. Q/E 31 March → 7 May).
  • Monthly returns: same 1m+7d rule (used by repayment traders).
  • Annual Accounting Scheme: one return per year + 9 monthly POAs (Module 14).
  • Payments on Account regime (turnover > £2.3m): monthly POAs based on prior year's liability.

13.7 Output and input VAT calculation basics

Output VAT on a VAT-exclusive price = price × rate. On a VAT-inclusive price = price × (rate / (1 + rate)). For the standard rate, the inclusive multiplier is 20/120 = 1/6.

13.7.1 Input VAT recovery — the four conditions

  1. The business is VAT-registered.
  2. The supply was made to the business (not to the director personally).
  3. The business holds a valid VAT invoice (or HMRC-accepted alternative for amounts below £25 / import documentation).
  4. The supply is used for taxable business purposes.

13.7.2 Blocked input VAT

Block Detail
Cars (purchase) Generally blocked unless used exclusively for business — narrow exception (taxis, driving school, car hire only)
UK client entertainment Fully blocked. Staff entertaining is recoverable
Goods/services for non-business or private use Apportioned
Costs supporting exempt supplies Subject to partial-exemption rules (Module 18)
Margin Scheme goods Input VAT on the goods themselves blocked

Module 13 — Summary

  • Four rates (20%, 5%, 0%, exempt) and the OoS concept.
  • Compulsory registration: £90,000 rolling 12-month taxable turnover (2024/25).
  • Tax point: basic = removal/performance; actual = earlier of invoice/payment, or invoice within 14 days.
  • 9-box VAT return; filing 1m+7d after quarter end.
  • Input VAT recoverable only with all 4 conditions met; specific blocks for cars, client entertainment.
Knowledge Check

Q1

Q2

Q3

Q4

Q5

Module 14 · Part 3 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

VAT Schemes — Standard, Cash, Annual, Flat Rate, Margin, TOMS, Retail

The UK has seven VAT schemes — not one — and choosing the right one for a client’s business can save them thousands a year, or hand HMRC money they need not pay. Most accountants default to Standard accruals because it’s the safe choice; but a service business with no stock can get a working-capital boost from Cash Accounting; a tiny consultancy with low costs can pay less under Flat Rate; a second-hand dealer must use the Margin Scheme or pay VAT on the full sale price they never received as profit; a tour operator uses TOMS; a retail shop uses one of the four retail schemes to deal with thousands of unidentifiable till transactions. Eligibility is strict for each — turnover caps, scheme-specific tests, “limited cost trader” rules for Flat Rate — and the wrong choice is often invisible until the year-end review. This module is each scheme, its eligibility, who it’s right for, and the recommendation framework.

Eligibility: turnover up to one hundred and fifty thousand including V A T at entry; leave when turnover exceeds two hundred and thirty thousand actual. The Limited Cost Trader trap: if goods spend is less than two percent of turnover or less than a thousand a year, you’re FORCED to use sixteen-and-a-half percent — which kills the saving for most service businesses. Recalculate annually. Sample rates: I T consultancy fourteen-and-a-half, management consultancy fourteen, bookkeeping fourteen-and-a-half, hairdressing thirteen, pubs six-and-a-half.” Discover
0:43–0:56 Margin + TOMS + retail schemes. “Mandatory for second-hand, tour, and high-volume retail” “Specialist schemes. Margin Scheme: V A T paid on the margin only, not the full sale price — mandatory for second-hand goods, antiques, art, collectibles, or you over-pay V A T enormously. T O M S, the Tour Operators’ Margin Scheme: travel packages combining bought-in transport, accommodation and so on — V A T on margin only; specialist territory and tour operators usually know they need it. Retail Schemes for thousands-of-till-transactions where you can’t identify the V A T rate per sale — Point of Sale is best where E P O S supports per-line V A T; Apportionment one and two and Direct Calculation one and two for everyone else, chosen by sector profile.” Fixed
0:56–1:10 Five recommendation questions. “Five questions. One scheme.” “Scheme recommendation in five questions. One: what’s the turnover? Above one-point-three-five million: Standard only. Two: how slow do customers pay? Slow means Cash Accounting wins on cashflow. Three: what’s the sector flat rate percentage versus actual input V A T? If the sector percentage saves more than the input V A T you’d reclaim — Flat Rate, unless Limited Cost Trader applies. Four: second-hand goods, art, or tour packages? Mandatory Margin or T O M S, or you over-pay massively. Five: retail volume without per-line V A T? Pick a retail scheme — Point of Sale if E P O S supports it. Five questions. The right scheme. The annual review.” Triumph

Learning Objectives

  • Distinguish the standard scheme from the alternative schemes.
  • Apply eligibility tests for each.
  • Calculate VAT under Flat Rate, Cash, Annual, Margin, TOMS and Retail schemes.
  • Recommend the correct scheme for a given client profile.

14.1 Standard accounting (accruals) scheme

Default scheme. Output VAT accounted for at the tax point of the sale (typically invoice date); input VAT recovered at the tax point of the purchase. Means VAT can be due on a sales invoice before the customer has paid — cashflow burden for businesses with long debtor days.

14.2 Cash Accounting Scheme

Output VAT due when payment received; input VAT recoverable when paid. Solves the cashflow issue. Eligibility: taxable turnover ≤ £1.35m (entry); leave when > £1.6m. Available to most but not for: imports, intra-NI/EU acquisitions, supplies more than 6 months overdue from supplier.

14.3 Annual Accounting Scheme

One annual return + 9 monthly (or 3 quarterly) interim payments based on prior-year liability. Final balancing payment with the return. Same £1.35m / £1.6m thresholds. Combine with Cash Accounting allowed.

14.4 Flat Rate Scheme (FRS)

You charge customers VAT at standard rates but pay HMRC a fixed flat-rate percentage of your VAT-inclusive turnover. You generally cannot reclaim input VAT (except on capital assets >£2,000 single transaction including VAT).

Entry: turnover (excl. VAT) ≤ £150k in next 12 months. Exit: VAT-inclusive turnover > £230k. First-year discount: 1% off published rate.

14.4.1 Limited Cost Trader (LCT) — anti-abuse rule

If goods cost <2% of VAT-inclusive turnover (or <£1,000/yr), the business is an LCT and pays a punitive 16.5% flat rate. Effectively eliminates FRS benefit for labour-only consultancies.

Worked Example 14.1 — FRS LCT

IT consultant, turnover £80,000+VAT (£96,000 incl.). Goods spend £200/year. LCT applies (200 < 2% of 96,000 = 1,920).

Output VAT charged 16,000
Pay HMRC: £96,000 × 16.5% 15,840
Net retained 160 vs. ~40 under standard with no input VAT — marginal

14.5 Margin Schemes

For dealers in second-hand goods, antiques, art, used cars. VAT calculated on the dealer's margin (sale − purchase price). Input VAT on the goods cannot be recovered.

14.6 TOMS — Tour Operators' Margin Scheme

Mandatory for businesses buying in and reselling travel/accommodation/passenger transport bundled as a package. VAT on the margin. Specialist sector.

14.7 Retail Schemes

For shops with mostly cash B2C sales. Variants: Point-of-sale (modern EPOS), Apportionment (mixed-rate till takings split), Direct Calculation. Allow accounting without per-transaction VAT invoices.

14.8 VAT Group Registration (VATA s.43)

Bodies corporate under common control may form a single VAT group (one VRN, one return). Internal supplies disregarded. Joint and several liability among members. Care needed with partially-exempt members.

Module 14 — Summary

  • Cash Accounting (≤£1.35m) helps cashflow when customers slow-pay.
  • Annual Accounting reduces admin — 1 return + interim payments.
  • FRS can save VAT but Limited Cost Trader rules block the benefit for labour-only businesses.
  • Margin, TOMS, Retail schemes for specialised sectors.
  • Group registration for commonly-controlled bodies corporate.
Knowledge Check

Module 14 — End-of-Section MCQ (6 questions)

Q1

Entry £1.35m, exit £1.6m.
Q2
A Limited Cost Trader on FRS pays:
LCT punitive rate effectively eliminates FRS benefit for labour-only.
Q3
Used-car dealer buys £6k, sells £8k. Output VAT under Margin Scheme:
Margin £2,000 × 20/120 = £333.33.
Q4
FRS exit threshold:
£230k VAT-inclusive on anniversary or 12-month rolling.
Q5
VAT group registration is for:
VATA s.43 — bodies corporate under common control.
Q6

Output follows cash receipt; input follows cash payment.
Module 15 · Part 3 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

VAT on Goods — Domestic, Imports, Exports, NI Protocol

Post-Brexit VAT on goods is built around four scenarios with different rules: domestic UK sales (standard tax-point rules); exports from GB to anywhere (zero-rated with proof of export); imports into GB from anywhere (now using Postponed VAT Accounting to avoid the old cash-flow hit); and the Northern Ireland Protocol’s special rules where goods between GB↔NI cross a notional VAT border, and NI↔EU continues to use EU acquisition/dispatch mechanics. Get the export proof wrong and zero-rating is denied retrospectively. Forget to use PVA on imports and the client pays VAT at the border that takes months to reclaim. Treat an NI Protocol acquisition as a normal UK purchase and you mis-state Boxes 2 and 9. This module is the four-scenario map: domestic, exports, imports with PVA, and NI Protocol — with the proofs, EORI numbers, commodity codes, and 9-box treatment that each requires.

Learning Objectives

  • Determine the VAT treatment of goods sold within UK, exported, imported, and moved between GB and NI.
  • Apply Postponed VAT Accounting (PVA) on imports.
  • Treat dispatches and acquisitions of goods to/from EU under the Northern Ireland Protocol.

15.1 Domestic supplies

Charge VAT at the appropriate rate (20%, 5%, 0%) per VATA Sch 8/Sch 7A. Standard tax point rules.

15.2 Exports of goods (UK to outside UK)

Zero-rated (Sch 8 Group 7) provided evidence of export within 3 months of supply. Evidence: shipping documents, courier proof of dispatch outside UK. Without evidence, must treat as standard-rated.

15.3 Imports — Postponed VAT Accounting (PVA)

Default since 1 Jan 2021. Account for import VAT on the VAT return rather than at the border:

  • Box 1: import VAT (output entry)
  • Box 4: same import VAT (input entry, subject to recovery)
  • Box 7: net value of imports

Net cash effect for fully-recovering business: nil. To use PVA, tick on the customs declaration; download monthly Postponed Import VAT Statement (PIVS) from CDS.

15.4 Northern Ireland Protocol — goods only

NI remains in EU VAT system for goods (not services):

  • GB ↔ NI: dispatched FROM GB TO NI generally zero-rated; arrival in NI subject to import VAT (PVA available).
  • NI ↔ EU: continues under EU rules (dispatch zero-rated to EU VAT-registered; acquisition Box 2/Box 9).
  • NI traders' VRN prefix: XI.

15.5 Distance selling B2C to EU consumers

Either: register in each EU member state above their distance-selling threshold; use OSS via NI registration; or use a fiscal representative. Specialist area — refer to a VAT specialist.

Module 15 — Summary

  • Exports zero-rated with proper evidence.
  • Imports use PVA — no cashflow drag for fully-recovering businesses.
  • NI remains in EU VAT for goods; XI VRN prefix.

Module 16 · Part 3 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

VAT on Services — Place of Supply & Reverse Charge

VAT on services lives or dies on one question: where is the place of supply? Because that’s the country whose VAT applies (or whose rules say no VAT at all). The general rule splits B2B and B2C. B2B: place of supply is where the CUSTOMER belongs — so a UK marketing agency invoicing a US client doesn’t charge UK VAT, and a UK SaaS company invoicing an EU business has the EU business reverse-charge it. B2C: place of supply is where the SUPPLIER belongs — so the UK marketing agency invoicing a US individual DOES charge UK VAT. Then there are the special rules: land-related services follow the land, events follow the event, restaurant follows the restaurant, electronic services to B2C consumers follow the consumer (MOSS / OSS rules). And the reverse charge mechanism: where the customer accounts for the VAT instead of the supplier. Includes cross-border services received (DR/CR in both Box 1 and Box 4 = net zero) and the CIS Domestic Reverse Charge for construction. Get place of supply wrong and you either charge VAT you shouldn’t (losing competitiveness, customer disputes) or fail to charge VAT you should (HMRC assessment later). This module is the framework that gets every cross-border service correct.

Cross-border B2B services received: UK reverse charges. CIS Domestic Reverse Charge for construction services between VAT/CIS-registered businesses, not end-user. Invoice must say reverse charge customer to account for VAT.

Learning Objectives

  • Apply general B2B and B2C place-of-supply rules.
  • Identify supplies subject to special POS rules.
  • Apply Reverse Charge for cross-border services received and CIS Domestic Reverse Charge.

16.1 Place of Supply (POS) foundations

Only supplies made in the UK are within UK VAT. POS rules determine where a service is treated as supplied.

  • General B2B: POS = where the customer belongs.
  • General B2C: POS = where the supplier belongs.

16.2 Special POS rules

Service POS
Land-related services Where the land is
Short-term hire of transport Where vehicle put at customer's disposal
Restaurant & catering Where physically performed
Cultural, artistic, sporting (B2C admission) Where carried out
Passenger transport Where transport takes place
Digital services to non-business EU consumers Where consumer is — use OSS

16.3 Reverse Charge — services received from overseas (RCSG)

UK customer self-accounts:

  • Box 1: VAT as if UK supply (e.g. £1,000 × 20% = £200)
  • Box 4: same £200 (subject to recovery)
  • Box 6: net value (£1,000)
  • Box 7: net value (£1,000)

Net cash nil for fully recovering. Mechanism prevents foreign suppliers undercutting UK suppliers by avoiding UK VAT.

16.4 CIS Domestic Reverse Charge (DRC)

From 1 March 2021. Applies when ALL of:

  1. Construction service within CIS scope
  2. Both parties VAT-registered
  3. Customer CIS-registered
  4. Customer NOT the end user

Subcontractor's invoice shows no VAT, with statement “Reverse charge: customer to pay VAT to HMRC”. Customer enters Box 1 + Box 4.

End-user statements

Get written confirmation from customer that they are/are not an end user. Without it, default to applying DRC.

Module 16 — Summary

  • Default B2B services: POS = customer; B2C: POS = supplier.
  • Special rules for land, transport, cultural, digital B2C.
  • Reverse Charge mechanism for cross-border B2B services received.
  • CIS DRC for construction between VAT- and CIS-registered businesses where customer not end user.
Knowledge Check

Q2

Reverse charge: equal Box 1 and Box 4; net cash nil.

Q4

Module 17 · Part 3 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

VAT on Land & Property

Property VAT is where almost every accountant’s first instinct is wrong — because the default is EXEMPT, not standard-rated. New residential builds are zero-rated. Existing residential lettings are exempt. Most commercial property transactions are exempt by default — UNLESS the owner has made an Option to Tax (a binding 20-year election that locks the property at standard rate). The reason a sane person makes that election is they’ve incurred significant VAT on the build/refurb and need to reclaim it — the OTT turns an exempt supply into a taxable one so input VAT can be reclaimed. Plus three more property-specific mechanisms every accountant must hold: the Capital Goods Scheme (10-year adjustment for buildings >£250k); Transfer of a Going Concern (TOGC — sells the property + tenants together at NO VAT, but strict conditions); and DIY housebuilders’ relief. This module is the residential vs commercial split, when OTT helps and when it hurts, CGS adjustments, TOGC mechanics, and the trap of changing a property’s VAT status mid-tenancy.

0:00–0:13 Residential: new build zero-rated, existing letting exempt, CMS conversions 5%. Commercial: default exempt, new builds under 3 years standard 20%, otherwise exempt unless OTT. The trap: exempt means you can’t reclaim input VAT — build a 500k office and lose 100k of input VAT permanently. The remedy is the Option to Tax on commercial property.
0:13–0:28 OTT. Why opt: significant input VAT on build or refurb, B2B tenants who fully reclaim. How: VAT1614A to HMRC within 30 days. For how long: 20-year binding from option date. When OTT is a mistake: B2C consumers, exempt-business tenants, residential conversions — they can’t recover and you push rent 20% higher forever. Six-month cooling-off; mandatory disapplication for residential conversion.
0:28–0:43 Capital Goods Scheme. Land and buildings over 250k acquired or refurbed, computers over 50k on a 5-year scheme. 10-year adjustment: each year measure percent use for taxable supplies vs exempt, adjust input VAT recovery up or down at one-tenth per year. Worked example: 500k building, 100k VAT reclaimed at Year 1 fully taxable. Year 5 use drops to 60%: pay back 100k times 40% times one-tenth equals 4,000.
0:43–0:56 TOGC. Sale of property plus tenants together as a going-concern letting business: no VAT charged on the sale, buyer steps into seller shoes. Conditions: same business continues, no significant break, buyer VAT-registered, and if seller OTT’d the buyer must OTT before completion AND notify seller before transfer. Savings: a 5m commercial sale saves 1m of VAT cash-flow plus the SDLT on the VAT.
0:56–1:10 Property VAT checklist. Residential or commercial? Is there an OTT? Does CGS apply over 250k? Could TOGC apply? Any change of use before completion? Status changes mid-deal blow up OTT, TOGC, and CGS — flag early.

17.1 Default treatment

Land and buildings are exempt by default (VATA Sch 9 Group 1). Exemption blocks input recovery on related costs.

17.2 Residential property

Transaction VAT
Sale or long lease of new dwelling by developer Zero-rated
Renting out residential property Exempt
Construction of new dwelling Zero-rated
Conversion of non-residential to residential 5% reduced
Renovation of empty dwelling (vacant ≥2 years) 5% reduced
Repairs and maintenance to dwellings Standard 20%

17.3 Commercial property

Transaction Default If OTT made
Sale of new commercial (<3 years) Standard 20% n/a
Sale of old commercial (≥3 years) Exempt Standard 20%
Lease of commercial Exempt Standard 20%
Construction of new commercial Standard 20% n/a

17.4 Option to Tax (OTT)

Election that converts a specific commercial property/land from exempt to standard-rated. 20-year lock with 6-month cooling-off and 20-year revocation. Notify HMRC on VAT1614A within 30 days. Used to unlock input VAT recovery on property costs.

Tenant impact: VAT on rent is an irrecoverable cost for partially-exempt or non-VAT-registered tenants (insurance brokers, banks, charities) — reduces achievable rent.

17.5 Capital Goods Scheme — buildings

For commercial buildings/refurbishments >£250k (excl. VAT), input VAT recovery monitored over 10 intervals. Annual adjustment if taxable use percentage changes.

Annual adjustment = (Total input VAT × 1/10) × (Current year's taxable% − Original year's taxable%)

17.6 Transfer of a Going Concern (TOGC)

A sale of a business (or part) as a going concern is OoS for VAT, provided:

  • Assets sold as a business capable of separate operation.
  • Buyer uses them in the same kind of business.
  • If seller VAT-registered, buyer is or becomes VAT-registered immediately.
  • For property: buyer must opt to tax (and notify) before the relevant date.

Module 17 — Summary

  • Property exempt by default with extensive exceptions.
  • OTT converts exempt commercial to standard to unlock input recovery — beware tenant impact.
  • CGS adjusts input recovery over 10 years for property >£250k.
  • TOGC takes a property transfer outside the scope of VAT if conditions met.

Partial Exemption

A business making BOTH taxable AND exempt supplies is partially exempt — and the input VAT it can reclaim is restricted. Input VAT on costs directly attributable to taxable supplies = fully reclaimable. Input VAT directly attributable to exempt supplies = NOT reclaimable. The complication is residual input VAT — rent, utilities, accountancy fees, all the shared costs that can’t be tied to one or the other. That residual VAT gets apportioned using the Standard Method (taxable supplies % of total supplies). Plus the de minimis tests — if exempt input VAT is less than £625/month AND less than 50% of total input VAT, you can reclaim it all anyway. And the annual adjustment — recompute on annual figures at year-end to true up quarterly approximations. Get this wrong and you over-claim (HMRC assessment + penalty) or under-claim (free money to HMRC). This module is the framework that every accountant for a property landlord, charity, financial services business, or healthcare provider must run.

0:00–0:13 Fully taxable: reclaim all input VAT, no PE issue. Mixed taxable and exempt: input VAT recovery restricted — the PE calculation kicks in. Classic businesses: charities, property landlords with mixed portfolios, education with commercial training, healthcare with retail. The trap is treating it as fully taxable — HMRC catches the over-claim at inspection.
0:13–0:28 Three types of input VAT. T directly attributable to taxable: reclaim in full. E directly attributable to exempt: not reclaimable. R residual or overhead: apportion using Standard Method. Step one of every PE return: split every input VAT line into T, E, or R.
0:28–0:43 Standard Method formula: taxable supplies divided by total supplies, round up to nearest whole percent. Worked example: 180k taxable, 60k exempt, 240k total, 75%. Residual input VAT 12k, reclaim 9k. Special methods require HMRC approval — don’t invent your own.
0:43–0:56 De minimis: if BOTH tests met, reclaim everything even on exempt input. Test 1: exempt input VAT 625 a month or less. Test 2: exempt input VAT 50% or less of total input VAT. Common error: pass on period basis but fail annual → clawback.
0:56–1:10 Annual adjustment: quarterly percentages vary, the annual figures give the true ratio. Re-calculate, recheck de minimis on the annual, adjust difference on the next return after year-end. Keep the T/E/R schedule, the Standard Method calculation, the de minimis tests, and the annual adjustment.

18.1 Partial-exemption principle

A business making both taxable and exempt supplies cannot recover all input VAT. Direct attribution + residual apportionment.

18.2 The Standard Method (Reg 101)

  1. Direct attribution: assign each input to taxable / exempt / residual.
  2. Recovery percentage on residual = Taxable supplies (excl. VAT) / Total supplies (excl. VAT) × 100, rounded UP to nearest whole percent (unless residual VAT > £400k/month).
  3. Recover: directly-attributable taxable + (residual × recovery%).

18.3 De minimis

If total exempt input VAT (direct + share of residual) is below de minimis, all exempt input VAT becomes recoverable. Test: exempt input VAT ≤ £625/month average AND ≤ 50% of total input VAT.

18.4 Annual Adjustment

Quarterly recovery uses provisional ratios; annual adjustment recalculates using full-year figures and adjusts in the next return after year-end.

Worked Example 18.1 — PE calculation

Period: taxable supplies £400k; exempt supplies £100k. Input VAT: directly taxable £30k; directly exempt £5k; residual £20k.

Recovery% = 400 / 500 = 80%.

Recovery = £30k + £20k × 80% = £46k. Blocked = £5k + £4k = £9k. De minimis: £9k > £625 × 3 months = £1,875 → fails. £9k blocked.

Module 18 — Summary

  • Direct attribution + residual apportionment by taxable/total.
  • De minimis allows full recovery if exempt input VAT is small.
  • Annual adjustment reconciles year's quarterly provisionals.

Module 19 · Part 3 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

VAT Errors, Inspections & Penalties

When you discover a VAT error six months after the return was filed, the question every accountant asks is: can I correct it on the next return, or do I have to disclose separately? The answer comes down to two thresholds — £10,000 net error (or up to 1% of Box 6 turnover, capped at £50,000) can be corrected on the next return; above that, mandatory disclosure on VAT652. And the new penalty regime since January 2023 changed the whole calculus — it’s now a points-based system: each late filing is a point, hit the threshold for your filing frequency (4 quarterly / 5 monthly / 2 annual) and a fixed £200 penalty bites, then every subsequent late submission is another £200 until points expire. Plus separate late-payment penalties — 2% at day 16, another 2% at day 31, then 4% annualised daily. The carry-over to a VAT inspection: HMRC turns up, picks a quarter, and tests every box against the underlying records. Behaviour-based penalties (no error / careless / deliberate / deliberate-and-concealed) follow at 30/70/100% of the under-paid tax. This module is the error thresholds, the points-based penalty system, the late-payment scaling, and how to manage a VAT inspection.

0:00–0:13 Method 1: adjust on next return if error 10k or less, OR up to 1% of Box 6 capped at 50k. Method 2: VAT652 separate notification for larger errors and any deliberate error. Time limit 4 years from end of period, 20 years if deliberate with concealment. Uncorrected error means assessment plus penalty plus interest.
0:13–0:28 Late filing: points system since 2023. Each late return is a point. Threshold: annual 2 points, quarterly 4, monthly 5. Hit threshold = 200 pound penalty plus 200 per subsequent late return. Points expire after 24 months of compliance. File even if you cannot pay — that’s the late-payment regime separately.
0:28–0:43 Late payment scaling. Days 1-15: no penalty if you pay or agree TTP. Day 16: 2% on unpaid. Day 31: additional 2%. Day 31 onwards: 4% annualised daily until paid. Plus late-payment interest at Bank Rate plus 2.5% daily, separate from penalty.
0:43–0:56 Behaviour-based error penalties. Reasonable care: no penalty. Careless: 0 to 30. Deliberate: 20 to 70. Deliberate plus concealed: 30 to 100. Unprompted disclosure pushes you to the bottom end of each range. Inspection etiquette: be present, engagement letter scope, document, ID-check the inspector.
0:56–1:10 Inspection process. Notice usually 7 days. Preparation: pre-check, brief client, line up docs. Visit: sample testing, judgement questions, keep minutes. Follow-up queries: respond in time, push back where wrong. Settlement or appeal: negotiate behaviour categorisation, ADR, FTT if needed.

19.1 Error correction thresholds

  • Net error ≤ £10,000: correct on next return (Box 1 or Box 4 adjustment).
  • Net error £10k–£50k or 1% of Box 6 (greater): can still be corrected on next return.
  • Net error > £50k or 1% of Box 6: report on form VAT652.
  • Deliberate errors: VAT652 always.

19.2 Points-based penalty regime (post Jan 2023)

  • Late submission: 1 point per missed deadline. Threshold (4 quarterly / 5 monthly / 2 annual) → £200 penalty + £200 each subsequent miss.
  • Late payment: 0–15 days nil; 16–30 days 3%; 31+ days 6% + daily 10% pa.
  • Late payment interest: BoE base rate + 2.5% from due date.

19.3 VAT inspections

HMRC selects on risk profile, random sample or intelligence. Typically 7 days notice. Reviews VAT control reconciliation, sample of sales/purchase invoices, treatment of cars/entertainment/property, apportionment workings.

Practitioner advice

Always attend the inspection with the client. Pre-inspection: review last 4 returns, identify any “known issues” first, brief client on what to say.

Module 19 — Summary

  • Errors ≤ £10k correctable on next return; larger or deliberate via VAT652.
  • Points-based late penalty regime since Jan 2023.
  • Inspections require active practitioner management.
Knowledge Check

Q1

Net errors ≤ £10k correctable on next return.
Q2
Late submission penalty at 4 points (quarterly):
£200 fixed at threshold + £200 each subsequent miss.
Q3
Late VAT payment 16–30 days late:
3% if 16–30 days; second 3% from day 31; daily charges thereafter.
Q4

Deliberate errors always require VAT652; behavioural penalties under FA 2007 Sch 24 also apply.
Module 20 · Part 3 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Making Tax Digital for VAT

Making Tax Digital for VAT — live for everyone VAT-registered since April 2022 — is two technical requirements packaged as one regime: records kept in digital form, and an unbroken digital link from source to the figure that lands in each of the 9 boxes on the return. A digital record includes the supply’s date, value, and VAT rate, kept in “functional compatible software.” A digital link is automated data transfer between software — including bridging software for users whose underlying records still live in spreadsheets. Re-typing a number across systems breaks the link. Cut and paste breaks it too (technically). XML, CSV import/export, API calls all preserve it. The compliance penalty isn’t huge per-incident but it can be assessed alongside any other VAT penalty and adds up. This module is the scope, the “functional compatible software” definition, the bridging-software workaround for legacy spreadsheet users, what counts as a digital link, the soft-landing periods (now closed), and the practical compliance check every accountant should run on each client’s VAT workflow.
