20.1 Scope

From 1 April 2022, all VAT-registered businesses (regardless of turnover) must comply with MTD VAT. Limited exemption for digital exclusion.

20.2 Digital records required

  • Designatory data (name, address, VRN, scheme).
  • Adjustments under FRS, partial exemption etc.
  • For each output supply: time, value, rate.
  • For each input supply: time, value, VAT recoverable.
  • Daily Gross Takings (retail scheme).

20.3 Digital links — the chain

Permitted: API connections; CSV/XML/XLS/XLSX export-import; linked cells in workbook; emailed file then imported.

NOT permitted: re-typing; copy-paste of values; transcribing printouts.

20.4 Bridging software

For spreadsheet users (Avalara, BX, VitalTax, Easy MTD VAT). Takes the 9 boxes from a workbook and submits via MTD API.

20.5 Penalties

Non-MTD compliance: up to £15/day plus standard late penalty regime.

Module 20 — Summary

  • All VAT-registered businesses in scope of MTD-VAT.
  • Digital records of designatory data, supplies and adjustments.
  • Digital links throughout — re-keying breaks compliance.
  • Bridging software keeps spreadsheet users compliant.

Module 21 · Part 4 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

PAYE Fundamentals — Tax Codes, NI Categories & RTI

Run payroll for a UK employer and you’re acting as HMRC’s unpaid tax collector: collect Income Tax via PAYE, collect employee National Insurance, pay employer NI on top, file the FPS the moment payment hits the employee’s bank, pay HMRC by the 22nd, and reconcile to a paying-account that runs in real-time. Every error has a 4-week feedback loop — HMRC’s next payroll-month statement shows the discrepancy and the underpayment notice arrives. The fundamentals every payroll-running accountant must hold: tax codes (the language HMRC uses to tell you how much to deduct — 1257L, BR, NT, K codes, S/C prefixes for Scottish/Welsh, week 1/month 1 emergency codes); NI categories (A is the default for working-age employee, H for apprentices under 25, M for under-21s, V for veterans, F for freeport, J for deferred, plus the four primary letters and three contracted-out states); RTI submissions (FPS on or before each payment, EPS for adjustments and CIS recovery); and the £5,000 Employment Allowance, which most one-director companies CAN’T claim. This module is each of those, the schedule of statutory dates, the EPS-vs-FPS distinction every newly-qualified bookkeeper gets wrong, and the recovery process when HMRC’s figures disagree with yours.

0:00–0:13 Tax codes are HMRC’s instructions to your payroll. 1257L is the standard 24/25 code with the £12,570 allowance. BR is basic rate for second jobs. D0 and D1 are higher and additional rate. NT means no tax for non-residents. K codes are negative allowances where BIK exceeds the allowance. S and C prefixes for Scotland and Wales. Emergency week-1 month-1 codes apply allowance for this period only, no cumulative reconciliation — stay on these too long and the employee gets a year-end bill.
0:13–0:28 NI categories. A is the default for most employees. H is apprentices under 25 with employer NI free up to the upper apprentice limit. M is under-21s with employer NI free up to the upper apprentice limit. V is veterans, first 12 months, employer NI free. Freeport letters F, I, S, L give employer NI relief up to the freeport limit. J is deferred employee NI for multi-job employees. The wrong letter on a 24-year-old apprentice costs the employer thousands of pounds a year.
0:28–0:43 RTI submissions. FPS, the Full Payment Submission, goes ON OR BEFORE every payment, per employee, reporting pay, tax, NI, pension. EPS, the Employer Payment Summary, goes by the 19th of the following month for adjustments — CIS recoveries, statutory pay reclaim. Late FPS triggers the penalty regime. Nil month? Send a no-payment-due EPS or HMRC chases.
0:43–0:56 Employment Allowance up to £5,000 off employer NI per year, claimed via EPS. Excluded: sole director PSCs and employers whose prior-year employer NI exceeded £100,000. Eligible: companies with two-plus directors or one director plus an employee on payroll. Requires the de minimis state aid declaration with sector since 2020. Claim from month 1 and it auto-applies.
0:56–1:10 The monthly cycle. Pay day, FPS before or on. 19th of following month, EPS deadline if any adjustments. 22nd, pay HMRC the PAYE plus NI plus student loan, less EPS recoveries. Reconcile to the HMRC Gateway account immediately. Year end on the week ending 5 April: final FPS, P60s to employees by 31 May. Module 25 covers year-end in detail.

21.1 PAYE in one paragraph

Pay As You Earn is the system by which employers deduct Income Tax and National Insurance from employees' wages and pay them to HMRC each month. Legal basis: Income Tax (PAYE) Regulations 2003 (SI 2003/2682) and the Social Security Contributions & Benefits Act 1992. Since 2013, RTI requires employers to report each pay event on or before the date payment is made.

21.2 Setting up a PAYE scheme

Register at gov.uk/register-employer. HMRC issues:

  • Employer PAYE reference (e.g. 123/AB45678)
  • Accounts Office reference (13 character, e.g. 123PA00012345)

Both required for RTI submissions and for employees' P60s/P45s. Allow 5 working days for issuance.

21.3 Tax codes (2024/25)

A tax code tells the employer how much tax-free pay an employee gets. Standard code 1257L = £12,570 PA.

Suffix / Prefix Meaning
L Standard PA
M Receiving 10% of partner's PA (Marriage Allowance recipient)
N Transferring 10% of own PA to partner
T Tax code includes adjustments — call HMRC if details needed
K (prefix) Negative allowance — additions to taxable pay (e.g. K475 means add £4,750 to taxable pay/year)
BR Basic Rate (20% on all earnings) — usually a 2nd job
D0 Higher Rate (40% on all)
D1 Additional Rate (45% on all)
NT No Tax
0T No PA — emergency or new starter without P45
S prefix Scottish taxpayer — Scottish rates apply
C prefix Welsh taxpayer (Welsh rates currently match English)

21.3.1 Cumulative vs Week 1/Month 1

Cumulative basis: tax on cumulative pay vs cumulative free pay. New starters or mid-year code changes may be put on W1/M1 (non-cumulative) until the next P6 from HMRC.

21.4 National Insurance — categories & rates 2024/25

Class 1 NI is split between employee (primary) and employer (secondary).

Category Who Primary (EE) Secondary (ER)
A Standard adult employee 8% / 2% 13.8%
C Over State Pension age 0% 13.8%
H Apprentice under 25 8% / 2% 0% up to UEL
J Deferring NI (multiple jobs) 2% / 2% 13.8%
M Under 21 8% / 2% 0% up to UEL
V Veteran in first year of civilian employment 8% / 2% 0% up to UEL
Z Under 21 deferring 2% / 2% 0% up to UEL

21.4.1 NI thresholds (2024/25)

Threshold Weekly Monthly Annual
Lower Earnings Limit (LEL) £123 £533 £6,396
Primary Threshold (PT) £242 £1,048 £12,570
Secondary Threshold (ST) £175 £758 £9,100
Upper Earnings Limit (UEL) £967 £4,189 £50,270
2025/26 — Employer NI changes

From 6 April 2025: Secondary Threshold drops to £5,000; Employer NI rises to 15%; Employer's Allowance rises to £10,500 with the £100k payroll cap removed. Re-model salary/dividend mix.

21.5 Employer's Allowance

Reduces ER Class 1 NI bill by up to £5,000 per tax year (2024/25). Eligibility:

  • Business or charity (not most public-sector).
  • 2024/25: prior year secondary NI bill ≤ £100k (cap removed from 2025/26).
  • NOT available for sole-director Ltd with no other employees above ST.
  • Connected employers share one EA.

21.6 Real Time Information (RTI)

  • FPS: on or before each pay date. Pay, tax, NI, NI category, YTD totals.
  • EPS: monthly for adjustments — statutory recoveries (SMP/SPP/etc.), Apprenticeship Levy, EA claim, no-payment flag.

21.7 Apprenticeship Levy

0.5% of pay bill for employers with annual pay bill > £3m, less £15,000 levy allowance.

Module 22 · Part 4 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Statutory Payments — SSP, SMP, SPP, ShPP, SAP, SPBP

When an employee goes off sick, becomes a parent, or loses a baby, the employer must pay statutory amounts — and can reclaim most of them. The six are: SSP (statutory sick pay, NOT reclaimable), SMP (maternity), SPP (paternity), ShPP (shared parental), SAP (adoption), SPBP (parental bereavement). Get any wrong and the employee either gets less than they’re entitled to (HR claim) or you over-pay and can’t reclaim from HMRC. The Small Employers’ Relief (Class 1 NI ≤ £45k previous year) lets you recover 103% of paid statutory pay (the bonus 3% covers your employer NI on it). Standard employers reclaim 92%. SSP is NOT reclaimable since 2014 — that’s an unrecoverable cost. The qualifying days for SSP, the qualifying week for SMP, the 26-week service requirement, and the SPP/ShPP/SAP windows are all eligibility tests an accountant must apply. This module is each payment’s trigger, rate, eligibility, qualifying period, and EPS recovery process.

0:00–0:13 Six statutory payments. SSP, sick pay, NOT recoverable since 2014. SMP maternity, SPP paternity, ShPP shared parental, SAP adoption, SPBP bereavement — all recoverable. Standard 92%, Small Employers’ Relief 103% if prior-year Class 1 NI 45k or less. Recovery happens via EPS.
0:13–0:28 SSP. £116.75 per week, max 28 weeks, paid from day 4. Earnings threshold £123 per week. First 3 qualifying days are waiting days unpaid. PIWs within 8 weeks link, no new waiting days. At 28 weeks issue SSP1 so the employee can claim ESA.
0:28–0:43 SMP. First 6 weeks at 90% AWE, then 33 weeks at the lower of £184.03 or 90% AWE. Qualifying week is the 15th week before EWC. 26 weeks service by end of QW, AWE at least LEL. Documentation: MATB1, 28 days notice, SMP1 if not eligible. Reclaim on EPS at 92% or 103%.
0:43–0:56 SPP: 1 or 2 weeks at £184.03 or 90% AWE if lower, 26 weeks service. ShPP: up to 37 weeks, parents share remaining maternity leave. SAP mirrors SMP exactly. SPBP: 2 weeks on loss of child under 18 or stillbirth from 24 weeks, no service requirement for leave.
0:56–1:10 EPS recovery in five steps. Pay statutory amount in payroll, treated as gross pay. File EPS by 19th with recovery figures. Pay HMRC the net — PAYE plus NI less recovery. Confirm SER status annually based on prior-year Class 1 NI. Keep evidence: MATB1, SSP records, SC3, SC7 for 6 years.

22.1 Overview

Payment Trigger Rate (2024/25) Recoverable?
SSP Sick ≥4 days £116.75/wk × max 28wks No
SMP Pregnancy 6wks × 90% pay; 33wks × £184.03 (or 90% if lower) 92% (103% via Small Employers' Relief if Class 1 NI ≤£45k)
SPP Birth/adoption partner 1 or 2wks × £184.03 (or 90% if lower) 92% / 103%
ShPP Shared parental Up to 37wks × £184.03 92% / 103%
SAP Adoption 6wks × 90%; 33wks × £184.03 92% / 103%
SPBP Loss of child <18 2wks × £184.03 92% / 103%

22.2 SSP detail

Eligibility: AWE ≥ £123/week. Sick 4+ days in a row (incl. non-working days). First 3 days = waiting days (unpaid SSP) unless linked to a previous SSP period within 8 weeks. Max 28 weeks.

22.3 SMP detail

Eligibility: 26 weeks continuous service ending with the 15th week before EWC; AWE ≥ £123 in 8-week period ending 15 weeks before EWC. MATB1 from midwife = evidence. Recovery: 92% standard; 103% Small Employers' Relief.

22.4 EPS recovery

Payroll software calculates and shows on FPS. EPS Box 11/12 claims recovery monthly, reducing the PAYE bill paid to HMRC.

Module 22 — Summary

  • SSP not recoverable (since 2014).
  • Family payments: 92% standard; 103% via SER (Class 1 NI ≤£45k).
  • SMP eligibility: 26 weeks service + AWE ≥ LEL.

Auto-Enrolment Pensions

Pensions Act 2008 made workplace pensions mandatory for every UK employer with at least one worker. Every employee is categorised on each pay date (eligible / non-eligible / entitled) and the employer must enrol the eligible ones into a qualifying scheme (NEST, NOW, The People’s Pension, or one a sponsor sets up), pay at least 3% employer contribution, deduct at least 5% employee contribution from qualifying earnings, and run a re-enrolment cycle every 3 years for anyone who’s opted out. Default the obligations and The Pensions Regulator’s fines start at £400 fixed and climb to £10,000 per day for serious or persistent non-compliance. Add: postponement (up to 3 months), salary sacrifice (saves employer NI and employee NI/tax), and the Declaration of Compliance to TPR within 5 months of duties start date. This module is the eligibility test (age + earnings), the contribution split, postponement mechanics, re-enrolment, salary sacrifice trade-offs, and the TPR Declaration of Compliance every employer must file.

0:00–0:13 Three worker categories assessed every pay date. Eligible jobholder: age 22 to State Pension Age, earnings 10k or more, auto-enrol with opt-out allowed. Non-eligible jobholder: age 16-21 or SPA-74, OR earnings 6,240-10,000, can opt in and employer must contribute. Entitled worker: any age 16-74, earnings under 6,240, can request to join but no employer contribution required. Check every pay date — payroll software does it automatically.
0:13–0:28 Contributions on qualifying earnings, the band from 6,240 to 50,270. Employer minimum 3%. Employee minimum 5%. Total 8%, made up of employer 3, employee 4 net, basic-rate tax relief 1. Employer can pay more — many SMEs voluntarily go 5% to total 10%.
0:28–0:43 Postponement delays assessment and enrolment for individual workers up to 3 months — useful for probationers and variable earners. Written notice within 6 weeks of postponement start. Employee can opt in during postponement and cancel the delay. Re-enrolment every 3 years — previously opted-out workers reassessed and re-enrolled, then a re-declaration to TPR within 5 months.
0:43–0:56 Salary sacrifice: employee gives up gross salary for employer pension contribution. Employee saves NI and PAYE; employer saves Class 1 NI at 13.8% on the sacrificed amount, often shared back. Don’t break NMW — post-sacrifice pay must not drop below the National Minimum Wage. Formal agreement, minimum 12-month commitment.
0:56–1:10 TPR compliance. Duties start date is the first day with at least one worker. Choose scheme: NEST default, People’s Pension, NOW, Smart, or sponsor scheme. Declaration of Compliance to TPR within 5 months, re-declare every 3 years at re-enrolment. Records kept 6 years. Penalties: 400 fixed escalating to 10,000 per day for persistent default.

23.1 The duty

Pensions Act 2008. Every employer must auto-enrol every “eligible jobholder” into a qualifying pension scheme. Failure: TPR fines from £400 fixed up to £10k/day.

23.2 Worker categories

Category Age Earnings Action
Eligible jobholder 22–SPA ≥£10,000/yr Auto-enrol
Non-eligible jobholder 16–21 or SPA–74 >LEL but <£10,000 Right to opt in; ER must contribute
Non-eligible jobholder 22–SPA ≥LEL but <£10,000 Right to opt in
Entitled worker 16–74 ≤LEL Right to join (no ER contribution)

23.3 Minimum contributions on qualifying earnings

Qualifying earnings band 2024/25: £6,240 to £50,270. Total minimum 8%: ER 3% + EE 5% (incl. tax relief).

Worked Example 23.1 — AE on £30k

QE: £30,000 − £6,240 = £23,760. Total contribution 8% × £23,760 = £1,900.80. ER £712.80; EE £1,188.

23.4 Cyclical compliance

  • Initial declaration of compliance within 5 months of duties start date.
  • Postponement up to 3 months allowed.
  • Triennial re-enrolment of opt-outs.
  • Re-declaration within 5 months of each re-enrolment date.

Module 23 — Summary

  • Eligible jobholders: 22–SPA earning ≥ £10k/year.
  • Total contribution 8% of QE; ER 3%, EE 5%.
  • Triennial re-enrolment + re-declaration of compliance to TPR.

Benefits in Kind & P11D Reporting

A benefit in kind is any non-cash advantage the employer provides “by reason of employment” — from a company car, to private medical, to a mobile phone that’s used personally. BIKs are taxable on the employee under ITEPA 2003 and trigger Class 1A NI on the employer (13.8% for 2024/25, rising to 15% in 2025/26). The annual reporting vehicle is the P11D — one per employee, filed by 6 July following the tax year, with the matching P11D(b) for the employer’s Class 1A liability. Common benefits each have their own valuation rule: company car uses list price × CO₂-based appropriate percentage, private medical uses cost to employer, fuel for private use uses the fuel multiplier × CO₂ %. Two efficiencies the accountant must surface: trivial benefits (£50 or less per event, certain conditions) escape charge entirely; and payrolling BIKs — tax the cash value through PAYE in real time, no P11D needed (P11D(b) still required for Class 1A). The optional choice becomes mandatory for most BIKs from April 2027. This module is the major BIKs, their valuation rules, the P11D/P11D(b) filing process, trivial-benefits & exempt-benefits maps, and the payrolling pivot.

Can’t payroll living accommodation or beneficial loans yet. Mandatory for all BIKs from April 2027 (announced 2024) — migrate clients now.

24.1 What is a BIK?

Non-cash benefit by reason of employment. Taxable on EE under ITEPA 2003; Class 1A NI on ER (13.8% in 2024/25; 15% from 2025/26). Trivial benefits (£50 or under) and certain exempt benefits escape charge.

24.2 Common benefits

Benefit Cash equivalent
Company car List price × CO₂-based AP
Free fuel for company car £27,800 (2024/25) × CO₂-based AP
Beneficial loan > £10,000 (Loan × HMRC official rate 2.25%) − interest paid
Living accommodation Annual value (or rent if higher) + interest charge if cost > £75k
Private medical insurance Cost to ER
Gym membership Cost to ER
Vouchers (non-cash) Cost to ER
Trivial benefit (≤£50, not cash, not contractual) Exempt

24.3 Company car AP table

CO₂ g/km 2024/25 AP (petrol)
0 (electric) 2%
1–50 (varies by EV range) 2–14%
51–54 15%
...incrementing 1% per 5g/km...
170+ 37% (cap)

Diesel non-RDE2: +4% surcharge (capped 37%). RDE2 diesels: no surcharge.

Worked Example 24.1

BMW 320d (RDE2) £40,000, 130 g/km, AP 30%. CE = £12,000. EE higher-rate tax £4,800. ER Class 1A £1,656.

Tesla Model 3 £40,000, 0 g/km, AP 2%. CE = £800. EE tax £320. ER NI £110. Saves ~£5,400.

24.4 Payrolling vs P11D

  • P11D: by 6 July file P11D per EE; P11D(b) for total Class 1A NI; pay Class 1A by 22 July.
  • Payrolled benefits: register before tax year start; tax collected through PAYE in real time. Still file P11D(b) for Class 1A. Mandatory from April 2026 for most BIK.

24.5 PAYE Settlement Agreement (PSA)

For minor / irregular / impracticable items. ER pays grossed-up tax + Class 1B NI. Application by 5 July following tax year; payment by 22 October.

Module 24 — Summary

  • BIK taxed on EE; ER pays Class 1A NI.
  • Company car CE = list price × CO₂ AP. Electric on 2% saves thousands.
  • Trivial ≤£50, mobile, workplace parking exempt.
  • P11D 6 Jul, Class 1A 22 Jul; payrolling mandatory from April 2026.

Module 25 · Part 4 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Year-End Payroll Process

Payroll year-end is the most date-driven event in the accountant’s calendar: five hard deadlines stacked across 12 weeks, each carrying its own penalty if missed. The tax year ends 5 April. Then: final FPS for the year must be marked “Final submission for tax year”; P60 to every employee on payroll at year-end by 31 May; P11D + P11D(b) for every employee with BIKs by 6 July; Class 1A NI paid by 22 July; final EPS if recoveries or adjustments by 19 April. The new tax year then starts on 6 April with updated tax codes, NI thresholds, rates and statutory pay multipliers — pension contributions check against new thresholds, NMW rates change on 1 April (also affecting age-banded NI categories), and Employment Allowance must be re-claimed each year via EPS. Get any deadline wrong and HMRC’s automatic systems trigger penalties, employees get incorrect P60s (claims against you), or the next tax year starts on wrong codes. This module is the 5-deadline calendar, the final-submission checklist, the new-year setup, and the reconciliation between what HMRC says you owe vs what your books say.

Five dates, twelve weeks, every missed one is an automatic penalty.

Send an Earlier Year Update via next year FPS adjustment. EOY EPS by 19 April for recoveries, CIS, Employment Allowance balance, and any nil-pay flag.

Wrong P60: correct, reissue marked Replacement, and EYU to HMRC.

Update payroll software early.

Pull HMRC your-view via Business Tax Account, PAYE for Employers, statement. Reconcile line by line — catch missing EPS allocations, timing differences, missed allowance claims. Settle any difference before the 19 April final EPS — HMRC ledger locks then.

25.1 Year-end checklist

  1. Final pay run for tax year ending 5 April; final FPS marked “Final submission for tax year”.
  2. Final EPS by 19 April.
  3. P60 to every EE on payroll at 5 April by 31 May.
  4. P11D for each EE with BIK; P11D(b) by 6 July.
  5. Class 1A NI by 22 July.
  6. Update tax codes for new tax year (P9X uplift = 1257L if no individual code).
  7. Update statutory rates (NMW/NLW, NI thresholds, statutory pay).

Module 26 · Part 4 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Construction Industry Scheme (CIS)

The Construction Industry Scheme is HMRC’s way of taxing subcontractor payments at source — designed in the 1970s to combat the cash economy in construction and still essential today. Every contractor (anyone whose business is construction, or who spends > £3m on construction in any rolling 12-month period) must deduct CIS at one of three rates from subcontractor payments and pay it across to HMRC monthly: 20% if verified standard, 30% if unregistered, or 0% gross payment status for established subcontractors who pass HMRC’s tests. Subcontractors then reclaim the deductions through their own returns — via tax credit (sole traders/partnerships) or against PAYE liability (Ltd companies). Plus the CIS Domestic Reverse Charge for VAT (M16) creates a second layer of complexity on the same transactions. Get it wrong and contractor faces penalties for under-deduction PLUS interest, AND the subcontractor over-pays tax that’s painful to reclaim later. This module is contractor vs subcontractor classification, verification, the three deduction rates, gross payment status tests, monthly CIS300 returns, the contractor pay/subcontractor reclaim flow, and the VAT reverse charge interaction.

Time Voiceover
0:00–0:13 Contractors deduct CIS at source. Mainstream contractor: business is construction. Deemed: non-construction business spending more than 3 million on construction in any rolling 12 months. Subcontractors get net, reclaim later. Construction operations per FA 2004 section 74: site prep, demolition, alteration, building, repair, decoration, installation. Excludes architecture, surveying, materials-only, transport-only. First step: register with HMRC as contractor.
0:13–0:28 Three deduction rates. Standard 20% for verified registered subby. Higher 30% for unverified or failed verification. Gross 0% for subby with gross payment status. Verify BEFORE first payment via HMRC’s CIS service with UTR, NINO or CRN, business name. Valid for 2 years inactivity. Deduct from LABOUR ONLY — not materials, VAT, or direct expenses. Itemise invoice.
0:28–0:43 Gross Payment Status. Why apply: paid gross, huge cashflow win. Three tests. Business test: UK construction with bank account. Turnover test: net 30k sole trader, 30k times partners, 30k times directors capped 100k for limited. Compliance test: no serious tax or CIS defaults in previous 12 months. HMRC reviews annually. Fail any test, status withdrawn, revert to 20% or 30%.
0:43–0:56 CIS300 contractor cycle. Monthly tax month ends 5th. List every subby paid, UTR or NINO, gross, materials, CIS deducted. File CIS300 by 19th of following month online — nil return required if no payments. Pay HMRC 22nd electronic or 19th post, same accounts office ref as PAYE. Issue CIS Payment and Deduction Statement to subby within 14 days. Late: 100 immediate, 200 at 2 months, tax-geared at 6 and 12.
0:56–1:10 Subby reclaim. Sole trader or partnership: CIS shown on SA return, offset IT/NI, refund if excess. Limited company: offset PAYE/NI via monthly EPS, refund excess after year-end. CIS Domestic Reverse Charge for VAT: B2B construction between VAT and CIS-registered businesses, subby doesn’t charge VAT, contractor reverse-charges. End-user flag is the exception — normal VAT applies, no reverse charge. Both CIS deduction AND VAT reverse charge can apply to the same invoice.

26.1 Who is in scope?

  • Mainstream contractors: business is construction.
  • Deemed contractors: non-construction businesses spending > £3m on construction in any rolling 12 months.

26.2 Verification

Status Deduction
Gross payment 0% — pay in full (subcontractor met turnover, business, compliance tests)
Standard rate 20% on labour element
Higher rate 30% (unverified or unregistered)

26.3 Calculating the deduction

CIS on labour only. Strip out: materials, VAT, plant hire (separately invoiced), CITB Levy.

Module 27 · Part 5 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

The Year-End Process

Year-end is when the running ledger gets transformed into a complete, corrected, statutory set of accounts that satisfies Companies Act 2006 s.396’s “true and fair view” requirement. It’s the most-scrutinised event in the accounting year — the accounts get filed to Companies House (public record), the CT600 derives from the same figures, and a year-end mistake is propagated downstream into every related filing. The professional year-end is an 11-step workflow : pre-year-end review (1-2 months ahead so issues can still be fixed), period close, trial balance extract, all the year-end adjusting journals (M28), control account reconciliations, fixed asset additions/disposals/depreciation, stock count + valuation, going-concern review, tax computation, draft accounts, approval and signing. Standard reporting framework depends on size — FRS 105 for micro (M29), FRS 102 Section 1A for small (M30), FRS 102 full for medium/large (M31). The discipline that separates senior from junior: cut-off testing, lead schedules for every balance sheet line, formal sign-off, and the working papers file that survives a Sch 36 enquiry years later. This module is the framework that every later year-end module builds on.

0:00–0:13 Year-end transforms the running ledger into a statutory set of accounts that satisfies Companies Act 2006 section 396 — the true and fair view. Used by Companies House public record, HMRC for CT600 basis, banks for covenants, investors, buyers, suppliers. Framework by size: FRS 105 micro, FRS 102 Section 1A small, FRS 102 full for medium-plus. A year-end mistake flows downstream.

Control account recs: debtors, creditors, VAT, bank, PAYE. Fixed assets: additions, disposals, depreciation. Stock count and valuation at lower of cost and NRV.
0:28–0:43 Steps 7-11: adjust, review, sign. Year-end adjusting journals from module 28. Going-concern review 12 months forward. Tax computation, CT provision posted. Draft accounts to client for review. Approval, signature, and filing. Same 11 steps every year for the same client.
0:43–0:56 Lead schedules. One working paper per balance sheet line — opening, movement, closing, supporting evidence, with a trail from TB to accounts and a reviewer signature. Fixed assets, debtors, stock, bank, creditors, equity. No lead schedule means no audit trail and you can’t defend the number in an enquiry years later.
0:56–1:10 Sign-off and filing. Accounts approved and signed by director with board minute. CT600 filed with HMRC within 12 months of year-end, CT paid 9 months plus 1 day. Accounts filed with Companies House: 9 months for private, 6 for PLC. CS01 confirmation statement annually on the confirmation date plus 14 days. Late penalties are automatic: 150 to 1,500 by lateness for private, doubles in consecutive late years.

27.1 Why year-end exists

CA 2006 s.396 requires “a true and fair view” of profit/loss for the financial year and the state of affairs at year-end. Year-end transforms running ledger into a complete, corrected, statutory set.

27.2 The 11-step year-end workflow

  1. Pre-year-end review (1–2 months before): aged debtors/creditors stale items, fixed asset register, stock count plan.
  2. Period close: final pay run, recurring journals, lock VAT period.
  3. Trial balance produced from accounting software.
  4. Reconcile balance sheet — every BS line has a working paper.
  5. Adjusting journals — accruals, prepayments, depreciation, stock, payroll, deferred income, dividend, CT, bad debts, DLA.
  6. Tax computation in TaxCalc / IRIS / Alphatax; agree CT charge with directors.
  7. Draft accounts in accounts production software.
  8. Internal QA: senior reviews TB, comparatives, lead schedules, disclosures.
  9. Client sign-off: directors review draft, sign accounts (CA s.414).
  10. iXBRL tag & submit: Companies House and HMRC (with computations + CT600).
  11. Archive working papers — 6 years (FA 1998 Sch 18 para 21).

27.3 The 9 standard balance sheet reconciliations

BS line Working paper
Tangible fixed assets Fixed Asset Register reconciled to TB; depreciation schedule
Intangible fixed assets Asset register; amortisation schedule; impairment review
Inventory Stock count valued at lower of cost and NRV (FRS 102 s.13)
Trade debtors Aged debtors; bad debt provision schedule
Bank & cash Bank reconciliation per account; petty cash count
Trade creditors Aged creditors; supplier statement reconciliations
VAT control VAT return reconciliation; outstanding return amount
PAYE/NIC control P32 reconciliation; final month liability
Director's loan account DLA schedule by director; s.455 assessment

Other Debtors — DLA £11,400

27.4 Materiality

Audit benchmarks: 5% PBT, 1% turnover, 1–2% total assets — auditor selects most appropriate. Non-audit SME: ~£100 per item or 0.5% turnover whichever lower. Don't agonise over immaterial items.

Year-End Adjusting Journals

A cash-basis ledger and an accruals-basis ledger can diverge by tens of thousands of pounds at year-end — and FRS 102 s.2.36 demands the accruals basis for every company set of accounts (only the smallest unincorporated traders may opt for cash basis tax filing). Year-end adjusting journals are the bridge: the nine standard adjustments that take a software-extracted trial balance and convert it into a true-and-fair P&L and balance sheet. Each journal has a recognition rule behind it — accruals from s.2.36, depreciation from s.17 (systematic basis matching consumption of economic benefit), stock from s.13 (lower of cost and NRV), bad debt provisions from s.11 (expected credit loss), and CT from s.29 (current tax payable on taxable profit). The discipline that separates a clean year-end from a messy one: every adjusting journal reverses on day 1 of the new period, so the new year’s P&L starts at zero and the same accrual isn’t recognised twice. Get the nine right, and the rest of the year-end (lead schedules, disclosure notes, tax comp) flows naturally.

FRS 105 — Micro-Entity Accounts

FRS 105 is the UK GAAP framework for the smallest companies — the micro-entity regime introduced by SI 2013/3008 and embedded in Companies Act 2006 Part 15. To qualify, the company must meet two of three thresholds for two consecutive years (or its first year): turnover ≤ £632k, total assets ≤ £316k, and average employees ≤ 10 — thresholds rising approximately 50% for accounting periods starting on or after 6 April 2025. What makes FRS 105 attractive: minimal disclosure — no directors’ report, no notes-by-line, no fair value remeasurement, no deferred tax, no revaluation. The filed accounts are essentially a stripped-down balance sheet and P&L plus two footnotes (director advances/credits and off-balance-sheet commitments). But FRS 105 excludes any company in an ineligible group, any PLC, financial institution, or charity. The accounts are also not subject to true and fair override if prepared in the format prescribed by FRS 105 — though they must still give a true and fair view. This module covers qualification, what’s in a FRS 105 set, the typical journal differences from FRS 102, and when a micro-entity should consider electing into FRS 102 1A anyway (for example, when bank covenants require fuller disclosure).

Two of three thresholds for two consecutive years (or first year):

Threshold Micro Small (FRS 102 1A) Medium
Turnover ≤ £632k ≤ £10.2m ≤ £36m
Total assets ≤ £316k ≤ £5.1m ≤ £18m
Average employees ≤ 10 ≤ 50 ≤ 250

Note: thresholds rising ~50% from accounting periods starting on or after 6 April 2025.

29.2 Excluded entities

Charities, PLCs, financial institutions, members of ineligible groups all excluded from FRS 105.

29.3 What's in a FRS 105 set

  1. Balance sheet (condensed, format A or B)
  2. Profit & loss (condensed)
  3. Footnotes on balance sheet:
    • Advances/credits to directors and any guarantees
    • Off-balance-sheet financial commitments

No notes, no accounting policies, no Strategic Report or Directors' Report (not required for micro-entities).

29.4 FRS 105 simplifications vs FRS 102

Area FRS 105 FRS 102
Investment property fair value Not permitted (cost only) FV through P&L
Revaluation model for tangibles Not permitted Permitted by class
Deferred tax Not permitted Required
Capitalisation of borrowing costs Not permitted Optional
Capitalisation of development costs Not permitted Required if criteria met
Government grants Performance model only Performance or accruals
Defined-benefit pensions Cash basis (contributions paid) Full FRS 102 s.28

29.5 Micro-entity declaration

Statement on the BS: “The accounts have been prepared in accordance with the micro-entity provisions and delivered in accordance with the small companies regime.”

Why FRS 105 exists

Introduced 2013 to reduce burden on smallest companies (~1.5m UK companies use it). Trade-off: extreme simplicity vs. uninformative accounts. Many banks now insist on full FRS 102 before lending.

FRS 102 Section 1A — Small Company Accounts

Section 1A is the most-used disclosure regime in UK practice — the regime that sits between FRS 105’s austerity and full FRS 102’s heavy disclosure burden. It applies to small companies (turnover ≤ £10.2m, assets ≤ £5.1m, employees ≤ 50 — rising to £15m / £7.5m / 50 from 6 April 2025) that want or need to use full FRS 102 recognition and measurement but qualify for reduced disclosure. The trick of Section 1A: full recognition and measurement of FRS 102 still applies — investment properties revalued, deferred tax recognised, financial instruments classified into basic/non-basic, going concern assessment formally done — but the disclosures filed are reduced to the “Appendix C” list of ~30 mandatory items. Section 1A also permits filleted accounts (P&L and related notes withheld from public filing), and from 2026 the ECCTA changes mean small companies will no longer be able to file BS-only abridged accounts — the filed pack must include the full P&L. This module walks through the Section 1A format, the 30+ Appendix C disclosures, accounting policy choices, the small-company audit exemption (CA 2006 s.477) and the typical Section 1A vs full FRS 102 trade-offs. It is the bread-and-butter framework of UK SME accounting.

30.1 What Section 1A is

Full FRS 102 recognition + measurement, but with reduced disclosure for small entities. Designed to balance true and fair view with proportionate burden.

30.2 Eligibility

Small company size limits: turnover ≤ £10.2m, total assets ≤ £5.1m, EE ≤ 50 (two of three for two years). Excluded: PLCs, financial institutions, ineligible-group members.

30.3 Mandatory Section 1A disclosures (Appendix C)

  1. Accounting policies — for each policy choice area
  2. Going concern statement (s.3.8)
  3. Significant judgements and estimation uncertainty (s.8.6, 8.7)
  4. Intangible assets — useful lives, additions/disposals
  5. Tangible fixed assets — cost, depreciation, NBV by class with movements
  6. Investments held as fixed assets
  7. Inventory — total, with material impairment
  8. Stocks/WIP if material
  9. Creditors due within / after one year
  10. Provisions — material provisions explained
  11. Share capital — classes, allotments, rights
  12. Director's loans & advances (CA 2006 s.413)
  13. Related party transactions (FRS 102 s.33)
  14. Average employee number
  15. Off-balance-sheet arrangements
  16. Post-balance-sheet events

30.4 Why each major disclosure exists

Accounting Policies

Source: FRS 102 s.10 + s.8.4. Why: Many areas allow policy choice (depreciation method, FV vs cost, grants). Users need to know choices to interpret figures and compare to peers.

Going Concern

Source: FRS 102 s.3.8 + ISA UK 570. Why: Accounts assume continuation 12+ months. If at risk, users must be warned — liquidation valuations would be materially different.

Significant Judgements & Estimates

Source: FRS 102 s.8.6/8.7. Why: Many figures depend on management estimates (useful lives, bad debt, fair values). Users need to identify the “hot spots”.

Tangible Fixed Asset Movement

Source: FRS 102 s.17.31 + CA 2006 Sch 1. Why: Capex investment, write-downs, depreciation policy — assess cash needs and replacement cycle.

Creditors split <1yr / >1yr

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 + FRS 102 s.4.5. Why: Liquidity assessment — what's payable next 12 months vs longer-term.

Director's Loans & Advances

Source: CA 2006 s.413. Why: Statutory transparency on transactions between company and officers — risk of value extraction. Lenders and minority shareholders need this.

Related Party Transactions

Source: FRS 102 s.33. Why: Non-arm's-length transactions can transfer value to a related party. Disclosure deters and exposes.

Average Employee Number

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 para 87. Why: Statutory size benchmark + scale indicator.

Post-Balance-Sheet Events

Source: FRS 102 s.32. Why: Adjusting events reflected in BS; non-adjusting events disclosed for user awareness even though no figures changed.

Module 30 — Summary

  • Section 1A: full FRS 102 R&M, reduced disclosures.
  • Mandatory disclosure list per Appendix C (~16 items).
  • Each disclosure ties to CA mandate or FRS 102 user-protection rationale.

FRS 102 Full

Full FRS 102 is the comprehensive UK GAAP standard — a 360-page reference issued by the Financial Reporting Council, organised into 35 numbered sections covering everything from concepts and pervasive principles (s.2) to specialised activities (s.34) and transition (s.35). It is mandatory for medium and large companies, charities (via the SORP), pension schemes, and any small entity that elects out of Section 1A. The March 2024 periodic review brings the biggest changes since 2015 — new Section 23 revenue aligned with IFRS 15’s five-step model, and new Section 20 leases aligned with IFRS 16 putting most operating leases onto the balance sheet as right-of-use assets. The full disclosure pack runs to a directors’ report, strategic report (medium+), profit & loss, balance sheet, statement of changes in equity, statement of cash flows (s.7), and typically 25-40 notes. This module gives you the section-by-section roadmap, the recognition and measurement principles that drive every adjustment, the audit interaction points, and the disclosure choices that turn a TB into a statutory pack. It’s the framework that every senior accountant must know cold.

The complete UK GAAP standard for medium/large companies and any small co electing out of Section 1A. Mandatory for entities outside small companies regime. ~360 pages.

  1. Statement of Financial Position (BS)
  2. Statement of Comprehensive Income (P&L + OCI)
  3. Statement of Changes in Equity
  4. Statement of Cash Flows (optional Section 1A)

31.4 The 2026 amendments — major changes

Effective for accounting periods starting on/after 1 January 2026:

  • s.23 Revenue: 5-step model (identify contract → POs → transaction price → allocate → recognise) aligned with IFRS 15.
  • s.20 Leases: lessee BS recognition of right-of-use asset and lease liability for almost all leases (mirrors IFRS 16).
  • Restate comparatives; recalculate covenants, bonuses, KPIs.

CA 2006 s.414A — required for medium/large. Contains:

  • Fair review of business — development, performance, position
  • Principal risks and uncertainties
  • KPIs (financial and non-financial)
  • Section 172(1) statement — long-term, employees, suppliers, community, environment, fairness
  • Climate-related financial disclosures (CFD) — large + PIE

31.6 Audit requirements

Required if any of: T > £10.2m, A > £5.1m, PLC, group exceeding small-group thresholds, regulated/financial sector, articles or 10%+ shareholder request.

Disclosure Reasoning — Why Each Note Is Required

Every line in a set of accounts is there because a specific law or standard mandates it — Companies Act 2006, FRS 102 (with Section 1A for small entities), FRS 105 for micros, or sector SORPs for charities/pensions. A senior accountant doesn’t copy a previous year’s notes; they reason from source → trigger → content. Note 1 (Statement of Compliance) exists because FRS 102 s.3.3 + CA 2006 s.474 require users to know which framework governs the figures . Note 2 (Significant Accounting Policies) exists because FRS 102 s.10.7 demands disclosure of any policy “relevant to an understanding of the financial statements.” The related party note exists because CA 2006 s.413 requires director loans/credits to be public, and FRS 102 s.33 extends that to all related parties. The going concern note exists because s.3.8 imposes a 12-month forward assessment. This module reasons through every note in a typical small-company set, gives the exact statutory or framework reference, and explains why the disclosure protects the user of the accounts. Master this and you can defend every note in an audit, an enquiry, or a peer review — and you can prune anything that isn’t required, keeping the disclosure pack lean.

Keep what’s legally required or material; prune what isn’t. The result is a disclosure pack you can defend line by line in audit, enquiry or peer review.”

This module is the user's specific request: every note in a typical FRS 102 / FRS 105 small-company set, the standard or law that requires it, and the rationale.

Note 1: Statement of Compliance

Source: FRS 102 s.3.3 + CA 2006 s.474. Why: Tells users which framework governs the figures so they know which R&M rules apply.

Note 2: Accounting Policies

Source: FRS 102 s.10. Why: Where a policy choice exists, users need to know the directors' choice. Examples: depreciation method, IP valuation, revenue trigger, grant treatment.

Note 3: Going Concern

Source: FRS 102 s.3.8. Why: Affirmation that accounts on going-concern basis. Material uncertainty disclosed.

Note 4: Critical Judgements & Estimation Uncertainty

Source: FRS 102 s.8.6, 8.7. Why: Estimates carrying significant risk of material adjustment in next 12 months — disclosed so users see the “hot spots”.

Note 5: Turnover Analysis

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 + FRS 102 s.5.7B. Why: Multi-segment analysis where material — concentration risk visibility.

Note 6: Operating Profit (Charges)

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 para 67 + FRS 102 s.5. Why: Disclosure of charges affecting operating profit — depreciation, amortisation, auditor fees, operating lease rentals, profit/loss on disposals. Profit quality.

Note 7: Auditor's Remuneration

Source: CA 2006 s.494 + Disclosure of Auditor Remuneration Regs 2008. Why: Audit fees + non-audit fees can compromise auditor independence. Exposed to deter threats.

Note 8: Staff Costs

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 para 88. Why: Wages, NI, pension costs — productivity computation, salary inflation, ER pension burden.

Note 9: Average Employees

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 para 87. Why: Size classification benchmark + scale indicator.

Note 10: Directors' Remuneration

Source: CA 2006 s.412. Why: Statutory transparency on directors' total remuneration. Aggregate for small co; per-director for medium/large + listed.

Note 11: Tax Charge Reconciliation

Source: FRS 102 s.29.27. Why: Reconciles P&L tax charge to standard CT × accounting profit. Explains disallowables, capital allowances vs depreciation, R&D credit, deferred tax.

Note 12: Tangible Fixed Assets Movement

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 + FRS 102 s.17.31. Why: Movement table by class showing capex, disposals, depreciation policy applied.

Note 13: Intangibles & Goodwill

Source: FRS 102 s.18.27, s.19.26. Why: Movement table; goodwill useful life (10 years presumed if not reliably estimated); impairment.

Note 14: Investments

Source: FRS 102 s.9 (subs), s.14 (assoc), s.15 (JVs), s.11/12. Why: Subsidiaries names, % held, country of registration; FV basis where used.

Note 15: Inventory

Source: FRS 102 s.13.22. Why: Categories, cost formula (FIFO, weighted avg), impairment, items pledged as security.

Note 16: Trade Debtors

Source: FRS 102 s.4.5 + s.11. Why: Analysis, ageing, past-due, bad debt provision movement. Collection efficiency + credit risk.

Note 17: Creditors <1yr

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 + FRS 102 s.4.5. Why: Liquidity. Categories: trade, accruals, taxation/NI, other.

Note 18: Creditors >1yr

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1. Why: Long-term debt structure. Loan repayment schedule (1–2yr, 2–5yr, >5yr).

Note 19: Provisions Movement

Source: FRS 102 s.21.14. Why: Movement table for each provision — opening, additions, used, released, closing. Exposes use as smoothing mechanism.

Note 20: Deferred Tax

Source: FRS 102 s.29.27. Why: Analysis — accelerated capital allowances, losses CF, OCI items. Predicts future tax cashflows.

Note 21: Share Capital & Reserves

Source: CA 2006 Sch 1 + FRS 102 s.4.12. Why: Number/class, nominal value, year movements (allotments, buybacks), rights. Reserves split: share premium, revaluation, retained earnings.

Note 22: Dividends

Source: FRS 102 s.6 + CA 2006 Part 23. Why: Dividend per share, interim/final, post-BS dividends declared but not yet paid.

Note 23: Capital and Other Commitments

Source: FRS 102 s.32.16. Why: Future commitments not yet on BS — capex contracted, operating lease commitments. Anticipates future cash.

Note 24: Related Party Transactions

Source: FRS 102 s.33. Why: Material transactions with related parties — nature, amount, balance. Exposes potential value transfer.

Note 25: Post-balance-sheet Events

Source: FRS 102 s.32. Why: Adjusting events reflected in BS; non-adjusting events disclosed for user awareness.

Module 32 — Summary

  • Each disclosure traces to a CA mandate or FRS 102 paragraph.
  • Disclosures inform users about liquidity, valuation choices, related-party risk, going concern, integrity.
  • Test: would a reasonable user be misled if omitted?

Module 33 · Part 5 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

iXBRL Tagging

Every set of UK statutory accounts is filed in iXBRL — Inline eXtensible Business Reporting Language — a hybrid format that delivers a human-readable XHTML document with machine-readable tags embedded inside. HMRC has mandated iXBRL for every CT600 since 2011; Companies House currently accepts it voluntarily but ECCTA 2024 makes iXBRL mandatory for all filings from 2027. The tags come from taxonomies — the UK GAAP (FRS 102 / FRS 105) taxonomy, the Charities SORP taxonomy, the IFRS taxonomy, the DPL (Detailed Profit & Loss) extension. A tagged P&L line for “Turnover” isn’t just text — it carries an XBRL element id, a context (period and entity), a unit (GBP), and possibly footnotes. Quality matters: HMRC’s automated checks reject filings with missing mandatory tags, and a poor tag job triggers manual review and enquiry risk. Modern accounts software (CCH, IRIS, TaxCalc, Sage, Xero Tax) auto-tags 70-90% of items; the accountant’s job is to review, correct, and complete the tagging before submission. This module covers the iXBRL standard, the UK taxonomies, the auto-tag workflow, the most-commonly-missed tags, and the audit trail for review.

Companies House Filing — Mechanics, Filleted, ECCTA

Filing accounts with Companies House is the final mechanical step of the year-end cycle — but it’s also the step where most penalty letters land. Private companies must file within 9 months of year-end; public companies within 6 months. Miss the deadline and the penalty escalates: £150 (within 1 month), £375 (1-3 months), £750 (3-6 months), £1,500 (over 6 months) — doubled if you also missed the prior year. Filing routes have collapsed to software-API for almost everyone: TaxCalc, IRIS, CCH, Xero Tax, Sage, FreeAgent all submit directly via the Companies House software filing API, returning an immediate accept/reject. WebFiling and paper routes are being phased out by ECCTA 2024. The big regulatory change is ECCTA 2024 — the Economic Crime and Corporate Transparency Act — which from 2026 ends abridged and filleted accounts for small companies (the filed pack must include the full P&L), introduces identity verification for directors and PSCs, and gives Companies House new powers to reject suspicious filings. This module walks through the mechanics: which forms file when, the small/dormant exemptions still permitted, the deadline calculator, late penalty mechanics, the ECCTA changes coming live in 2025/26, and how to handle resubmissions and corrections via second filing mechanism.

Part Six

Corporation Tax

6 modules · ~15 hours · From accounting profit to filed CT600

Corporation Tax is the tax on company profits, computed under CTA 2009 (income, deductions) and CTA 2010 (rates, reliefs, group rules). Filed on form CT600 within 12 months of period end via iXBRL-tagged accounts.

Module 35 · Part 6 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Corporation Tax Fundamentals

Corporation Tax is the levy on UK company profits, governed by the Corporation Tax Act 2009 (income/expense) and the Corporation Tax Act 2010 (rates, reliefs, groups). The basis period is the Accounting Period (AP) — usually the company’s year-end, but a long period (>12 months) splits into a 12-month AP plus a remainder AP, each with its own CT600 and computation. From 1 April 2023 the regime returned to a two-rate structure: 19% small-profits rate for profits ≤ £50k, 25% main rate for profits ≥ £250k, and marginal relief tapering between (effective marginal rate ~26.5%). Augmented profits include franked investment income and associated-company thresholds are divided by (1 + number of associates) — a critical trap for groups and family holdings. The filing/payment chain: file CT600 within 12 months of period end, pay 9 months and 1 day for non-large companies, or quarterly instalments (QIPs) for large (taxable profits >£1.5m) and very large (>£20m). This module is the conceptual scaffold for everything in Part 6 — the language of CT, the deadlines, the rate map, and the framework you carry into every CT600 you ever prepare.

  • Period: an Accounting Period (AP) — typically the company's accounting period; long period >12 months split into 12-month AP + remainder.
  • CT600 within 12 months of end of AP.
  • Pay 9m+1d after AP end (non-large); large companies (taxable profits >£1.5m) pay quarterly Instalments (QIPs).

35.2 Rates 2024/25 & 2025/26

Profit band Rate
Up to £50,000 (Small Profits Rate) 19%
£50,001 – £250,000 (Marginal Relief) Effective marginal 26.5%
Above £250,000 (Main Rate) 25%

35.3 Marginal Relief

Marginal Relief = (Upper limit − Augmented profits) × (Augmented profits ÷ Total taxable profits) × 3/200

Compute CT at 25% then deduct MR.

Worked Example 35.1 — Marginal Relief

Profit £150,000. Single company, no associates.

CT @ 25% 37,500
MR: (250,000 − 150,000) × (150,000/150,000) × 3/200 (1,500)
CT due 36,000
Effective rate 24.0%

35.4 Associated companies

£50k/£250k limits divided by number of associated companies (51% group, common control). Reintroduced from 1 April 2023.

35.5 CT600 supplementary forms

  • CT600A: loans to participators (s.455 charge)
  • CT600B: controlled foreign companies
  • CT600C: group/consortium relief
  • CT600E: charities/CASCs
  • CT600J: DOTAS

Module 35 — Summary

  • CT600 supplementary forms for special cases.

Adjusting Accounting Profit to Taxable Profit

Accounting profit is not taxable profit. The CT computation bridges the two via two columns — add backs (items expensed in accounts but disallowed for tax) and deductions (items allowed for tax that aren’t in the P&L, or that are tax-free income to back out). The classic add-backs: depreciation (replaced by capital allowances under CAA 2001), goodwill amortisation (generally disallowed since FA 2002), client entertaining (CTA 2009 s.1298), fines and penalties (not wholly & exclusively trade), political donations, and capital expenditure expensed in error. Deductions: capital allowances on qualifying P&M (replacing depreciation), pension contributions paid (s.196 FA 2004), and statutory reliefs. The “wholly and exclusively” test (CTA 2009 s.54) is the workhorse principle — if expense isn’t wholly and exclusively for trade purposes, it’s disallowed. Get this column right and the rest of the computation flows; get it wrong and HMRC discovery-window risk follows you for 6 years. This module covers every standard add back, every standard deduction, the wholly-and-exclusively test in practice, and the structured pro-forma that every CT computation should follow.

Module 37 · Part 6 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Capital Allowances

Capital allowances are the tax substitute for depreciation — the system by which the cost of qualifying capital expenditure on plant and machinery (P&M) is written off against taxable profits, governed by the Capital Allowances Act 2001. The core toolkit: Annual Investment Allowance (AIA) at 100% on the first £1m of qualifying P&M (any business); Full Expensing at 100% with no cap on new main-pool P&M (companies only, permanent from April 2023); 50% First-Year Allowance on new special-rate P&M (companies); Writing-Down Allowances (WDA) at 18% main pool / 6% special rate (reducing balance), and a structures and buildings allowance (SBA) at 3% straight-line. Special rules apply to cars (CO2-banded WDA, no AIA), integral features (lifts, electrical, A/C — special pool), and short-life assets. Get capital allowances right and the CT charge drops materially; get them wrong and you either overpay tax or trigger a balancing charge on disposal. This module walks through the full toolkit, the pool mechanics, the qualifying-cost rules, the AIA-allocation strategy, and the standard worked example you’ll use on every CT computation.

Module 38 · Part 6 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

R&D Tax Relief

R&D Tax Relief is one of the most generous — and most abused — UK tax reliefs. From 1 April 2024 the old SME and RDEC schemes have merged into a single regime : a 20% above-the-line expenditure credit, with a separate ERIS (Enhanced R&D Intensive Support) route for loss-making R&D-intensive SMEs (R&D ≥ 30% of total expenditure). The technical test is BEIS Guidelines (now DSIT): a project must seek to resolve scientific or technological uncertainty through systematic investigation aimed at advancing the field. Qualifying costs: staff costs, subcontracted R&D, consumables , cloud computing & data licences (added 2023), and EPWs (Externally Provided Workers). Major changes from April 2024: contracted R&D rules now favour the principal (the one with project intent), subsidised expenditure rules tightened, and a mandatory Additional Information Form (AIF) must be filed BEFORE the CT600. HMRC has dramatically increased compliance activity since 2022 — enquiry rate now ~15-20% on first-time claims. This module walks through the new regime, the qualifying activity test, the cost categories, the AIF mechanics, and how to build a defensible claim file from the ground up.

  • ERIS: Enhanced R&D Intensive Support — for loss-making SMEs with R&D ≥ 30% of total expenditure. 86% additional deduction (so 186% total); payable credit at 14.5%; net cash up to ~27% of qualifying spend.

  3. Compute relief in CT computation
  4. Claim on CT600 within 2 years of end of AP

38.6 Patent Box

Profits attributable to qualifying patents taxed at 10% rather than 25%. Election required.

Module 39 · Part 6 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Loss & Group Relief

Losses are the most valuable asset on a CT balance sheet you can’t see. The UK system gives five separate trading-loss reliefs (CTA 2010 s.37 and onward): current year against total profits (s.37(3)(a)), 12-month carry back (s.37(3)(b)), carry forward against total profits from 1 April 2017 (post-reform s.45A — previously trading-only), terminal loss relief for cessation (3-year carry back, s.39), and group relief — surrendering losses to a 75%-owned consortium or group member (CTA 2010 Part 5). The Restriction: from 1 April 2017, brought-forward losses can only relieve up to £5m of profits plus 50% of the excess — a major restriction for large groups. Group relief rules (75% group, 75% consortium) require both companies UK-resident or chargeable to CT and run on a strict ownership test. Trading losses, non-trading loan relationship deficits, property losses, and management expenses all have their own carry-forward and surrender rules — this module maps every relief, every restriction, and the decision tree for “which relief should I claim and in what order?”

39.1 The five trading loss reliefs

Relief Section Effect
Current year CTA 2010 s.37(3)(a) Loss against total profits of same AP
Carry back CTA 2010 s.37(3)(b) Against total profits of preceding 12 months
Extended carry back FA 2021 s.18 3-year carry back, capped (mostly expired)
Carry forward CTA 2010 s.45A onwards Against future total profits (post-Apr 2017 losses; LRR)
Group relief CTA 2010 Part 5 Surrender to 75% group company

39.2 Loss Relief Restriction (LRR) — c/f losses

From 1 April 2017:

  • £5m Deductions Allowance per group, used freely
  • Losses above allowance restricted to 50% of remaining profit

So £20m profit + £20m b/f losses = offset £5m + 50%×£15m = £12.5m → £7.5m taxable.

39.3 Group relief — 75% group

Parent owns ≥75% of subsidiary's ordinary share capital, ≥75% beneficial entitlement to distributable profits and assets on winding-up. Losses surrendered between members applied against overlapping AP.

39.4 Other losses

  • Capital losses: only against capital gains; carry forward indefinite; cannot be group-relieved.
  • Property business losses: ring-fenced.
  • Loan relationship deficit: similar 5 reliefs but ring-fenced.

39.5 Anti-avoidance

CTA 2010 s.673 — losses denied if major change in nature of trade within 5 years of change in ownership. Prevents “loss buying”.

Module 39 — Summary

  • 5 routes for trading losses: CY, 12m carry back, c/f, group relief, extended carry back.
  • LRR caps c/f use above £5m group allowance to 50% remaining profit.
  • 75% group: capital, profit, asset rights.
  • Capital losses ring-fenced.
  • Anti-avoidance on change of ownership + change in trade.

CT600 Walkthrough in TaxCalc

The CT600 is the Corporation Tax Return — a 12-section, ~100-box form covering every type of UK company income, deduction, and payment. The CT600 attaches the iXBRL accounts and iXBRL computation; supplementary pages (CT600A close-company loans, CT600B group, CT600C losses, CT600J disclosure of tax avoidance) attach where relevant. This module demonstrates: setup & data import from accounts production, completion sequence for a typical small company, validation, e-submission via HMRC gateway, and what the receipt looks like.

Module 41 · Part 7 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

SA100 Main Return

The SA100 is the headline personal tax return — the document every UK Self Assessment client files annually, supplemented by source-specific pages (SA102 employment, SA103 self-employment, SA104 partnership, SA105 UK property, SA106 foreign, SA108 capital gains, SA109 residence). The legal hook is TMA 1970 s.8: any person who receives a notice to file must file. Filing routes: online via HMRC Personal Tax Account or commercial software (TaxCalc, Sage Personal Tax, BTCSoftware, Andica); paper SA100 still accepted for some categories. Deadlines: 31 October (paper) and 31 January (online), with balancing payment and first payment on account both due 31 January, second POA 31 July. Penalties escalate fast: £100 immediate, £10/day after 3 months (max £900), then 5% or £300 at 6 and 12 months. The SA100 captures income across all sources, pulls deductions and allowances, calculates tax due, and triggers POAs for the following year. This module walks the structure, who must register, when registration is triggered, the income/allowances flow, and the end-to-end software workflow.

SA103 — Self-Employment

The SA103 reports self-employed income on the SA100 — in two flavours: SA103S (Short) for turnover up to ~£85k and SA103F (Full) for turnover above the threshold or anyone claiming CIS deductions, capital allowances on cars, or unusual reliefs. From 2024/25 the basis period reform is fully effective: sole traders now report profits on a tax-year basis (6 April to 5 April), replacing the old “current year basis”. Traders with non-31-March accounting periods need transition profit calculations (FA 2022) spread over 5 years. Class 4 NIC removed at £12,570-£50,270 threshold (8% from 6 April 2024, down from 9%); Class 2 NIC abolished from April 2024 for trading profits above the small profits threshold. Cash basis is now the default for sole traders and partners (FA 2023). Trading allowance (£1k) shelters small-side incomes. This module walks the SA103, the basis-period reform mechanics, NIC changes, cash vs accruals decision, AIA on the self-employed return, and how to handle CIS deductions for subbies.

Module 43 · Part 7 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

SA105 — Property Income

The SA105 reports UK property income for individuals — covering buy-to-let landlords, rent-a-room hosts, and historically furnished holiday lettings (FHL, abolished from 6 April 2025). Two big regime features dominate: the Section 24 mortgage-interest restriction (FA 2016) which since 2020/21 has fully replaced mortgage-interest deduction with a 20% basic-rate tax credit — brutal for higher-rate residential landlords who now pay tax on gross rents; and the property allowance of £1,000 letting income tax-free (or deduct actual expenses, not both). The Rent-a-Room scheme shelters up to £7,500/year for letting a furnished room in your main home. From April 2025 the FHL regime is abolished — ex-FHL properties become standard residential lets with all the s.24 disadvantages, no BADR on disposal, no full mortgage interest, no capital allowances. Commercial property and corporate landlords are largely unaffected. This module walks through the s.24 mechanics with a worked example, the property allowance, Rent-a-Room, the post-2025 FHL position, and the structural question every landlord eventually asks: incorporate or stay personal?

43.1 Section 24 mortgage interest restriction

Critical for residential landlords. Mortgage interest no longer deductible from rental profit; replaced by 20% basic-rate tax credit. Higher-rate landlords lose significant relief. Does NOT apply to commercial property or corporate landlords (or FHL pre-April 2025).

43.2 Furnished Holiday Lettings (FHL) — abolished from April 2025

Until April 2025, qualifying FHLs had favourable treatment (full mortgage interest, capital allowances, BADR, pensionable income). FHL regime abolished 6 April 2025 — properties become standard residential lets.

£1,000 — first £1k of property income tax-free. Above £1k: actual expenses OR £1k allowance (not both).

43.4 Rent-a-Room scheme

Up to £7,500/year tax-free for letting furnished room in main home.

SA108 — Capital Gains

The SA108 reports capital gains and losses for individuals, governed by TCGA 1992. The Annual Exempt Amount (AEA) has been slashed: from £12,300 (22/23) to £6,000 (23/24) to £3,000 (24/25). Rates are bifurcated: 10% / 20% for most assets (basic / higher rate), 18% / 24% for residential property — the residential higher-rate cut from 28% to 24% in April 2024. Business Asset Disposal Relief (BADR) gives a 10% rate on qualifying business sales up to £1m lifetime allowance — but rising to 14% in April 2025 and 18% in April 2026. Residential property gains require a 60-day separate CGT return via HMRC Online (not on SA108) plus reporting on SA108 at year-end. Share matching rules (s.106A): same day, then 30 days, then the s.104 pool. PPR relief exempts your main home; letting relief only applies if you lived in the property during the letting period (post-April 2020). This module walks all rates, AEA, BADR mechanics, share pooling, PPR, letting relief, and the 60-day reporting obligation that catches landlords out every year.

SA104 — Partnership Income

Partnerships are transparent for tax — the partnership itself doesn’t pay tax; each partner’s share of profit is taxed on their own personal return. Two filings are required: the SA800 partnership return (with a nominated partner submitting profit allocation) and each partner’s SA104 supplementary on their SA100. Partners can be individuals (SA104) or companies (CT600 share). The salaried members rule (ITA 2007 s.863A) is critical for LLPs: if a member meets all three tests (Disguised Salary >80% of pay-out, no significant influence, contribution <25% of pay-out), they’re deemed employee for PAYE/NI — expensive surprise from HMRC re-classifications. Basis-period reform equally applies to partners: tax-year basis from 2024/25, transition profit spread, overlap profits used up. Corporate partners trigger TCGA 1992 special rules and SI 2014 PIE (partnership income element) anti-avoidance. Mixed-membership rules (ITA 2007 s.850C) catch profit-shifting between non-corporate and corporate partners. This module walks SA104, SA800 mechanics, LLP salaried members test, mixed membership, and the partner-vs-employee distinction that HMRC scrutinises closely.

SA109 — Residence & Domicile

The SA109 reports residence and domicile status — the gatekeeper for whether the UK taxes a person on worldwide income or only on UK source. The Statutory Residence Test (SRT) in FA 2013 Schedule 45 is a 3-tier flow: automatic overseas (under 16 days, or under 46 if non-res in 3 prior years, or full-time overseas work) → automatic UK (183+ days, only home in UK, or full-time UK work) → sufficient ties test combining family, accommodation, 90-day, work, and country ties. Split-year treatment applies in years of arrival/departure with 8 cases. The big news: the non-dom remittance basis abolished from 6 April 2025 — a 200-year-old regime replaced by a 4-year FIG (Foreign Income & Gains) regime for new arrivals plus transition rules. Deemed domicile rules (15/20 years UK residence) made many non-doms tax-resident for IHT already; the FIG regime now ends the income-tax shelter too. This module walks SRT mechanics with worked examples, split-year, FIG regime, transition rules (50% rebasing election, TRF), and the SA109 boxes that report all of it.

46.1 Statutory Residence Test (SRT)

  1. Automatic Overseas Test: e.g. <16 days; <46 days if non-res in 3 prior; full-time work overseas
  2. Automatic UK Test: 183+ days; only home in UK; full-time work in UK
  3. Sufficient Ties Test: combine family, accommodation, work, 90-day, country ties

46.2 Domicile reform

From 6 April 2025, remittance basis abolished. New 4-year FIG regime: new UK residents not UK-resident in any prior 10 years get 100% relief on foreign income/gains for first 4 years.

Tax Calculation & Payments on Account

UK personal tax is not a flat charge — it’s the result of income segregated by type, allowances tapered, and bands stacked in a specific order. The 2024/25 rates: Personal Allowance £12,570 (tapered £1 per £2 above £100k income; fully gone at £125,140), basic rate 20% to £50,270, higher rate 40% to £125,140, additional rate 45% above. Savings income has its own band: 0% starting rate for £5k stacking under earned income, plus £1,000 PSA (BR) or £500 (HR) tax-free. Dividend tax: £500 allowance 2024/25 (down from £1k), then 8.75% / 33.75% / 39.35% by band. The order of income matters: earned/property income first, then savings, then dividends — each fills its bands in turn. Payments on account (POAs): each due 31 Jan and 31 Jul, calculated as 50% of prior-year liability, waived if <£1,000 due or >80% taxed at source. Class 2 NIC abolished 24/25; Class 4 on SE profits at 8% / 2%. This module walks the calc step-by-step with worked examples for typical client profiles (employee with side income, BTL landlord with PAYE, business owner taking salary + dividends).

  • Balancing payment 31 Jan 2026

Module 48 · Part 7 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

SA Reliefs — Pension, Gift Aid, EIS, SEIS, VCT

Personal tax planning lives in the SA reliefs — the levers that extend tax bands, reduce tax due, and shelter capital. The big four: pension contributions (FA 2004 s.196), Gift Aid (ITA 2007 s.413+), EIS/SEIS (ITA 2007 Parts 5+5A), and VCT (ITA 2007 Part 6). Pensions: tax relief at marginal rate, AA £60k from 2023/24 (was £40k), tapered if threshold income >£200k and adjusted income >£260k (down to £10k AA). Lifetime allowance abolished from 6 April 2024, replaced by lump-sum allowance £268,275 and lump-sum-and-death-benefit allowance £1,073,100. Gift Aid: extends BR band by 1.25 × gift (mechanically grossing up via 20% reclaim). SEIS: 50% income tax relief on up to £200k, 100% CGT exempt after 3 years. EIS : 30% on up to £1m (or £2m if KIC). VCT: 30% on up to £200k, tax-free dividends, CGT exempt. Plus Marriage Allowance (£1,260 transfer) and blind person’s allowance. This module covers each relief mechanism, the boxes on SA100/supps, and the order to maximise benefit.

Tax relief at marginal rate. Limit: lower of 100% UK earnings or Annual Allowance £60k. Mechanisms: relief at source, net pay arrangement, salary sacrifice.

48.4 Gift Aid

48.5 EIS

  • 30% IT credit on subscription up to £1m/year (£2m if >50% knowledge intensive)
  • CGT exempt after 3 years
  • CGT deferral on other gains
  • IHT relief after 2 years (BPR)

48.6 SEIS

  • 50% IT credit up to £200k/year (raised from £100k April 2023)
  • Smaller, earlier-stage companies (raise ≤£250k SEIS)
  • 50% CGT exemption on rolled-in gains
  • CGT exempt after 3 years

48.7 VCT

  • 30% IT credit up to £200k/year
  • Tax-free dividends
  • CGT exempt on disposal
  • 5-year hold to retain IT relief

One of the most common questions a UK accountant gets asked: “Should I incorporate?” — and once the answer is yes, how exactly to do it without losing tax reliefs, triggering unwanted CGT, or leaving stranded liabilities. Module 49 · Part 8 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Choosing a Structure — The Decision Framework

Structure choice is the highest-leverage decision in UK business advisory — it sets tax exposure, liability shield, privacy posture, capital flexibility, and compliance burden for years. The five canonical options: sole trader (zero set-up, full liability, SA only), partnership (joint & several liability, SA800 + SA104s), LLP (limited liability + tax transparency, accounts public), private Ltd (limited liability, CT regime, public accounts), and PLC (listed-ready, full disclosure). The decision turns on five questions: liability appetite, profit profile (low/lumpy/growing), privacy concerns, capital plans (need shares?), and operational complexity. Tax-driver heuristics: profits <£30k typically sole trader wins (no double tax, no public accounts), £30-50k grey zone (depends on extraction), >£50k Ltd usually wins via salary+dividend optimisation, >£1m Ltd essential for capital allowances and growth investors. Many advisors choose poorly because they default to “Ltd” without modelling. This module is the framework, the worked example, and the cheat-sheet for first-meeting client conversations.

1 · Five-option menu 0:00–0:13 5 stacked tiles: sole trader, partnership, LLP, Ltd, PLC; footer for charities. “UK business structures: sole trader, partnership, LLP, private limited company, and PLC. Each has different liability, tax, and disclosure profiles. Charities and fund GPs covered in M50.”
2 · Five questions 0:13–0:28 5 question tiles: liability, profit profile, privacy, capital, complexity. “Five key questions: how much could creditors take, is profit low, lumpy or growing, is public accounts ok, will you need equity finance, and can the owner manage compliance? Score each one to five.”

Above fifty thousand, limited company typically wins via salary plus dividend optimisation and pension contributions.”

Limited company with nine thousand salary plus dividends pays just under nineteen thousand for twenty four percent. Limited company saves about four thousand.”
5 · Cheat sheet 0:56–1:10 4 structure-fit tiles + change-later footer. “Cheat sheet: sole trader for under thirty thousand or low liability. LLP for two-plus professional partners. Limited company for profits above fifty thousand, investor plans, or asset protection. Partnership is falling out of favour. Always changeable.”

49.1 The five key questions

  1. Liability: how much could the business lose to creditors? Higher = limited structure.
  2. Profit profile: low / lumpy / steadily growing? Higher and growing = company often beats sole trader.
  3. Privacy: do owners care about public accounts? Sole trader = total privacy; Ltd = public.
  4. Capital: equity finance needed? Investors expect shares, not partnership interests.
  5. Exit: planning sale within 5–10 years? BADR (10% CGT) needs trading-company structure for 2 years pre-disposal.

49.2 The £30k–£60k pivot zone

The “sole trader vs Ltd” tax math typically inverts somewhere between £30k and £60k profit. Below: sole trader cheaper after software/accountancy. Above: Ltd dominates IF profit can be retained or extracted as dividends.

Worked Example 49.1 — £80k profit comparison (2024/25)
Sole Trader Ltd (£9.1k salary + dividend)
Profit 80,000 80,000
Salary deducted — (9,100)
Profit before CT — 70,900
CT @ 19%/marginal — ~14,290
Profit available as dividend — 56,610
IT on profit (sole trader) 17,432 —
Class 4 NI (sole trader) 2,841 —
IT on dividend — ~5,400
Total tax 20,273 ~19,690
Net to owner 59,727 60,310

Tiny difference at £80k. From 2025/26 the Ltd's advantage erodes due to ER NI changes — re-model.

49.3 Beyond tax — qualitative factors

  • Bank lending: Ltd more credible to lenders
  • Customer perception: large customers prefer Ltd suppliers
  • DLA flexibility: Ltd allows owner to lend money in/out
  • Pension funding: Ltd can pay employer pension contribution for owner-director
  • Spousal income split: Ltd shares can be issued to spouse
  • Risk separation: trade litigation stays in the company

49.4 Six valid reasons NOT to incorporate (yet)

  1. Profit too low — Ltd costs outweigh tax savings
  2. Significant losses expected — sole trader can sideways-relief; Ltd losses ringfenced
  3. Need to pull all profit out — dividend/salary tax narrows the gap
  4. Privacy critical — sole trader figures aren't public
  5. Trade involves regulated activity that Ltd would complicate
  6. Likely cessation in 1-2 years — incorporation + closure within 2 years can lose BADR

Module 49 — Summary

  • Decision driven by 5 questions: liability, profit, privacy, capital, exit.
  • Tax math typically tips around £30k–£60k profit.
  • Qualitative factors often more important than marginal tax saving.
  • 6 valid reasons to delay incorporation.

Module 50 · Part 8 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Sole Trader Setup

Sole-trader setup is deceptively simple — no registration with Companies House, no Articles, no shareholders, no minutes — but the tax compliance still requires precision. The legal status: the trader IS the business — no separate legal person, full personal liability for debts and creditors. Step 1 register for Self Assessment via CWF1 by 5 October after the tax year of commencement (or face failure-to-notify penalty up to 100% of tax due). HMRC issues a UTR in ~10 days, plus NIC Class 4 registration (Class 2 abolished from 24/25 for profits above small-profits threshold). Step 2: activate Government Gateway. Step 3: separate business bank account (strongly recommended, not legally required). Step 4: VAT registration if turnover > £90k threshold (2024/25). Step 5: PAYE registration if hiring employees. Step 6: choose cash basis (default from 24/25 reform) or accruals election. Step 7: basis period reform — new sole traders now report on tax-year basis from day one. Cheap to set up, cheap to run, but full IT + Class 4 NIC on profits. This module covers each setup step, the registration mechanics, MTD ITSA delayed timeline, and the year-1 checklist every sole trader needs.

Module 51 · Part 8 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Partnership Setup

A general partnership exists the moment two or more persons carry on a business in common with a view of profit (Partnership Act 1890 s.1). No registration with Companies House needed — but partnership setup needs care because joint and several liability exposes every partner personally to the debts and acts of every other partner. The Partnership Agreement overrides the default 1890 rules (equal shares of profit, equal capital, no salaries) — without one, the defaults govern, often badly. Step 1: draft the agreement covering profit/loss share (PSR), capital contributions, drawings, salaries, admission/retirement, dispute resolution, dissolution. Step 2: register the partnership with HMRC via SA400 (gets partnership UTR). Step 3: each partner registers individually for SA via SA401. Step 4: nominate a partner to handle the SA800 submission. Step 5: open a partnership bank account with all partners on the mandate. Step 6: VAT, PAYE, and other registrations as needed. LLP setup follows a parallel but more formal process — register with Companies House via LL IN01, member agreement (binding), and account-filing obligations apply. This module covers both routes, the salaried-members trap from M45, and the year-1 checklist.
