Module 52 · Part 8 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Ltd Company Setup

Setting up a limited company under Companies Act 2006 is the bread-and-butter advisory task — and the single decision that exposes a client to 30+ years of compliance obligations. Pre-incorporation decisions: name (WebCheck for availability; not sensitive without permission; cannot imply Crown/charity status), registered office (UK, public record), service addresses for directors and PSCs (accountant office for privacy), initial directors (16+, not disqualified), PSCs (people with significant control), share capital (typically £100 in 100 × £1 ordinary), SIC codes (1-4). Incorporation via IN01 form online (£50 standard, £78 same-day) gets CRN within hours. Post-incorporation week 1: certificate of incorporation, set up bank account (PSC/UBO checks slow this), HMRC CT registration (auto-triggered, get UTR), shareholder/director records, PSC register, statutory books. ECCTA 2024 changes live from autumn 2025: identity verification mandatory for all directors and PSCs — unverified directors cannot file or act. Software-only filing from 2027. This module walks every step, the practical pitfalls (PSC inheritance, share classes, articles), and the first-year compliance calendar.

Module 53 · Part 8 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

LLP Setup

An LLP — Limited Liability Partnership — is the hybrid form: legal person like a company (sues, owns assets, contracts), but tax-transparent like a partnership (members taxed on their share). Created by Limited Liability Partnerships Act 2000 . The big draw: limited liability for members, but with partner-style profit allocation flexibility — ideal for solicitors, accountants, architects, investment managers. Setup steps: (1) draft the Member Agreement (LLPA 2000 defaults are very sparse — without an agreement, all members share profit equally and consent to all decisions); (2) file LL IN01 at Companies House (£50, ~24h); (3) appoint at least 2 designated members with statutory duties (sign accounts, appoint auditors, file CS01); (4) register with HMRC via SA400 + each member via SA401; (5) open bank account. Critical traps : the salaried members rule (M45 — ITA 2007 s.863A) can re-classify members as employees; annual accounts public at CH (FRS 105/102 framework); ECCTA 2024 identity verification applies to all members. LLP vs Ltd calculus: LLP wins where partner-style allocation flexibility matters AND members are individuals (corporate members trigger mixed-membership). This module covers setup, post-incorp checklist, designated member duties, ECCTA implications, and the LLP vs Ltd decision.

Module 54 · Part 8 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Charity Registration

UK charity setup is more complex than a Ltd company because it’s dual-regulated — by the Charity Commission for England & Wales (or OSCR Scotland, CCNI Northern Ireland) AND by HMRC for tax. Three structural choices: unincorporated charity (trustees personally liable, no separate legal person, sparse for very small charities); charitable company limited by guarantee (CLG) (dual-registered at CH + CC, classic form for medium/large); Charitable Incorporated Organisation (CIO) — introduced 2013, single-regulated at CC only, two flavours (Foundation CIO and Association CIO). The income threshold for CC registration: £5,000 annual income (excluding CIOs which register from day 1 regardless). Setup steps: (1) define the charitable purposes from Charities Act 2011 s.3 list (13 heads); (2) draft the governing document (trust deed/constitution/articles); (3) appoint trustees (min 3 typically, must be fit-and-proper); (4) register with CC via online portal; (5) register with HMRC for tax exemption + Gift Aid. Accounting framework: Charities SORP (FRS 102) for income >£500k; receipts & payments for smaller. Audit thresholds: £1m gross income or £500k+ income with >£3.26m assets. This module walks structural choice, registration mechanics, and the trustee compliance year-1 calendar.

54.1 Choosing the form

  • Unincorporated charity — trustees personally liable; no separate legal personality.
  • Charitable company limited by guarantee — dual-registered (CH + Charity Commission).
  • CIO — single regulator (Charity Commission). Foundation CIO (members = trustees) or Association CIO (separate membership).

54.2 The CIO route (most common for new charities)

  1. Draft constitution (CC model templates).
  2. Confirm objects exclusively charitable (Charities Act 2011 s.3 — 13 purposes).
  3. Identify 3+ trustees (unrelated, willing, fit).
  4. Apply online to Charity Commission (~6–12 weeks).
  5. Receive Charity Number.
  6. Register with HMRC for charity tax exemptions (online HT2).
  7. Open bank account (charity bank, CAF Bank, Co-op).
  8. Bookkeeping with Charities SORP (FRS 102).
  9. Annual: accounts + Trustees' Annual Report; Annual Return to CC.

54.3 Tax treatment

  • Most income exempt under CTA 2010 Part 11 if used for charitable purposes
  • Gift Aid: 25% gross-up on cash donations from UK taxpayers
  • Trading exemption: small-scale or in furtherance of objects exempt; non-primary trading often via wholly-owned trading subsidiary
  • VAT: not automatically exempt; partial exemption common; specific reliefs (advertising, fundraising)
  • Business rates: 80% mandatory relief on premises used for charitable purposes

Module 54 — Summary

  • CIO is the modern default.
  • CC registration ~6–12 weeks; HMRC tax exemption separate.
  • Charities SORP (FRS 102 + extensive narrative).
  • Most income exempt; trading subsidiaries for non-primary trading.
Module 55 · Part 8 of 12 · ~3 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Sole Trader → Ltd Company Incorporation

Sole-trader-to-Ltd is the most common UK transition — and the most commonly botched. Done badly: triggers CGT on goodwill transfer, leaves stranded VAT , creates inefficient extraction structures, wastes loss relief, and creates years of compliance pain. Done well: preserves trading losses via election (CTA 2010 s.86), secures BADR eligibility on later disposal, transfers stock at value, creates tax-efficient extraction (salary + dividends + pension) from day one. The 9-step process: (1) prepare cessation accounts, (2) value the business (goodwill + tangible assets), (3) incorporate Ltd, (4) execute the sale agreement (assets + goodwill in return for shares + DLA credit), (5) transfer trade + employees (TUPE), (6) handle VAT (transfer-as-going-concern or new registration), (7) terminate sole trader registrations, (8) start company compliance cycle, (9) elect for loss carryover (s.86). Critical tax mechanics: CGT on goodwill — usually triggered as market value disposal, but incorporation relief (TCGA s.162) defers if whole business transferred for shares; SDLT on property; VAT TOGC rules (no VAT charged if conditions met); DLA mechanism credits the trader for net assets transferred. This module walks every step, the s.162 vs s.165 election choice, and the TUPE/employee considerations.

Section 162 incorporation relief defers if whole business transferred for shares. Section 165 gift relief is selective. DLA credits trader for net assets transferred, tax-free withdrawal.”
4 · VAT & employees 0:43–0:56 TOGC banner; TUPE banner; stock/debtors transfer; SDLT warning. “VAT TOGC: no VAT if same trade continues and Ltd VAT-registered — transfer via VAT68 or new reg. TUPE means employees transfer automatically with existing terms. Stock and debtors at value. SDLT applies on property transfer at market value.”
5 · New compliance 0:56–1:10 5-step post-incorp ladder + loss c/f footer. “Post-incorp: final SA100 cessation return, CT600 from incorporation date forward, PAYE for director salary, dividends from reserves, track DLA repayment to avoid s.455 trap, pension contributions from company. Section 86 loss c/f offsets future profits of same trade.”

The most common transition. Done badly: triggers CGT on goodwill, leaves stranded VAT, creates a tax-inefficient extraction structure for years. Done well: preserves losses, secures BADR eligibility, creates tax-efficient extraction from day 1.

55.1 The 9-step process

  1. Form the new Ltd (Module 52).
  2. Value the business assets: tangible (book value), inventory (cost), debtors (face value), goodwill (see 55.2).
  3. Sale agreement: written contract sole trader → Ltd transferring assets and goodwill.
  4. VAT TOGC: if VAT-registered, structure as TOGC (Module 17) to avoid VAT on transfer.
  5. CGT: s.162 incorporation relief: where consideration is wholly shares, s.162 applies automatically to defer entire gain on goodwill into share base cost. Mixed consideration → partial s.162 (relief proportional to share value / total consideration).
  6. HMRC notify cessation: file final SA103 marking cessation.
  7. VAT: VAT68 to transfer VRN to Ltd, OR sole trader deregisters and Ltd applies for new VRN.
  8. Bank, contracts, insurance, suppliers: novate or reissue in Ltd's name. Some (commercial leases, finance) require landlord/lender consent.
  9. Open BS of Ltd: post asset transfer journal.

55.2 Goodwill — the technically tricky bit

Goodwill = value beyond identifiable assets. On incorporation, technically a CGT disposal at MV (s.18 TCGA 1992 — connected-party at MV).

Two main treatments:

  • Pure share consideration → s.162 incorporation relief: gain rolled into share base cost; no immediate CGT. Required: all assets transferred to Ltd in exchange for shares.
  • Mixed (shares + cash/DLA): s.162 partial (£ shares ÷ £ total × gain). The cash/DLA portion of gain is taxable now but BADR may apply (10% up to £1m lifetime) provided 2-year qualifying trade.

55.3 Goodwill amortisation in Ltd

Acquired goodwill amortised under FRS 102 s.18/s.19 (presumed 10-year life). However goodwill amortisation generally non-deductible for CT since 2002 (FA 2002 reform). From April 2019 narrow corporate intangibles regime allows 6.5% write-down where goodwill acquired alongside “qualifying IP” — most plain incorporations don't qualify.

55.4 Other transfer considerations

  • Trading stock: transfer at higher of cost or MV (TCGA s.161). MV creates P&L credit in sole trader's final accounts.
  • Plant & machinery: usually elect TWDV transfer to avoid balancing charge/allowance (CAA 2001 s.266).
  • Property: SDLT applies on land at MV between connected parties (FA 2003 s.53). Often property left in personal name and licensed to Ltd to avoid SDLT.
  • VAT TOGC: meet conditions or face VAT on entire asset transfer.
  • DLA: if Ltd buys assets but doesn't pay cash, the unpaid balance is a credit to Director's Loan — drawable tax-free as repayment of loan in future.

55.5 Loss treatment on transition

  • Sole trader losses: carried forward to set against future income from same trade — but the trade has ceased! Limited use; can elect under s.86 ITA 2007 to relieve against income from new Ltd only if consideration ≥80% shares.
  • Capital losses: remain personal; no transfer.

55.6 Practitioner's incorporation checklist

  1. “Is incorporation worth it” tax model on actual numbers?
  2. 2 years' trade for BADR eligibility?
  3. Goodwill valuation defensible?
  4. VAT TOGC structuring confirmed?
  5. Property treatment decided?
  6. Sale agreement drafted/signed?
  7. Final sole trader SA filed (cessation noted)?
  8. New Ltd opening BS posted?
  9. DLA / share base cost recorded?

Module 55 — Summary

  • Sole trader → Ltd is a CGT event on goodwill at MV (s.18 TCGA).
  • s.162 defers gain if wholly shares; partial if mixed.
  • BADR may cover taxable portion at 10% (2-year qualifying period).
  • TOGC for VAT; elect P&M at TWDV; consider leaving property in personal name.
  • Goodwill amortisation in Ltd usually non-deductible.
  • Final sole trader SA marks cessation.
Knowledge Check

Wholly shares → automatic full s.162.
Q2

Connected-party transactions deemed at MV.
Q3

Q4

Q5

Module 56 · Part 8 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Partnership → LLP / Partnership → Ltd

Partnership-to-LLP is mostly painless — both are tax-transparent — while partnership-to-Ltd involves the harder transition from transparency to a separate taxable entity with all the goodwill, CGT, and TUPE issues. Partnership → LLP: form the LLP mirroring the partnership’s membership and PSR, then HMRC’s concession D33 generally treats it as continuation (no cessation, no transfer-pricing, no CGT). Existing partnership assets continue at carrying value; capital allowance pools roll over; trading losses can be claimed against LLP members on the same continuation basis. Partnership → Ltd: now a real transition — treated like sole-trader-to-Ltd for each partner. Each partner’s share of partnership goodwill triggers CGT (s.162 incorporation relief available if whole business for shares), partnership assets transferred at market value with possible balancing charges, trading losses survive via election (CTA 2010 s.86), CSCH (Capital Account Sale-and-Buy-Back) sometimes useful. SDLT on property, VAT TOGC for new Ltd. LLP → Ltd: same mechanics, plus dealing with LLP wind-down at Companies House. Critical: profit-sharing changes can trigger CGT on goodwill — structure carefully. This module covers each route with worked examples and the partnership-agreement amendments needed pre-transition.

56.1 General partnership → LLP

Mostly painless. Both tax-transparent. Steps:

  1. Form the LLP, mirroring partnership members and PSR.
  2. Draft LLP Agreement.
  3. Transfer assets at book value (no CGT — partnership treated as continuing).
  4. VAT68 to transfer VRN.
  5. Notify clients/suppliers.
  6. Final SA800; new SA800 starts for LLP.

HMRC treats as continuation of trade (provided members substantially same) — no balancing charges, no goodwill CGT.

56.2 Partnership → Ltd

Mechanically similar to sole trader → Ltd, but each partner makes a CGT disposal of their partnership share.

  1. Form Ltd; share allocation typically mirrors PSR.
  2. Each partner's share of business assets transferred at MV.
  3. s.162 if all-shares; partial if mixed.
  4. BADR may cover taxable goodwill at 10% (each partner's £1m lifetime).
  5. Final SA800; cessation; new CT600 for Ltd.
  6. Novate partnership creditors/contracts.

Module 56 — Summary

  • GP → LLP: tax-transparent, treated as continuation.
  • Partnership → Ltd: each partner's share = CGT disposal; s.162 / BADR available.
Module 57 · Part 8 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

First-Year Filings — Compliance Calendar

Every newly-set-up UK business has a year-one filing avalanche — multiple registrations, multiple deadlines, multiple authorities, all overlapping. Miss any one and penalties trigger automatically. The structure of the calendar varies by entity: sole trader — CWF1 by 5 Oct, first SA100 + SA103 by 31 Jan ~15 months later, balancing payment + first POA same day, second POA 31 Jul. Ltd company incorporated 1 Jan 2025 → CS01 confirmation statement due ~1 Jan 2026, first accounts due 1 Oct 2026 (21 months from incorp), CT600 due 12 months after first AP end, CT paid 9 months + 1 day after AP end, plus directors’ SA100s, plus PAYE/RTI from month 1, plus VAT quarters once registered. Partnership/LLP — SA800 for the partnership + SA104 inside each member’s SA100 + LLP CS01 + LLP accounts at CH. Charity — CC annual return + accounts + trustees’ report at CC. Critical traps: registration deadlines before tax-year deadlines (CWF1 5 Oct; VAT <30 days of breach; PAYE before first payday); first accounts long-period for Ltd (split into two APs for CT); director SA100 separate from CT600; auto-enrolment from day 1 of hiring. This module is the compliance calendar by entity type, the deadline tracker, and the year-1 escalation plan.

Part Nine

Cessation Scenarios

9 modules · ~12 hours · Closing every kind of UK business cleanly

Closing a business is its own discipline with distinct compliance, tax and timing rules. Get cessation wrong and clients face stranded VAT, denied losses, surprise tax bills, or director disqualification.

Module 58 · Part 9 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Sole Trader Cessation

Sole-trader cessation is mechanically simple but tax-rich. The final SA103 needs the ceased-trading box ticked + cessation date, final accounts run to the cessation date, plus several special items: balancing charge or allowance on disposal of P&M (CAA 2001 s.55), terminal loss relief (ITA 2007 s.89 — 3-year carry-back), post-cessation receipts taxed in year received (ITA 2007 s.241), NIC adjustments, VAT deregistration via VAT7 (within 30 days of ceasing), and final PAYE if any. Reasons for cessation: retirement, ill-health, business failure, sale to third party, incorporation (covered separately in M55), death of trader. Order of post-cessation actions: (1) stock disposed/transferred, (2) debtors collected/written off, (3) creditors settled, (4) P&M disposed with balancing entries, (5) VAT7 within 30 days, (6) HMRC notification, (7) final SA103 + SA100, (8) close business bank, (9) records kept 5+ years (CTA 2009 s.387 equivalent). Critical: terminal loss calculation extends 12 months before cessation date — can offset prior 3 years of taxable income, often valuable for retirees with prior strong years. This module covers each step, the special-item mechanics, and the year of cessation pro-forma.

58.1 Final SA103 — special items

  • Tick “ceased trading”; enter cessation date
  • Final accounts to cessation date
  • Closing stock at MV (TCGA s.161)
  • Balancing CA charge / allowance
  • Outstanding debtors → post-cessation receipts taxed as income from previous trade

58.2 Capital allowances on cessation

Pools closed. Disposal proceeds vs TWDV: balancing allowance (proceeds < TWDV) or balancing charge (proceeds > TWDV).

58.3 Loss reliefs

  • Terminal loss relief (ITA 2007 s.89): last 12 months of trading loss carried back 3 years (latest first), set against profits of same trade.
  • CY / 12m carry back / sideways s.64 also available.

58.4 VAT deregistration

Within 30 days of ceasing taxable supplies (VAT7).

  • Deemed self-supply: assets retained > £6,000 (excl. VAT) — output VAT due on stock + capital assets retained
  • Final VAT return covers period to dereg date
  • VAT427 for post-dereg input VAT recovery (4 years for some items)

58.5 Other compliance

  • PAYE: close scheme, final FPS marked final, P45s
  • CIS: deregister
  • HMRC notify cessation
  • Insurance: PII run-off (~6 years)

Module 58 — Summary

  • Final SA103 with cessation date.
  • Closing stock at MV; balancing CA on cessation.
  • Terminal loss relief: last 12m carry back 3 years.
  • VAT deregister 30 days; deemed self-supply on retained assets >£6k.

Module 59 · Part 9 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Partnership Cessation

Partnership cessation has TWO layers: the partnership itself winds up (final SA800 with cessation flag, partnership UTR deregistered), and each partner has their own cessation event (final SA104 inside their SA100, terminal loss relief calculated per partner). For LLPs, add a third layer: LLP wind-down at Companies House via LL DS01 strike-off or formal liquidation. Common scenarios: full dissolution (all partners leave, business stops), partial change (one partner retires, remaining partners continue — not a cessation if at least one continues), conversion to sole trader (one partner buys out others — partnership ceases, sole trader emerges), conversion to Ltd (handled in M56). Capital account settlement — each partner’s capital + reserves + share of goodwill paid out, often phased; CGT on disposal of capital interest; BADR available if 2-year ownership + whole/most of business interest. Terminal loss relief (ITA 2007 s.89) applies separately to each partner’s share. VAT, PAYE, public-register dereg all required. This module walks the partnership-level mechanics, per-partner mechanics, LLP wind-down, and the “continuation vs cessation” test that determines which path applies.

Module 60 · Part 9 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Ltd Strike-Off (DS01) — Voluntary Dissolution

Voluntary strike-off via DS01 (Companies Act 2006 s.1003) is the cheapest, simplest route to close a Ltd company — a £33 form to Companies House, 2-3 months of public-notice period, then dissolution. But it’s strictly limited to solvent, simple-affairs companies: not traded in the last 3 months (no recent name change), no insolvency proceedings pending, no CVA, no creditors agreements. The killer constraint: distributable reserves <£25k for tax-efficient distribution via “ESC C16-style” mechanism — over £25k requires MVL (M61) instead. Even with low reserves, TCGA s.1030A from FA 2012 limits the £25k cap to genuine distributions; anti-avoidance rules (TAAR — ITTOIA 2005 s.396B) catch “phoenix” arrangements where shareholders restart the same trade within 2 years. The 5-step process: (1) clear creditors and tax liabilities, (2) distribute reserves, (3) file DS01 + send copies to interested parties (creditors, employees, shareholders, pension trustees), (4) wait 2-3 months for objection window, (5) confirmation of strike-off. Director duties continue throughout. This module walks eligibility, the £25k cap mechanics, BADR availability, anti-phoenixing rules, post-dissolution issues (bona vacantia for missed assets), and the strike-off vs MVL decision.

5 · Post-dissolution 0:56–1:10 Bona vacantia warning; director duties; restoration banner; records footer. “Post-dissolution: undistributed assets go to Crown as bona vacantia. Director duties continue until strike-off. Restoration available within six years via RT01 plus court order. Keep records six years post-dissolution.”

60.1 Eligibility (CA 2006 s.1003)

  • SOLVENT, dormant or simple-affairs Ltd
  • Not traded or changed name in last 3 months
  • Not subject to insolvency proceedings
  • No agreement with creditors (e.g. CVA)

60.2 Process

  1. Settle all known creditors (HMRC for VAT/CT/PAYE).
  2. Distribute remaining assets BEFORE applying for strike-off.
  3. Final CT600 (period to cessation of trade).
  4. Final VAT return; deregister.
  5. Close PAYE; final FPS.
  6. File DS01 (£33 fee online from May 2024); signed by majority of directors.
  7. CH publishes notice in The Gazette; if no objection within 2 months, strike-off complete.
  8. Notify creditors, shareholders, employees within 7 days of DS01.

60.3 £25,000 capital distribution rule (CTA 2010 s.1030A)

  • Pre-strike-off distributions ≤ £25k → capital (CGT, often BADR 10%)
  • > £25k → income dividend (8.75/33.75/39.35%)
  • For larger capital extraction → MVL is the route

60.4 HMRC objection

HMRC objects to strike-off if tax outstanding. Always check HMRC clearance before DS01.

60.5 Restoration if struck off in error

CH (administrative, 6-year limit) or court (CA 2006 s.1024 / s.1029) restoration.

Module 60 — Summary

  • DS01 for solvent simple closure; £33 fee.
  • Settle creditors and distribute assets first.
  • £25k capital cap (s.1030A); above use MVL.
  • HMRC objects if tax outstanding.

Module 61 · Part 9 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Members' Voluntary Liquidation (MVL)

MVL — Members’ Voluntary Liquidation — is the tax-efficient exit route for solvent companies with reserves above the £25k strike-off cap. All distributions to shareholders are treated as capital not income — meaning BADR at 10% (rising to 14% April 2025, 18% April 2026) on the entire reserves, vs dividend tax at 33.75-39.35%. On £500k of reserves that’s ~£100k saved. Process: directors sign Declaration of Solvency (debts paid within 12 months — criminal offence if false), 75% shareholders pass resolution to wind up, appoint Insolvency Practitioner (IP) as liquidator. IP fees: typically £3-7k — worth it if BADR savings > fees. IP takes control, settles creditors, distributes net assets to shareholders. TAAR (ITTOIA s.396B) still applies — same trade within 2 years recharacterises distribution as dividend, killing BADR. Pre-MVL planning: clear DLAs, recover R&D refunds, manage employment status of director-shareholders. Process timeline: 2-6 months typically, occasionally longer if HMRC clearance needed. This module covers eligibility, IP appointment, the £25k threshold decision vs strike-off, TAAR avoidance, BADR mechanics, and post-MVL compliance.

61.1 When MVL is the route

  • Solvent (Declaration of Solvency by directors; debts payable in 12 months)
  • Distributable funds > £25,000
  • Shareholders want capital treatment (CGT/BADR) over dividends

61.2 Process

  1. Directors prepare Declaration of Solvency (sworn).
  2. Members pass special resolution to wind up + appoint IP as liquidator.
  3. Notice in Gazette.
  4. IP gathers assets, settles creditors, distributes surplus to members.
  5. Final meeting; IP files final account at CH.
  6. Company dissolved 3 months after final account.

61.3 Tax treatment

Distributions = CAPITAL:

  • BADR 10% up to £1m lifetime if conditions met
  • AEA £3,000 (2024/25)
  • Higher CGT 20% otherwise

61.4 TAAR (Targeted Anti-Avoidance Rule, 2016)

Distribution re-classified as income dividend if:

  1. Recipient connected (5%+)
  2. Recipient continues same/similar trade within 2 years
  3. Reasonable to assume one main purpose is income tax avoidance

Genuine retirement / sale: not affected.

61.5 IP costs

£1,500–£5,000 typical. BADR savings on £500k distribution can be £100k+.

Module 61 — Summary

  • MVL: solvent, >£25k, capital tax treatment.
  • Declaration of Solvency by directors; IP appointed.
  • TAAR re-classifies as dividend if owner continues similar trade within 2 years.
  • IP costs £1.5k–£5k; BADR savings often substantial.

Creditors' Voluntary Liquidation (CVL)

CVL is the insolvent-company exit — directors recognise the company can’t pay its debts and voluntarily choose liquidation rather than wait for a creditor petition (compulsory liquidation under IA 1986 s.124). Insolvency tests: cash-flow (can’t pay debts as they fall due) and balance-sheet (liabilities exceed assets). Critical timing: from the moment of insolvency, wrongful trading liability begins (IA 1986 s.214) — directors personally liable for additional losses if they continue trading when no reasonable prospect of avoiding liquidation. Process: directors call board meeting → appoint insolvency practitioner → convene shareholders’ meeting (75% to wind up) → hold creditors’ meeting within 14 days (s.100) → IP nominated by creditors becomes liquidator. Director conduct review follows: any breach of duty (wrongful trading, fraudulent trading s.213, preference payments, transactions at undervalue s.238) can result in personal liability AND director disqualification up to 15 years (CDDA 1986). HMRC preferential creditor status restored from 1 Dec 2020 for VAT, PAYE/NIC, CIS — HMRC ranks ahead of floating-charge holders. This module walks the insolvency tests, the timing-critical director duties, the CVL process, and post-CVL disqualification risks.

Insolvent company — debts cannot be paid. Directors choose voluntary liquidation rather than wait for creditor petition.

62.2 Process

  1. Directors decide insolvent.
  2. Members resolve to wind up.
  3. IP appointed (often by directors, with creditor approval).
  4. S.100 creditors' meeting within 14 days.
  5. Liquidator settles creditors in statutory order:
    1. Liquidator's costs & expenses
    2. Secured creditors (fixed charge)
    3. Preferential creditors (employees up to £800 each; HMRC for VAT/PAYE/NI since Dec 2020)
    4. Secured (floating charge) with prescribed part for unsecureds
    5. Unsecured creditors (pro rata)
    6. Members
  6. Final account; dissolution.

62.3 Director consequences

  • Disqualification (CDDA 1986) if conduct “unfit”: 2–15 years
  • Wrongful trading (IA 1986 s.214): personal liability if knew/should have known
  • Fraudulent trading (IA 1986 s.213): personal liability + criminal
  • Personal guarantees crystallise

Module 62 — Summary

  • CVL: insolvent voluntary liquidation; director-initiated.
  • Statutory order of creditor payment.
  • HMRC moved to preferential status for VAT/PAYE/NI from Dec 2020.
  • Wrongful/fraudulent trading risks personal liability + disqualification.
Module 63 · Part 9 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Compulsory Liquidation

Compulsory liquidation is court-ordered winding up — the involuntary version of CVL, triggered by a winding-up petition (IA 1986 s.122). The most common petitioner is a creditor: any debt >£750 + statutory demand unpaid for 21 days = grounds for petition. Other petitioners: the company itself (rare — CVL is faster), directors (joint), shareholders (under just-and-equitable ground), HMRC (significant tax debt), The Secretary of State (public interest under CDDA 1986). Process: petition filed at High Court (or county court for smaller companies), advertised in The Gazette, hearing within ~8 weeks. Court appoints Official Receiver initially (Insolvency Service officer), who may then appoint a private IP. From petition to liquidation order : company assets effectively frozen, transactions can be voided (s.127), bank accounts often frozen by banks. Directors have 21-day window to convert to CVL or otherwise dispose. Director conduct review typically more aggressive than CVL given creditor petition. Same post-liquidation regime as CVL (SoCID2, CDDA 1986, phoenix rules). This module covers petition mechanics, the s.127 freeze, conversion options, the OR’s role, and what to do when a winding-up petition arrives.

Module 64 · Part 9 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Administration & CVA

Administration and CVA are the rescue tools — alternatives to liquidation when the business has rescuable value. Administration (IA 1986 Sch B1) puts the company under court protection while an administrator (licensed IP) restructures or sells it as a going concern. The big benefit: moratorium — creditor action halted, no winding-up petition can be presented, no security can be enforced without consent. Three statutory purposes ranked: (1) rescue as going concern, (2) better result for creditors than liquidation, (3) realise property to distribute to secured/preferential creditors. CVA (IA 1986 Part 1) — Company Voluntary Arrangement — is a deal between company and creditors: typically pay reduced amount over 3-5 years instead of full debt. Approved by 75% by value of creditors. Continues trading throughout. Cheaper than administration but limited: no moratorium except the 28-day “Part A1 moratorium” introduced by CIGA 2020. CIGA 2020 reforms introduced the Restructuring Plan (Part 26A CA 2006) for larger restructurings with cross-class cramdown. Pre-pack administration: sale of business arranged before administration begins, often to connected party — requires SIP 16 statement + new viability statement under SoCV regulations 2021. This module covers administration mechanics, CVA structure, CIGA changes, and when each tool applies.

Module 65 · Part 9 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Final Accounts on Cessation

Final accounts on cessation differ from ordinary year-end accounts in critical ways: going-concern basis no longer applies, so FRS 102 s.3.9 requires the break-up basis — assets at net realisable value, liabilities at settlement amount. For sole traders/partnerships: closing stock at market value (FA disposed of in S.1 of CTA 2010 / equivalent for unincorporated), balancing capital allowance entries on disposed P&M, debtors at recoverable value, write off uncollectible, partnership capital accounts settled. For Ltd companies: prepare to cessation date (often mid-year), include final period AP for CT600, mark balance sheet “Prepared on a break-up basis” if appropriate, recognise liabilities at amounts likely to settle (provisions for dilapidations, redundancy, contingent claims), reverse deferred tax as no future profits, include going-concern note explaining cessation basis. The auditor (if applicable) gives a modified going concern opinion — usually emphasis of matter with cessation paragraph. Cessation-cost provisions: redundancy (when constructive obligation arises, IAS 37 / FRS 102 s.21), lease exit / dilapidations, warranty obligations, contract termination. Asset write-downs — impairment of intangibles, goodwill, PP&E to recoverable amount. This module walks the break-up basis, the disclosures required, the auditor implications, and the bridge to CT600 / SA105 / SA800 closure.

Module 66 · Part 9 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Capital Distributions & BADR

The capital vs income treatment of distributions on company closure determines the tax bill — potentially saving owners 40% of every distribution £. Capital treatment (10% BADR up to £1m, 18% non-BADR) beats dividend tax (33.75-39.35%) at all but the lowest income bands. The routing decision: strike-off DS01 — capital up to £25k, income above (s.1030A); MVL — full capital treatment with BADR (subject to s.396B TAAR); share buy-back — capital treatment if conditions met (CTA 2010 s.1033-1043); liquidation as part of sale — capital. BADR conditions: 2-year ownership period + 5% shareholding + officer/employee status throughout + qualifying business (s.169I TCGA). BADR rates : 10% currently — rising to 14% from 6 April 2025, 18% from 6 April 2026. Lifetime limit £1m. TAAR (ITTOIA s.396B): same trade within 2 years recharacterises distribution from capital to dividend — killing BADR and adding 30 percentage points of tax. Planning rules: clean break, document genuine retirement intent, allow time gap before any new venture, careful clearance applications for borderline cases. This module covers each capital-distribution route, BADR mechanics, TAAR avoidance, the timing decision pre-April-2025 BADR-rate-rises, and the practical decision framework.

Module 67 · Part 10 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Ltd → Sole Trader (Disincorporation)

Disincorporation — reversing a Ltd back to a sole trader — is the rare but tax-expensive transition that catches advisors out. Common reasons: simplification (owner tired of CT, accounts, CH filings), profits dropped below break-even (M49), client decided incorporation didn’t suit, regulatory change. The big problem: there’s no equivalent of s.162 incorporation relief in reverse. Disincorporation triggers: CGT on transfer of company assets to shareholder at market value, balancing charge on P&M disposed (CAA 2001 s.55), VAT TOGC only if conditions met, income tax on undistributed reserves as dividends, BADR if conditions met. The Disincorporation Relief (FA 2013) was a limited time-window relief (2013-2018, never extended) — expired and not available now. Order of operations: clear DLAs, distribute distributable reserves, transfer assets to shareholder at MV, formally cease Ltd trade, strike-off or MVL, register sole trader (CWF1). Cost-benefit: often the “de-incorporation tax cost” exceeds the long-term compliance saving — clients commonly keep dormant Ltd or change to non-trading instead. This module covers the mechanics, the absent reverse-relief, the practical decision tree, and alternatives like dormancy.

3 · 8-step process 0:28–0:43 8-tile grid + TUPE banner + timing note. “Eight steps: clear DLAs, distribute reserves, value assets at market value, transfer to shareholder, VAT TOGC or dereg, register sole trader via CWF1, cease Ltd trade, strike-off or MVL. Plus parallel PAYE cessation and TUPE for any employees.”
4 · Alternatives 0:43–0:56 Dormant/outsource/disincorp options; rare-scenario note. “Three alternatives: dormant Ltd preserving shield and name at low annual cost; outsource compliance to accountant with fixed fee; or actual disincorporation only when tax cost less than multi-year compliance saving. Most clients pick A or B.”
5 · Post-disincorp 0:56–1:10 CWF1 banner; assets-at-MV banner; VAT banner; liability resumed. “Post-disincorporation: register sole trader via CWF1 by 5 October. Assets sit on new sole trader books at market value — new CA pools start. VAT68 transfer or new registration. Personal liability resumes — update insurance.”

67.1 Why disincorporate

  • Simplification — owner tired of CT, CH filings
  • Profits dropped below break-even (Module 49)
  • Cost of compliance exceeds tax saving
  • Owner doesn't need limited liability

67.2 No clean tax route

Unlike sole trader → Ltd (s.162 incorporation relief), there is no equivalent reverse relief. Disincorporation Relief (2013–2018) expired.

Ltd transferring business to director triggers:

  • CGT on goodwill at MV (s.18 TCGA — connected parties)
  • Balancing CA charge on P&M
  • Stock at MV
  • VAT issues (TOGC may apply)
  • Distribution to shareholder (capital if MVL, dividend if direct)

67.3 Practical steps

  1. Value business assets and goodwill.
  2. Decide route: MVL (capital + BADR) or wind-down + DS01 (capital ≤£25k).
  3. Sole trader registers for SA.
  4. Ltd transfers assets to sole trader at MV.
  5. Apply VAT TOGC if applicable.
  6. Final CT600 covers period to cessation.
  7. Distribution to shareholder.
  8. CH closure (DS01 or post-MVL dissolution).
  9. Sole trader operates from new VRN (or transferred VRN).

67.4 Practical reality

Many owners either: (a) leave Ltd dormant rather than disincorporate; or (b) MVL for capital extraction at BADR, then continue as sole trader if TAAR doesn't apply.

Module 67 — Summary

  • No reverse equivalent of s.162 — disincorporation is taxed.
  • Disincorporation Relief (2013–2018) not renewed.
  • Common route: MVL distribution + sole trader continues if TAAR allows.
  • Alternative: leave Ltd dormant.

No reverse incorporation relief.
Q2

s.18 TCGA — connected-party at MV.

MVL exploits BADR; TAAR risk if same trade resumed within 2 years.
Module 68 · Part 10 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Sole Trader → Partnership

Sole-trader-to-partnership is the tax-light transition — both regimes are tax-transparent, both file SA. The sole trader brings their existing trade into a new partnership with one or more incoming partners. Critical tax point: this is treated as a cessation of sole trader trade + commencement of partnership trade, but basis-period continuation generally applies (no balancing charges if assets pass at carrying value). However, the incoming partner acquires a share of goodwill at market value — potential CGT for the original sole trader if a market-value consideration is received. The 5 setup steps: (1) draft Partnership Agreement covering PSR, salaries, drawings, dispute resolution; (2) register partnership for SA via SA400 (gets partnership UTR); (3) each new partner registers for individual SA via SA401; (4) nominate a partner for SA800 filing; (5) update VAT registration (VAT68 transfer or new). Final SA103 for sole trader closes the unincorporated trade; first SA800 with SA104s for all partners. Basis-period reform (M42) applies — tax-year basis from 24/25. Common scenarios: bringing in spouse or child (income-splitting), bringing in service partner for capital injection, professional firm formalising existing arrangement. This module covers the mechanics, the goodwill mechanics, basis continuation, and the Partnership Agreement essentials.

Module 69 · Part 10 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Partnership → Ltd (cross-reference Module 56)

The partnership-to-Ltd route is comprehensively covered in M56; this module is the quick-reference recap emphasising the partner-specific mechanics. Each partner makes a CGT disposal of their partnership interest — goodwill, premises, intangibles, all transferred to Ltd at market value. Section 162 incorporation relief defers CGT if consideration is wholly shares; section 165 gift relief available where shares are gifted; BADR may cover any taxable element (10%, rising 14%/18%). Process: final SA800 cessation with all partners’ allocations, incorporate Ltd with shares allocated per partner’s pre-incorporation share, sale agreement transferring assets+goodwill, TUPE for employees, VAT TOGC, deregister partnership UTR, each partner files final SA104. Critical timing: align partnership year-end with incorporation date to simplify final allocation; consider basis-period reform position; LLP wind-down at Companies House via LL DS01 strike-off if LLP. Loss preservation: CTA 2010 s.86 allows trading losses to carry forward into the Ltd if same trade continues. Reserve distribution timing: capital accounts settled BEFORE or AFTER incorporation — pre-incorp better for clean ledger but post-incorp can be DLA-credit mechanism. This module sketches the structure; deep mechanics in M56.

Module 70 · Part 10 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Group Restructuring

Group structures — HoldCo + multiple subsidiaries — serve risk separation, sale optionality, tax planning, and operational separation. Typical patterns: HoldCo + trading sub + IP sub + property sub; trading group with separate brand entities; family investment company (FIC) + trading sub . Key tax reliefs: group relief (CTA 2010 Part 5) for trading losses; SSE (Substantial Shareholding Exemption) (TCGA Sch 7AC) for trading-co share disposals — the “capital gains exemption” for groups, 10%+ shareholding for 12+ months; intra-group asset transfers no gain/no loss (TCGA s.171) — can move assets within group without CGT; SDLT relief on group transfers (FA 2003 Sch 7); VAT group registration simplifies intra-group supplies. Anti-avoidance traps: SSE “trading” test (no >20% non-trading activities), depreciatory transaction rules, transfer-pricing for connected company transactions. Setting up: insert HoldCo via share-for-share exchange (TCGA s.135 + s.136 + CTA s.110), or direct subscription (SDLT issue if shares paid in cash). This module covers group structures, the major reliefs, the SSE conditions, intra-group transfers, VAT grouping, and the demerger options (covered M73).

70.1 Why create a group

  • Risk separation (trading sub, IP sub, property sub)
  • Sale optionality
  • JV vehicle
  • Investor protection (Holdco shares simpler)
  • BADR optimisation

70.2 Holdco over existing TradingCo (share-for-share, s.135)

Existing shareholders transfer their shares in TradingCo to a new HoldCo in exchange for new HoldCo shares. HoldCo shares inherit base cost — no immediate CGT (s.135 exchange relief). HMRC clearance (s.138) advisable.

70.3 Inter-group asset transfers — TCGA s.171

Transfers of capital assets between members of a 75% group: no gain / no loss. Allows asset reorganisation without CGT.

70.4 Stamp Duty

  • 0.5% Stamp Duty on share transfers
  • FA 1930 s.42 group relief: 75% group transfers exempt
  • FA 1986 s.75 reconstruction relief

70.5 Substantial Shareholding Exemption (SSE)

Corporate parent disposing of 10%+ shares in trading subsidiary held 12+ months: gain exempt from CT (TCGA Sch 7AC). Major incentive for grouping pre-sale.

Module 70 — Summary

  • s.135 share-for-share creates HoldCo without CGT trigger.
  • s.171 inter-group asset transfers no gain / no loss.
  • Stamp Duty group relief s.42 FA 1930.
  • SSE exempts qualifying corporate disposals.

Module 71 · Part 10 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Ltd → Charity / CIO Conversion

Ltd-to-charity is the mission-shift transition — a trading Ltd becomes a registered charity to access tax exemption, Gift Aid, grant funding eligibility, and legacies. Two routes: (1) convert existing Ltd to CLG — change articles to charitable purposes, register with CC + HMRC, may need court order; (2) incorporate new CIO + transfer trade — simpler, common preferred route post-2013. The critical issue: existing shareholders cannot benefit after conversion — charitable purpose means no private benefit. Disposal of shares by founders to charity: TCGA s.257 gift-to-charity relief (no CGT) + income-tax relief (s.431 ITA) for the donor. Property transfer : SDLT relief if transferred to charity for charitable purposes (FA 2003 Sch 8). Asset transfer to CIO: structured carefully to maintain HMRC charity tax status; trading subsidiary often retained for revenue-generating activities. Compliance shift: from CT600 + CH accounts to CC online return + Charities SORP accounts. Trustees appointed (fit-and-proper test). VAT: charities have partial exemption + reduced rate access. This module covers both routes, the share-disposal mechanics, the asset transfer, and the year-1 compliance calendar.

Module 72 · Part 10 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Sale of Business — Asset Sale vs Share Sale

The asset-sale vs share-sale decision in M&A is the most consequential structuring choice for both buyer and seller — affecting tax cost, deal complexity, liability transfer, and consideration mechanics. Asset sale: buyer cherry-picks specific assets + assumes specific liabilities — seller’s Ltd retains residual exposure, leftover cash, the legal entity. Tax for asset sale: seller faces double-tax friction (CT on gains in Ltd, then dividend/MVL tax on extraction); buyer gets step-up on asset base costs + new CA pools + goodwill amortisation deduction (post-1 April 2002 goodwill). Share sale: buyer acquires the company itself — gets all assets + ALL liabilities (warranties + indemnities cover unknown risks). Tax for share sale : seller gets single-tax (CGT on shares, BADR available); buyer inherits historic base costs, no step-up, but no double-tax. SSE (M70) applies if seller is corporate. Buyer typically prefers asset sale (control over what’s taken, step-up, no historic liabilities); seller typically prefers share sale (cleaner exit, single tax, BADR). Deal structuring : warranties, indemnities, completion accounts, locked-box, escrow, deferred consideration, earn-outs. SDLT on property in asset sale; VAT TOGC for asset sales of going concerns. This module covers the comparison, mechanics, and the inevitable negotiation tension.

72.1 The two structures

Asset Sale Share Sale
What's sold Individual assets + goodwill Shares in the company
Seller The company Shareholders
Tax on seller CT on company gain + then dividend/distribution CGT (often BADR 10%) direct
Buyer Picks specific assets, leaves liabilities Inherits everything (known + contingent)
Buyer's CT base Higher cost base — CAs, goodwill amortisation if applicable Inherits company's existing tax base
VAT TOGC available VAT exempt (sale of shares)
Stamp duty SDLT on land; nil on goodwill 0.5% on shares
Typical preference Buyer Seller

72.3 Earn-outs

Marren v Ingles principle:

  • Estimated value included in disposal proceeds at sale date
  • Difference on actual receipt = separate disposal of chose in action
  • s.279A election to defer where contingent becomes “ascertainable” later

72.4 Loan notes / QCBs

Qualifying Corporate Bonds defer gain until QCB redeemed. BADR can apply on subsequent disposal.

Module 72 — Summary

  • Asset sale: company taxed; shareholder then taxed on extraction. Buyer-friendly.
  • Share sale: shareholder direct CGT/BADR. Seller-friendly.
  • Stamp duty: 0.5% shares; SDLT on land in asset sale.
  • Earn-outs: Marren v Ingles + s.279A election.
  • Loan notes / QCBs can defer gain.

Module 73 · Part 10 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Demergers

Demergers split a single corporate group into two or more independently-owned entities — typically to separate trading and investment activities, prepare for sale of one business, resolve shareholder disputes, or unlock SSE eligibility. Three statutory routes: (1) Distribution-in-specie demerger (CTA 2010 s.1075-1086) — HoldCo distributes shares in subsidiary to its shareholders; (2) Capital reduction demerger (CA 2006 s.641-653) — court-confirmed reduction creates demerger reserve to distribute; (3) Liquidation demerger (TCGA s.137) — HoldCo liquidates, assets distributed to new HoldCos via s.110 IA 1986. Tax treatment requires careful structuring: distribution-in-specie generally tax-neutral if conditions met (TCGA s.139); shareholders deemed to dispose of original shares + acquire new shares with cost-basis split; HMRC clearance mandatory via SP3/16 advance assurance. Stamp duty: usually relieved via CTA s.77 reconstruction relief. SDLT: relieved for group transfers if within 75% group at relevant times. Anti-avoidance: Transactions in Securities rules (ITA s.684), TAAR. Common scenarios: trading + investment split, family disputes splitting family co, partial divestment ahead of trade sale. This module sketches each route, tax mechanics, clearance requirements, and the typical demerger timeline.

ITA s.684 transactions in securities anti-avoidance. Commercial reasons critical. Timeline three to six months. Specialist tax counsel essential.”

73.1 Three statutory routes

  1. Distribution-in-specie (s.1075 CTA 2010): split group's trading subs into two Holdcos owned by original shareholders.
  2. Reduction of capital demerger (CA 2006 s.641): court-confirmed capital reduction.
  3. Liquidation demerger (s.110 IA 1986): liquidator splits the trade.

73.2 Use case

Owner-managed group has Trading Co A and Trading Co B; founders want to separate so daughter takes A, son takes B. Demerger creates two Holdcos owned separately, without an immediate CGT trigger.

73.3 Conditions

Statutory demerger (s.1075) needs HMRC clearance + conditions about trading nature and post-demerger holding. Failure → distribution treated as income dividend.

Module 73 — Summary

  • Three demerger routes: distribution-in-specie, capital reduction, liquidation s.110.
  • HMRC clearance and trade-nature conditions required.
Module 74 · Part 10 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Reconstructions

A reconstruction moves a trade and assets from one company to another without losing tax continuity — the recipient carries on the same trade and shareholders are substantially identical. Legal hook: CTA 2010 s.939 (continuation of trade) and CTA 2010 s.940A-947 (transfer of trade) set out the relief, which lets the recipient inherit the transferor’s trading-loss position, capital allowances pools, and various other tax attributes. Stamp duty relief: CTA 2010 s.77 reconstruction relief on the share-for-share exchange. SDLT : FA 2003 Sch 7 reconstruction relief on property transfers. CGT relief: TCGA s.139 covers business reconstructions where shares are issued. Typical uses: moving trade between group companies, hive-down of trade to a new sub before sale, reorganisation prior to listing, separating trade from non-trading assets. Conditions to qualify: same shareholders, same trade continues, consideration substantially in shares, commercial reason . HMRC clearance via SP3/16 again advisable. Distinguishing from demerger : reconstruction preserves single-entity outcome (trade moves but ownership doesn’t change); demerger creates separate ownerships. This module covers the relief framework, conditions, common scenarios, and the “hive-down + sale” case study.

Module 75 · Part 11 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

IR35 / Off-Payroll Working Rules

IR35 (the Intermediaries Legislation) is the UK’s anti-avoidance regime preventing individuals from avoiding employee taxes by interposing a Personal Service Company (PSC). If the engagement “would be employment” absent the PSC — full PAYE + NIC applies on the deemed employment income. Originally introduced by FA 2000 (Chapter 8 ITEPA 2003), the off-payroll working rules (Chapter 10 ITEPA 2003) shifted the IR35 assessment + tax-deduction burden to the end client from April 2017 (public sector) and April 2021 (medium/large private sector). Small companies (CA 2006 size) still apply Chapter 8 — PSC determines own status. Status tests from Ready Mixed Concrete v MoP 1968 : mutuality of obligation, personal service / substitution, control, plus other factors (financial risk, equipment, integration). HMRC’s CEST tool gives a (sometimes-binding) determination. Status Determination Statement (SDS): client must issue to PSC + fee-payer (often the agency) before first payment + on change. Penalties : deemed payments triggered, PAYE/NIC due, interest + penalties on under-payment. Practical impact: many PSCs have shut down post-2021; rise of umbrella companies for contractor markets. This module covers the legal framework, status tests, SDS mechanics, CEST limitations, and the post-2021 contractor market shifts.

75.1 What IR35 is

Anti-avoidance: prevents individuals avoiding employee taxes by interposing a personal service company (PSC). If the engagement “would be employment” absent the PSC, IR35 applies — full PAYE/NI on deemed employment income.

75.2 Status tests (Ready Mixed Concrete v MoP 1968)

  1. Personal Service: must the worker do the work, or can they substitute?
  2. Mutuality of Obligation (MOO): ongoing offer/accept obligation?
  3. Control: how, what, when, where over the work?

Plus secondary: financial risk, equipment, exclusivity, integration, intention.

75.3 Who decides status

  • Pre-April 2017 private sector: worker (via PSC).
  • Public sector since April 2017: client (SDS — Status Determination Statement).
  • Private sector since April 2021: medium/large clients determine; small clients = worker still decides.

75.4 If inside IR35

  • Fee payer (client/agency) deducts PAYE/NI on deemed direct payment to worker
  • Employer NI applies (fee payer = NI employer)
  • Worker offsets deemed employment income against PSC income to avoid double tax

75.5 CEST

HMRC's status check tool. HMRC stands by results if answers honest. Many disputes; tribunals have overturned.

Module 75 — Summary

  • IR35 prevents disguised employment via PSCs.
  • Tests: Personal service, MOO, Control + secondary.
  • Determination: medium/large clients in private sector since April 2021.
  • Inside IR35 → fee payer deducts PAYE/NI.
Module 76 · Part 11 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Inheritance Tax

Inheritance Tax (IHT) is the UK’s charge on transfers of value — primarily death estates but also lifetime gifts within 7 years. Headline rates: 40% on death , 36% if 10%+ left to charity, 20% on lifetime chargeable transfers (e.g., transfers into discretionary trusts). The Nil Rate Band (NRB) is £325,000 (frozen since 2009 until 2030 per latest Budget); spouses can transfer unused NRB giving £650k. Residence Nil Rate Band (RNRB): extra £175k if main residence passes to direct descendants — tapered above £2m estate. Key reliefs: Spouse exemption (unlimited if both UK domiciled), Charity exemption, Business Property Relief (BPR) — 100% on trading-business assets held 2+ years, Agricultural Property Relief (APR) — 100% on owner-occupied farms (50% if tenanted), annual exemption £3k, small gifts £250/person, marriage gifts, normal expenditure out of income exemption. PETs vs CLTs: gifts to individuals are PETs (potentially exempt) — full relief if donor survives 7 years; gifts to trusts are CLTs (immediate 20% if exceed NRB). April 2026 changes: BPR cap at £1m (50% above), APR also capped, pension funds becoming taxable in estate. This module covers the regime, reliefs, planning, and the 2026 reform impact.

  • Tax on transfers of value: death estate + lifetime gifts within 7 years
  • 40% on death; 36% if 10%+ to charity; 20% on lifetime CLTs
  • NRB: £325k (frozen until April 2030)
  • RNRB: £175k (qualifying main residence to direct descendants); tapers when estate > £2m

76.2 Lifetime gifts

  • PETs: gifts to individuals — exempt if donor survives 7 years
  • CLTs: gifts into trusts — 20% lifetime (or 25% if donor pays)
  • Taper relief: gifts 3-7 years before death taxed at 80/60/40/20/0% of full rate

76.3 Annual exemptions

  • £3,000/year (carry forward 1 year)
  • £250 small gifts per recipient
  • Wedding: £5k parent / £2.5k grandparent / £1k other
  • Normal expenditure out of income (regular pattern)
  • Spouses/CPs: unlimited if both UK-domiciled

76.4 Business Property Relief (BPR)

  • Unquoted trading shares: 100%
  • Quoted controlling holding (50%+ voting): 100%
  • Quoted minority: nil (limited exceptions)
  • Sole trader/partnership trading business: 100%
  • Land/buildings used by business owned by deceased: 50%

2-year ownership; trading not investment.

76.5 Agricultural Property Relief (APR)

100% or 50% on agricultural land/buildings; 2-year (owner-occupied) or 7-year (let).

76.6 Spring Budget 2024 IHT changes

  • NRB and RNRB frozen until April 2030
  • BPR/APR limited to £1m combined (Autumn 2024 announcement)
  • Residence-based regime replaces domicile-based from April 2025

Module 76 — Summary

  • NRB £325k + RNRB £175k frozen to April 2030.
  • 40% death; 20% lifetime CLT.
  • BPR 100% on unquoted trading shares (subject to upcoming £1m cap).
  • Residence-based regime from April 2025.
Module 77 · Part 11 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Stamp Duty Land Tax

SDLT is a transaction tax on UK property purchases (England + Northern Ireland; Scotland uses LBTT, Wales uses LTT). Residential rates 2024/25 (post-1 April 2025 changes): standard bands at 0% £0-£125k, 2% £125k-£250k, 5% £250k-£925k, 10% £925k-£1.5m, 12% above. First-time buyer relief: 0% up to £300k, 5% £300k-£500k (relief lost above £500k). Additional Property +3% for BTL, second homes, corporate purchases — rising to +5% surcharge announced in 2024 Budget. Non-resident +2% for individuals not UK-resident. ATED for >£500k residential held by corporates. Non-residential rates: 0% to £150k, 2% £150k-£250k, 5% above. Mixed-use: non-residential rates apply (~30% saving) — HMRC heavily disputes. Reliefs: group relief (FA 2003 Sch 7), incorporation relief, Multiple Dwellings Relief (MDR abolished June 2024), shared ownership relief. Filing: SDLT1 return + payment within 14 days of completion. Late filing penalties: £100 then escalating. This module covers rates, surcharges, reliefs, the mixed-use battle, and the SDLT1 mechanics.

CGT — Reliefs Deep Dive

M44 covered the SA108 mechanics — this module is the reliefs deep dive . The major CGT reliefs: BADR (Business Asset Disposal Relief) — 10% rising to 14% April 2025, 18% April 2026, £1m lifetime; Investors’ Relief — separate £10m lifetime cap for newly-subscribed unquoted trading-co shares held 3+ years; Rollover Relief (TCGA s.152) — defer gain on disposal of business asset reinvested in qualifying replacement within 12m before / 36m after; Holdover Relief (TCGA s.165) — gift of business asset defers gain to recipient; Incorporation Relief (s.162) — M55; PPR — M44 main residence exemption; EIS deferral relief — defer gain by reinvesting in EIS shares; SEIS reinvestment relief — 50% exemption on gains reinvested. Stacking : reliefs can combine — e.g., BADR on sale + EIS deferral on portion. Conditions per relief: ownership period, qualifying activity, trader status, reinvestment timing. Anti-avoidance : TAAR catches BADR phoenix patterns. Hold-over: only on assets used in trade or in a trading company; investment assets excluded. Letting relief: only if shared occupancy post-April 2020. This module is the practitioner’s CGT-relief cheat-sheet.

Module 79 · Part 11 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Trusts

A trust is a legal arrangement where trustees hold assets for the benefit of beneficiaries under terms set by the settlor. Four main types: bare trust (transparent for tax — income/gains taxed on beneficiary), interest in possession (IIP) (beneficiary entitled to income as it arises), discretionary trust (trustees decide what/when to distribute), accumulation trust (income reinvested for future generations). Tax treatment: IIP — income taxed on beneficiary (45% if over band), trustees pay 20%/8.75% then beneficiary credits. Discretionary trusts — trustees pay 45% income tax + 39.35% dividends, beneficiaries get tax credit on distribution. Capital gains: trustees pay 20% (24% residential), £1.5k AEA (half individual). IHT treatment: relevant property regime — 10-year periodic charge up to 6%, exit charges, entry CLT at 20% if above NRB. Trust Registration Service (TRS) mandatory for most trusts since 2022. Common uses: protect minor inheritance, vulnerable beneficiary, family wealth preservation, charitable giving, IHT planning. Settlor-interested trust: anti-avoidance — income taxed on settlor. Practitioner role: trust accounts, trustees’ SA900 return, distribution planning. This module covers types, tax, TRS compliance, and the planning angles.

Module 80 · Part 11 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Non-Domiciled Status (Until April 2025)

The non-dom regime was abolished from 6 April 2025 — but legacy planning for clients who relied on it continues for years to come. Pre-2025: UK-resident-but-non-UK-domiciled individuals could elect remittance basis — UK tax only on UK-source income/gains + amounts remitted to UK. Remittance basis charge (RBC): £30k/year if UK resident 7 of last 9 tax years, £60k if 12 of 14. Deemed domiciled: long-term residents (15 of last 20) treated as UK-dom for IT/CGT/IHT. From April 2025: replaced by 4-year FIG regime (Foreign Income & Gains) for new arrivals with 10+ years overseas — first 4 years UK-resident, foreign income/gains exempt. Existing non-doms transition: 50% rebasing election for capital assets, Temporary Repatriation Facility (TRF) — bring offshore funds at 12% (2025/26-2026/27) then 15% (2027/28). IHT shift: long-term residents (10+ years) face IHT on worldwide assets — major hit for offshore trusts. Excluded property trust protection lost. Planning: trust restructuring, asset sales pre-2025 for old base costs, FIG elections, family relocation. This module covers the legacy regime, transition rules, FIG election mechanics, and current planning considerations.

Module 81 · Part 11 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

HMRC Enquiries

An HMRC enquiry is a formal investigation under TMA 1970 / FA 1998 into a tax return. Types: aspect (single area), full (entire return), cross-tax (multiple regimes), code of practice 8 (suspected fraud, civil), code of practice 9 / contractual disclosure facility (CDF) (suspected serious fraud, immunity for disclosure). Section 9A TMA 1970 (SA enquiry): HMRC has 12 months from filing to open enquiry (or 12m from later filing if amended). FA 1998 Sch 18 para 24 (CT600): same 12-month window. Discovery assessment: longer windows — 4 years (innocent), 6 years (careless), 20 years (deliberate). Schedule 36 FA 2008: HMRC information powers — can issue formal notices for documents/info, third-party notices to banks/agents, with tribunal pre-approval for some. Practitioner duties: PCRT compliance, AML reporting if uncovers tax evasion. Process: opening letter → information gathering → meeting → settlement discussions → closure notice + assessment OR appeal. Settlement: COP 9 immunity for full disclosure, otherwise penalty regime (M82) applies. This module covers enquiry types, time limits, Schedule 36 powers, and practitioner client-handling.

Module 82 · Part 11 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Penalty Regimes

UK tax penalties fall into three broad categories: late filing, late payment, and error/inaccuracy. Late filing: SA £100 immediate + £10/day after 3 months (max £900) + 5% or £300 at 6m and 12m. CT600: £100 + £200 + 10%/20% of CT at 6/12 months. Late payment: 5% surcharge at 30 days late + 5% at 6 months + 5% at 12 months + interest from due date. Error penalties (FA 2007 Sch 24): 0% for innocent error (genuine mistake despite reasonable care), up to 30% for careless, up to 70% for deliberate, up to 100% for deliberate concealed. Disclosure mitigation: unprompted disclosure reduces minimum penalty significantly — e.g., careless 0% min vs 15% prompted. Behaviour assessment: HMRC categorises based on records, advisor use, prior warnings. Suspension: careless penalties suspendable if specific improvements made within 24 months. Offshore penalties: higher rates — up to 200% on offshore matters under FA 2016 Sch 18. VAT default surcharge: 2-15% on late VAT. Worldwide Disclosure Facility: ongoing voluntary disclosure with penalty mitigation. This module covers the penalty matrix, behaviour assessment, mitigation strategies, and the suspension regime.

Module 83 · Part 12 of 12 · ~2 hours · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

AML & MLR 2017

AML is the gateway compliance for every UK accountant and bookkeeper. MLR 2017 (Money Laundering, Terrorist Financing and Transfer of Funds Regulations) implements EU 4th AMLD, with later 5th AMLD updates. Practising without supervision = criminal offence (reg.56, up to 2 years). Three lines of defence: (1) Customer Due Diligence (CDD) — identify + verify clients before onboarding (regs.27-28); (2) Ongoing monitoring + transaction review; (3) Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) to NCA when knowledge/suspicion of money laundering or terrorism. CDD types: Standard, Simplified (low risk), Enhanced (EDD) for PEPs, high-risk countries, complex structures. Beneficial owner identification: 25%+ ownership thresholds, ultimate human owners. Practice obligations: written risk assessment, AML policies, MLRO (Money Laundering Reporting Officer), staff training, record-keeping 5+ years. Supervisors: ICAEW, ACCA, AAT, CIOT, HMRC (for unregulated). POCA 2002: SAR + tipping-off offence under s.333A. Failure to disclose: 5 years prison (s.330 POCA). Penalties: civil + criminal + supervisory action including practising certificate revocation. This module covers MLR framework, CDD mechanics, SAR reporting, and the practice-level compliance infrastructure.

Module 84 · Part 12 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Professional Ethics

UK accountancy ethics is governed by the IESBA Code of Ethics (International Ethics Standards Board for Accountants) implemented by professional bodies (ICAEW, ACCA, AAT, CIOT, CIMA). Five fundamental principles: (1) Integrity — straightforward and honest in professional/business relationships; (2) Objectivity — no bias, conflict of interest, undue influence; (3) Professional Competence + Due Care — maintain knowledge, apply diligently; (4) Confidentiality — protect client information unless legal duty / authorised; (5) Professional Behaviour — comply with laws + avoid discrediting the profession. Conceptual framework: identify threats → evaluate significance → apply safeguards → if not at acceptable level, decline / withdraw. Threats: self-interest, self-review, advocacy, familiarity, intimidation. Safeguards: regulatory (CPD, supervision), firm-level (engagement quality reviews, second partner reviews), engagement-level (rotation, partners-only meetings). Common dilemmas: conflicts of interest, client pressure to participate in tax avoidance, discovery of client fraud, fee dependency . PCRT applies to tax specifically. Whistleblowing: protected disclosure under PIDA 1998. This module covers principles, conceptual framework application, common dilemmas, and the disciplinary process.

Module 85 · Part 12 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Engagement Letters

The engagement letter is the contractual foundation of every accounting relationship — required by all professional bodies (ICAEW, ACCA, AAT, CIOT). Without one, professional indemnity insurance may not respond, fee recovery is harder, and scope disputes become acrimonious. Standard contents: parties, scope of services, fee basis, payment terms, respective responsibilities (client’s vs accountant’s), information & record requirements, confidentiality, complaints procedure, limitation of liability, termination, governing law. Scope precision matters: separate letters for audit, statutory accounts, tax, payroll, advisory. Tax-specific clauses: PCRT compliance, who initiates HMRC contact, post-cessation responsibilities. Fee mechanisms: hourly, fixed-fee, value-based, retainer. Limitation of liability: cap typically 2-3x annual fee or specific amount per ICAEW guidance. Annual review + update for scope or fee changes. Disengagement letter when relationship ends. Reliance letter when third party (bank) wants comfort. Sub-contracting: notify client + maintain confidentiality + check supervisor permissions. Specimen letters from ICAEW, ACCA available. This module covers structure, key clauses, fee mechanisms, liability caps, and the engagement lifecycle.

Module 86 · Part 12 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

GDPR for Accountants

UK GDPR + Data Protection Act 2018 apply to all accountants handling personal data — which is basically every practice. Most practices are data controllers for client data (decide purpose + means); outsourced functions like payroll bureaux are data processors acting on the controller’s instructions. Six lawful bases for processing: consent , contract, legal obligation (MLR records), vital interests, public task, legitimate interests. Special category data (health, biometric, etc.) needs additional Article 9 condition. Data subject rights: access, rectification, erasure, restriction, portability, objection, automated decisions. Practice obligations : ICO registration + annual fee, privacy notice on website, retention schedule, DPIA for high-risk, data processing agreement with processors. Breach reporting: within 72 hours to ICO if risk to data subjects. Subject Access Request (SAR): 1 month free response (extendable). International transfers: post-Brexit safeguards, SCCs or adequacy. Penalties: up to 4% of global turnover or £17.5m. ICO enforcement: investigations, audits, monetary penalty notices. Cloud practice: check provider locations, encryption, access controls. This module covers controller/processor distinction, lawful bases, subject rights, breach response, and practice-level compliance.

Module 87 · Part 12 of 12 · ~1 hour · with 65-second animated explainer + MP4 storyboard

Professional Indemnity Insurance (PII)

PII is the mandatory practice insurance covering professional negligence, errors, breach of duty and the resulting client claims. Required by all UK accountancy bodies (ICAEW, ACCA, AAT, CIOT). ICAEW minimum cover: 2.5x fee income, £1.5m floor, £5m max. ACCA : similar tiered structure. Cover scope: civil liability arising from professional services rendered — includes errors, omissions, breach of confidentiality, dishonesty of employees. Common exclusions: criminal acts, intentional dishonesty by principal, war/terrorism, asbestos, regulatory fines. Claims-made basis: cover applies when claim made (not when act committed) — continuous cover essential including run-off cover (typically 6+ years) when practice closes. Premium drivers: fee income, claims history, services offered (advisory + tax higher), staff numbers, supervisor type. Excess/deductible: amount practice pays per claim. Claims process: notify insurer immediately of circumstance + claim, do not admit liability, cooperate fully. Practical points: maintain accurate disclosure on renewal, declare past claims, review limits annually, consider cyber + employers liability + management liability add-ons. Without PII: cannot practice + supervisor disciplinary + personal liability for losses. This module covers requirements, cover, exclusions, premium drivers, and the claims process.

1 · Why PII 0:00–0:13 Covers vs excludes; ICAEW minimum; claims-made. “PII is mandatory practice insurance covering negligence, errors, breach of duty. ICAEW minimum two and a half times fee income with one point five to five million limits. Claims-made — continuous cover essential. Without PII: cannot practice.”
2 · Cover detail 0:13–0:28 Civil liability; employee dishonesty; key exclusions; excess. “Cover: civil liability from services including tax errors, audit failures, missed deadlines. Defence costs included. Employee dishonesty sub-limit. Excludes criminal acts, war, asbestos, HMRC penalties. Excess one to twenty five thousand typical.”
3 · Premium drivers 0:28–0:43 6 driver tiles + tax high-risk + run-off banner. “Premium drivers: fee income base, claims history, services offered, staff numbers, supervisor, risk management. Tax and investigations high-risk surcharge. Run-off cover six plus years post-closure essential.”
4 · Claims process 0:43–0:56 5-step claims ladder + notify warning. “Claims process: notify insurer immediately, do not admit liability or pay, insurer appoints panel solicitor, cooperate fully, settlement or defence. Failure to notify can void cover — report even uncertain matters.”
5 · Risk management 0:56–1:10 Engagement letters; quality controls; cyber add-on; review limits. “Risk management: clear engagement letters with liability cap, quality controls under ISQM with second partner reviews, cyber PII add-on for ransomware. Review limits annually as practice grows.”

87.1 Why PII

Required by professional bodies. Covers negligence, errors, breach of duty.

87.2 Cover (ICAEW)

  • Minimum: 2.5× gross fee income; capped £1.5m for fees ≤£600k
  • Minimum £100k for smallest practices
  • Aggregate cap typically 1× cover
  • Excess: £1k–£10k

87.3 What PII covers

  • Civil claims for damages
  • Defence costs
  • Loss of client documents
  • Some include cyber and run-off

87.4 Run-off cover

6 years post-cessation (matches Limitation Act period). Significant cost — budget into closure plan.

Module 87 — Summary

  • PII mandatory; 2.5× gross fees minimum (ICAEW).
  • Covers negligence, errors, defence costs.
  • Run-off 6 years post-cessation.

Appendix B

UK Compliance Calendar (Annual Cycle)

April

  • 5 April: end of UK tax year
  • 6 April: new tax year — apply new tax codes, NI thresholds, statutory pay rates
  • 19 April: final EPS for prior tax year
  • 22 April (electronic): March PAYE payment

May

  • 3 May: previous month's CIS300 + PAYE/NIC
  • 7 May: VAT return Q/E 31 March
  • 31 May: P60s issued to employees

July

  • 5 July: PSA agreement application
  • 6 July: P11D + P11D(b) filed
  • 22 July (electronic): Class 1A NI on BIK
  • 31 July: 2nd Self Assessment Payment on Account
  • 7 July: VAT return Q/E 31 May

October

  • 5 October: register for SA (new SA taxpayers)
  • 22 October: PSA payment
  • 31 October: paper SA returns; partnership paper SA800

December / January

  • 30 December: SA return online if owe <£3,000 collected via PAYE
  • 31 December: many companies' year-end; CS01 due 14 days after anniversary
  • 31 January: SA online + balancing payment + 1st POA
  • 7 January: VAT return Q/E 30 November

Monthly

  • 22nd (electronic): PAYE/NIC + CIS deductions
  • 19th: CIS300 monthly return
  • FPS on or before each pay date
  • EPS by 19th of following month

Per-company schedule (varies by ARD)

  • Confirmation Statement: 14 days after annual review period
  • Statutory accounts at CH: 9 months after ARD (or 21 months from incorporation if first)
  • CT600: 12 months after end of AP
  • CT payment: 9 months + 1 day after end of AP (non-large)
